Executive director | Deloitte Research Center for Energy & Industrials | Deloitte Services LP

Deloitte United States

Kate Hardin is the executive director for the Deloitte Research Center for Energy & Industrials. In tandem with Deloitte’s energy, resources, and industrials leadership, she drives energy research initiatives and manages the execution of the center’s strategy as well as its eminence and thought leadership.

Carolyn Amon

Research leader, Power, utilities & renewables

Deloitte United States

Carolyn Amon leads Power, Utilities & Renewables’ projects at the Deloitte Research Center for Energy and Industrials, where she focuses on decarbonization strategies. She has 20 years of experience delivering international advisory services and developing thought leadership across the Energy, Electric Vehicle, and Manufacturing sectors. She is passionate about empowering people to partake in the energy transition to a net-zero world.

Article

•

8-min read

•

21 September 2026

•

Deloitte Center for Energy & Industrials

For every new entrant under 25 years, there are more than five utility workers who are 45 years and older—more than double the economywide ratio.1 No other major growth industry is simultaneously expanding and preparing to replace most of its experienced workforce.2 Artificial intelligence–driven growth and workforce aging have converged as AI transforms the workforce and the work itself in an “AI-ging” moment. Utilities must now address aging, growth, and AI all at once. Success hinges on workforce redesign to enable effective human-machine collaboration across a new generation of talent and technologies. Utilities that act now may find that the retirement wave presents an opportunity to reinvent how work gets done.

30-second “AI-ging” readiness check

How many of these statements are true for your organization?

We know where and when retirements will create the greatest operational risk.

We have captured the knowledge that would leave with exiting employees.

We have quantified the workforce gap between retirements and growth.

We understand which work AI can help automate, augment, or leave to people.

We have a strategy to attract and develop new talent in an AI-enabled workplace.

Scoring guide:

5 checks: Your workforce strategy looks to be well positioned for the “AI-ging” transition.

3–4 checks: Capabilities are in place, but key vulnerabilities likely remain.

0–2 checks: Your workforce strategy may not keep pace with the combined pressures of growth, retirements, and AI.

Show more

Historic growth ahead

AI has sparked a momentous surge in the utilities industry, building on long-term structural growth from electrification. The sector is among the nation’s fastest-growing, as are many of its occupations.3 Related careers may require some of the fastest-changing skills.

Deloitte estimates that the announced expansion of utility-scale grid-connected generation could create the equivalent of more than 1.2 million additional jobs in the United States by 2035.4 These include temporary construction jobs measured in job-years5 and permanent operational jobs in labor-intensive nuclear, hydroelectric, and geothermal generation, in addition to the solar, wind, storage, and gas projects that account for the bulk of planned generation (figure 1). Many jobs involved in the AI economy buildout are in this power infrastructure, which Deloitte estimates could create more than 12 times as many jobs as planned data centers.6

Utilities are the fastest-growing major industry sector of the US economy.7 Moreover, in terms of employment growth, the top three fastest-growing industries are tied specifically to electric power, with electric equipment manufacturing in the top five, and other electric power generation in the top ten (figure 2).8

Within these industries are the nation’s second and fourth fastest-growing occupations—solar photovoltaic installers and wind turbine service technicians—which also have rapidly evolving skill requirements.9 Over the past three years, about three-quarters of the skills required for these occupations have changed.10 Energy and nuclear engineers also rank among the top 20 occupations experiencing the highest levels of skill change.11

The utilities sector is short of both workers and the skills it needs to grow.12 And the shortfall is deepening at a time of intensified competition for the same talent pool from other AI infrastructure builders and operators.13 Also standing in the way of utilities seizing the opportunities that the AI economy has opened is a looming retirement cliff.

Historically, long tenures have contributed to utilities’ outlier workforce. Median employee tenure peaked at 9.5 years in 2018, the highest for any industry across private and public sectors and more than double the national median.16

While tenure has since declined, the ratio of retiring workers to young entrants remains high due to low turnover among the experienced workforce. As retirements accelerate, that imbalance could become one of the industry’s defining workforce challenges.

A closing window for action

These aging trends leave utilities with a limited window to act. There are more than five utility workers age 45 and older for every new entrant under age 25, compared with the economywide ratio of less than 2:1.17 With half of their workers being over 45 years, utilities could lose much of their current talent and knowledge base to retirements within the next decade (figure 4).

Complicating workforce planning is the uneven timing and distribution of utility workforce aging. The largest age cohort in utilities has shifted five times over the past decade, compared with just once for the US workforce overall (figure 5).18 Utilities should anticipate not only how many workers are expected to exit but also the moving target of when and where transitions will occur.

The challenge is uneven geographically too. Utility workforce trends do not align with broader state aging trends.19 The largest age cohort may be over 45 years for a state, but under 45 years for utilities in the state, and vice versa. Yet, in nearly half of the US states, older age groups already dominate their utilities sector (figure 6).

In business-as-usual times, a large generation of older workers exiting the sector without younger workers entering could pose an operational challenge. Today, it indicates a workforce shortage as the industry grows. Rapid expansion in capital investment has further impacted traditional approaches to building the workforce needed to keep pace with AI infrastructure execution demands.

Utilities may need to leverage AI itself to multiply what each worker can do.

“AI-ging” the utilities workforce

As it drives industry growth, AI is also redefining workforce capabilities. An aging workforce managing an aging grid under legacy models is not likely to deliver growth at the pace needed. Utilities could leverage AI to help.

Securing a future-ready workforce likely goes beyond like-for-like replacement of retiring workers and headcount growth. For utilities, the path forward may include redesigned processes that can unlock true human-machine collaboration in managing knowledge and delivering value. As utility work is broken into tasks, effort can gradually shift from today’s aging workforce to a new generation of workers in redefined roles, supported by AI that becomes increasingly embedded in workflows as it matures across generative, agentic, and physical forms. Orchestration of AI-enabled people and processes toward outcomes will likely become a premium human skill, as will the ability to operate assets manually if needed.

AI is expected to impact most utility roles, albeit in different ways and on different timelines.20 Foundational data capabilities should be in place to help enable AI-assisted, -augmented, and -powered solutions. Resistance to adopting new processes that change decades-long practices can also be a challenge. But once these solutions are implemented alongside operating model changes, they can help counter workforce aging through “AI-ging”—the transformation of workforce roles and skills and the work itself as AI reshapes talent needs (figure 7).

While AI can help utilities maximize the capabilities of each worker, it will likely also be important to help address the underlying talent pipeline issues. Few organizations have succeeded in offsetting workforce aging and related outflows while attracting sufficient new talent to meet historic growth. But if utility firms can close the gap with AI-fluent workers, their odds of rising to the occasion might improve.

A gen AI to Z opportunity

Untapped opportunities exist to connect AI-fluent workers’ capabilities with the industry’s growing workforce needs. Demand for AI talent is accelerating: The share of utility job postings requiring AI skills rose by more than 44% between 2024 and 2025.21 Utility workers are adopting gen AI faster than the US workforce overall, yet they report saving less than half as much time as AI users economywide (figure 8).22 This suggests that realizing AI’s full value may first require improved processes and workforce readiness.

Younger workers may be well positioned to help meet these needs. Gen Z leads in AI adoption, ease of use, and productivity gains.23 Gen Z’s familiarity with AI could help accelerate effective adoption, while experienced workers could contribute domain expertise and operational judgment. Research suggests that Gen Z achieves its greatest productivity gains when advancing AI initiatives on generationally diverse teams.24

Intergenerational collaboration can be especially valuable for utilities. Workers who are new to the industry may benefit from greater guidance in an industry where AI implementation often proceeds with limited communication from leadership—the complexities of utilities’ regulated operating environment may help explain this “stealth adopter” behavior.25 This type of collaboration can also help bridge generational divides. Utilities have an opportunity to intentionally pair experienced workers’ institutional knowledge with AI fluency to strengthen knowledge transfer, accelerate effective AI adoption, and improve productivity. The result might be capabilities that no single generation could achieve alone.

The Gen Z talent equation

Winning Gen Z talent will be important for this opportunity. Backfilling retiring workers and accelerating the industry’s AI transformation may depend on attracting a generation that remains underrepresented in utilities.26 It will likely take more than posting open positions. With relatively low appeal among Gen Z,27 utilities should consider both the career opportunities they offer and how they communicate them to help compete for the next generation of talent.

Despite recruiting challenges, utilities possess strong early-career value propositions in the economy, particularly for the growing number of Gen Z workers choosing trades over a four-year degree.28 These core trade roles are where the retirement wave is arriving first and hiring demand is growing fastest.29 In plant operator and trade occupations, Gen Z entrants can advance quickly and earn more than peers in other occupations requiring a certificate or associate degree.30 Construction and technical trades are among the four certificate programs whose graduates earn more within five years of enrollment than comparable individuals who never enrolled, and they are also the two associate-degree fields with the largest earnings gains (figure 9).31

Competitive compensation is only part of the equation. To attract Gen Z, utilities should also align with the generation’s workplace expectations. Work/life balance ranks among the top workplace priorities for Gen Z, reflecting a broader emphasis on well-being.32 Meeting those expectations can be challenging in field operations, which offer less flexibility than the hybrid and remote arrangements that office roles may offer. Even where work from home is possible, it can constrain progression unless utilities provide mentorship and on-the-job learning.33

Purpose is even more important.34 Gen Z considers a sense of purpose crucial to both job satisfaction and well-being, with 80% of Gen Z adults surveyed seeking careers centered on making a positive impact, although fewer than half of Gen Z workers surveyed say they have found one.35 Here, utilities may be underselling one of their strengths. While the industry’s current growth story centers on powering AI, younger workers may connect more strongly with a broader mission such as the energy transition. Indeed, Gen Z’s engagement with renewable energy suggests that this mission may be resonant: According to the March 2026 Deloitte ConsumerSignals survey, 53% of US Gen Z respondents regularly power their home with renewables, compared to 17% for Gen X, boomers, and older generations combined.36

Finally, there are gaps between Gen Z expectations and experiences with their supervisors in the workplace. Fifty-three percent of US Gen Zs surveyed in the energy and industrials sector expect managers to coach employees, but only 33% experience such coaching.37 Meanwhile, 42% of US Gen Zs in the sector expect close supervision of day-to-day tasks, but 58% experience it.38

An industry’s age profile can shape workplace norms, technology adoption, and employee expectations, reinforcing itself over time. Workers of the same age tend to cluster, creating a workplace that reflects their preferences.39 Without stronger recruitment, utilities could risk becoming more digitally constrained just as AI capabilities become increasingly important. On the other hand, attracting and empowering more Gen Z workers could inject the digital fluency, evolving workplace expectations, and cultural momentum needed to transform utilities into truly AI-native organizations.

Pathways to close the talent gap

In utilities, an acute workforce aging trend has run up against explosive growth. To help manage both, utilities should look to redesign work with AI-enabled processes that augment knowledge transfer and skill development. Utility leaders can consider the following actions (figure 10).

Test transition timelines. Scenario plan around workforce turnover, demographic trends, and AI usage and exposure. This can help define the windows for action to maintain and manage knowledge by role. It can also lay the foundation for longer-term strategic workforce planning.

Capture, codify, and communicate knowledge. Identify critical and concentrated core role knowledge. Accelerate the capture of siloed knowledge. Consolidate and codify content to help it be consumable and usable across age cohorts, platforms, and worksites.

Gauge the gap to growth. Assess ways to fill the gap between retirement-driven workforce losses and AI-driven demand. Rethink the size, scope, and complexity of roles across the core, contingent, and contractor workforces. Segment categories of talent to recruit, onboard, train, and retrain for existing and new roles and skills. Compare these needs with local workforce and skill availability, especially as manufacturers increasingly compete for the same talent.

Draw out hidden and ladder skills. Recognize skills learned on the job that may not be documented. Quantify the operational continuity risk of these hidden skills sliding down the chute as talent retires. Identify ladder skills that workers could climb more quickly by leveraging AI.

Tailor training to top off and attract. Develop appealing, accessible, and calibrated training that tops off uncovered skills and employees’ existing skills. Implement new forms of delivery informed by real-time workforce analytics. Tie training more closely to industry purpose. Partner with educational and workforce development institutions, unions, manufacturers, and tech companies to create training centers and expand the locally available talent pool for shared core roles facing shortages.

In a broader national context of workforce aging and “AI-ging”—trends that could complement, complicate, or compound each other—utilities can act based on measured realities and the unknowns those measurements reveal. Utilities facing the paradox of aging fast while growing faster could integrate gen AI and Gen Z to help resolve it. The retirement wave could become an opportunity to reinvent the organization.

‘AI-ging’ in action: How Deloitte is helping clients get there

Deloitte is working with some of the larger players in the AI infrastructure buildout on “AI-ging” the workforce.

Example 1

The goal: Achieve enterprisewide AI transformation.

The problem: The business was looking to embed AI across all its functions and businesses to accelerate business processes; increase efficiencies from the back-office to front-office engineering, production, and construction delivery; and improve client delivery speed. It sought to position itself at the forefront of AI innovation and adoption to expand the business amid resource constraints and client demand for accelerated delivery.

The approach: A forward deployed engineering program was developed to build agents, fully integrate AI applications, and deploy AI across the core of the business. Forward deployed engineering embeds engineering, business leadership, risk, and adoption into a single delivery system focused on measurable outcomes.

Value delivered: The operating model, decision-making, leadership, talent, and ways of working are evolving in lockstep as AI reinvents the business.

Example 2

The goal: Deliver a road map for an AI work-design program with measurable outcomes across revenue growth, operating margin, asset efficiency, and cost management.

The problem: Return on investment did not materialize at the pace warranted by AI spend. The business was deploying AI capabilities into roles, structures, and behaviors that had not been redesigned to absorb them.

The approach: A structured analysis of the company’s largest workforce concentrations was conducted, including a task-level decomposition across functions. Each process was scored across six work-type dimensions and mapped to the three-tier model: AI-powered, AI-augmented, and AI-assisted. The analysis produced heatmaps pinpointing where AI impact would land first within each process and what work design changes could help capture that value.

Value delivered: AI value was captured across the finance, information technology, human resources, and supply chain functions.

Example 3

The goal: Stand up a scalable, agent-first operating model for customer care that enables AI agents, automation operations, and targeted human oversight to work together to drive reliable outcomes and continuous performance improvement as agentic capabilities mature.

The problem: As customer expectations continued to rise, the client’s current operating model had not kept pace with the expanding role of automation. Risk and complexity were growing as a result of inconsistent ways of working across functions, unclear accountability between AI agents and people, and a staffing model that was struggling to flex as capabilities matured.

The approach: A scalable global customer care model was built to help strengthen human and AI roles, improve visibility and consistency, and ultimately shift capacity from repetitive tasks to higher-value, customer-focused work.

Value delivered: This approach led to a reshaped organization where roles shifted from transactional processing toward higher-value oversight and judgment, freeing people to focus on protecting recurring revenue and supporting growth alongside the sales organization.

An ‘AI-ging’ READY assessment

How prepared is your organization for the “AI-ging” era? Are you confident in your organization’s ability to navigate the convergence of historic industry growth, workforce aging, and AI adoption?

Rate your organization on each of the five dimensions of the “AI-ging” READY workforce maturity model (figure 11). The model assesses five capabilities across a maturity curve ranging from reactive workforce management to a continuously regenerating human-machine workforce. Select the description that most closely reflects your current state. Your overall readiness is determined by your lowest-scoring areas, not your highest.

D: Demand planning

Level 4: Scaling

Y: Young talent pipeline

Attract, develop, and retain the next generation of digitally fluent utility workers.

Level 1: Exploring

Level 2: Experimenting

Retention remains inconsistent.

Level 3: Establishing

AI-enabled learning accelerates onboarding.

Cross-generational mentoring is common.

Level 4: Scaling

Engaging—the workplace is designed for emerging talent

Work, learning, flexibility, and purpose are intentionally defined for emerging talent.

AI fluency is treated as a strategic capability.

Regenerating—the utility has created a talent flywheel

AI, experienced workers, and young talent accelerate each other’s productivity.

The organization has become a destination employer for digitally native energy talent.

The organization has broken down roles to skill levels and stitched them back together. It more effectively leverages skill sets to plug gaps while creating solid recruitment pathways for new skills needed as a result of AI enablement.

Identify your lowest maturity level. That is likely your organization’s biggest constraint. In the “AI-ging” era, utilities are unlikely to fail because they lack technology. They often struggle when retirement risk, workforce planning, AI adoption, and talent strategy mature at different speeds. Competitive advantage can come from advancing all five together.

text:
Written by Martin Lynch, European News Editor for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas)

Summary

Google has committed to taking half of the electricity produced by Finland's Loviisa nuclear power plant for the next two decades as part of a major data center push in the country.

Major Investment in Data Centers

Google plans to invest €13 billion (US$15 billion) in building data centers in Finland and has agreed a 20-year power offtake deal that secures the future for the country's oldest nuclear power plant. The investment will happen over 2027-2028 across four municipalities: Hamina (expanding the existing campus), plus three new sites in Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala. It is the company's largest data center investment in Europe and one of the largest ever in the Finnish economy. During the initial construction phase in 2027 and 2028, it is claimed that more than 37,000 jobs nationwide will be supported and will contribute €3.6 billion (US$4.1 billion) annually to Finland's GDP. According to Industrial Info Resources data, there are 121 data center projects in Finland worth almost US$69 billion in investment.

The Company Take

"Since we converted a former paper mill in Hamina into a data center 15 years ago, Finland has been a vital hub for Google," said Bikash Koley, vice president for Google Global Infrastructure. "Today, we're deepening that commitment with a €13 billion investment in digital infrastructure, clean energy projects and economic partnerships across Finland over the next two years, to help meet growing demand for Google's core services - such as Search, Maps, and Gemini. Today's announcement, our largest single investment in Europe, will provide a significant boost to the Finnish economy." Industrial Info is tracking four active Google projects at Hamina worth US$780 million in investment.

Prime Minister's Welcome

Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said: "This is a very important day for Finland. Google's historically large investment in Muhos, Vaala, Kajaani and Hamina is a strong vote of confidence in Finland. Decisions on investments of this scale are not made by chance. Countries with stable operating environments, a skilled labour force and reliable infrastructure are the ones that succeed in international competition. In an increasingly digitalised world, data centres are vital infrastructure. They provide the foundation for artificial intelligence, cloud services, industrial digitalisation, research, and the digital services that people and businesses use every day. For this reason, international competition for data centre investments is hard. Finland has done well in this competition."

The Nuclear Connection

The company has committed to taking half of the electricity produced by Finland's Loviisa nuclear power plant in a deal that will secure the expected €1 billion (US$15 billion) of investment that owner Fortum said it will need to keep the plant running. The 20-year power purchase agreement (PPA) provides "economic certainty for the lifetime extension and power upgrade of the plant through 2050 by contracting for up to 50% of Loviisa nuclear power plant's capacity." Loviisa is one of two nuclear power plants in Finland, along with the larger Olkiluoto facility, which supply 37% of the country's power. "Without the lifetime extension investment program, the Loviisa plant -- which currently employs approximately 580 people and provides 10% of Finland's electricity -- could not continue operations beyond 2030, " Fortum admitted. "Keeping this fossil-free energy asset online for decades to come will help stabilize electricity prices and support long-term resilience of Finland's grid."

Fortum's President and Chief Executive Officer Markus Rauramo said: "Finland has a unique opportunity to turn its decarbonised, reliable electricity system and robust industrial infrastructure into a foundation for the next wave of sustainable industrial growth. Long-term partnerships like the one between Fortum and Google are essential to making that happen, especially in today's uncertain market environment characterized by low visibility and highly volatile electricity prices. "Our collaboration with Google provides a strong foundation for the continued development and reliable operation of our Loviisa power plant for decades to come."

Key Takeaways

Google is investing €13 billion (US$15 billion) to build data centers in Finland.

It includes a 20-year power offtake deal for half the power at the Loviisa nuclear power plant.

Industrial Info Resources is tracking 121 data center projects in Finland worth almost US$69 billion in investment.

title: Opportunities: why fusion energy needs architects
description:
Architects as strategic leaders for fusion Architects have always worked at the intersection of complexity.
A fusion power plant is not just another piece of energy infrastructure.
That continuity of thinking, from Culham to West Burton, is already shaping our approach to the UK’s first prototype fusion power plant.
Fusion is becoming a global movement The UK is part of a worldwide race to commercialise fusion energy, supporting STEP as a “world-first” prototype fusion plant.
Jason Boyle is chief architect for STEP, the UK's prototype fusion power plant programme
text:
Commercial fusion energy is often described as the next chapter in clean power. It is something far wider than that.

If it succeeds, fusion will not simply generate electricity. It will create an entirely new industrial sector, complete with new technologies, supply chains, institutions and places. Like the railways or the digital revolution before it, fusion has the potential to reshape economies and redefine how nations innovate.

The UK government has made fusion an important part of its industrial strategy, committing £2.5 billion commitment to its development until 2030, including facilities to develop fusion fuel technology, and a £200 million Construction Partner contract to ILIOS to build a fusion energy plant in West Burton, Nottinghamshire, to be completed in the 2040s.

That is why the conversation about fusion must extend beyond plasma physics and engineering, and into design, leadership and place. The challenge is not simply to build a power station, but to create the physical and organisational framework for an industry that does not yet exist. That is where architects have an essential role.

For decades, architecture has followed engineering; invited in once the technical decisions are made, to organise the spaces and soften the public image of complex infrastructure. Too often, we have accepted that role ourselves.

Fusion offers a chance to change the narrative. For perhaps the first time in nuclear infrastructure's history, architects have the opportunity to help define the vision before the first concrete is poured. We are not inheriting an established building type; we are helping create an entirely new architectural typology, and with it, the places that will support one of the defining industries of the century. This is not about aesthetics; it is about leadership.

What is fusion?

It is the coming together of two readily available atoms of hydrogen in a plasma state at 1500 million degrees Celsius, within magnetic confines of a doughnut-shaped machine called a tokomak, to release huge amounts of low carbon power which can be converted to electricity.

Architects as strategic leaders for fusion

Architects have always worked at the intersection of complexity. Our training does not make us specialists in a single discipline; it teaches us to synthesise competing priorities into coherent solutions, reconciling engineering with human experience and technical constraint with long-term adaptability.

That ability has never been more relevant. Fusion is frequently described as one of the greatest engineering challenges of our age, and it is, but it may be an even greater design challenge, demanding the integration of advanced science, engineering, digital technology, manufacturing, regulation and public engagement, none of which exists in isolation.

Success depends on bringing them together into a coherent whole, and that is precisely what architecture does: not design buildings, but organise complexity, creating order where multiple systems intersect and giving long-term direction to projects that evolve over decades.

Lessons from history and the global fusion community

Every great technological revolution has required architects to imagine new forms of place. The railways gave Victorian Britain stations that became civic landmarks, electrification changed how cities functioned, and the digital revolution produced typologies of its own, from data centres to innovation districts.

Fusion belongs in that lineage. A fusion power plant is not just another piece of energy infrastructure. It is the beginning of an industrial ecosystem that will extend far beyond the reactor itself, drawing in advanced manufacturing, robotics and entirely new communities of expertise. The places we design today will shape how that ecosystem develops for generations.

The UK is not pursuing fusion alone. ITER in southern France shows that fusion has already evolved beyond scientific experiment into a long-term international enterprise, requiring sophisticated campus planning and environments capable of supporting thousands of researchers over decades. Meanwhile, the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory and the Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics show the same principle at a different scale. Research quality depends not only on scientific excellence but also on carefully planned environments that support long-term collaboration, international partnerships, specialist manufacturing and knowledge exchange. The physical setting plays an important role in attracting talent and enabling innovation over decades.

Closer to home, AL_A's design for General Fusion’s demonstration plant at the UK Atomic Energy Authority’s Culham Campus has challenged assumptions about how nuclear infrastructure should present itself. Working with Arup, Amanda Levete's practice wrapped a 38m-high fusion hall in translucent fabric, designed to project confidence in the technology rather than conceal it.

AL_A now sits alongside our team within the ILIOS consortium developing STEP. That continuity of thinking, from Culham to West Burton, is already shaping our approach to the UK’s first prototype fusion power plant.

Design intent established from the start

When UK Fusion Energy established its design authority, it made a significant decision: it appointed an architect, me, at the outset of the programme, not at the end of the design process.

My first responsibility was not to produce drawings but to develop the UKFE design guide, establishing principles that would influence decisions from masterplanning to workplace environments and long-term design governance. Rather than following procurement, we first established design intent. That is not a procedural adjustment; it is a cultural one, and the decision I am proudest to have been part of.

Large infrastructure programmes involve multiple organisations, changing technologies, and delivery spanning many years. Without a consistent design vision, they risk becoming fragmented, driven by individual packages rather than a coherent whole. Architecture provides that continuity. The architect's role is not to dictate every technical decision, but to ensure thousands of individual decisions continue to serve a common purpose.

That kind of stewardship has largely vanished from our towns and cities, where fragmented decision-making has produced fragmented places we all now live with. Fusion offers a rare chance to prove its value again, at national scale. This is not architectural authorship in the traditional sense; it is architectural governance.

Leadership through collaboration with engineers

None of this diminishes engineers’ extraordinary contribution. Fusion remains one of the most ambitious engineering programmes ever attempted, and without exceptional engineering there is no fusion industry. But engineering alone cannot determine how a new industrial sector should inhabit the landscape or inspire public confidence.

The strongest programmes are never driven by a single profession. They emerge from genuine collaboration, where architects, engineers, scientists and manufacturers each contribute different expertise towards a common ambition, and the relationship between them is never hierarchical. Engineers bring precision; architects bring spatial intelligence. Neither replaces the other, and together they produce outcomes that neither could achieve alone.

Designing a new global typology

Fusion does not inherit an established architectural language. Unlike airports, hospitals or even conventional nuclear power stations, there is no accepted image of what a commercial fusion facility should be, or how these campuses should relate to the communities around them. We are not refining an existing typology. We are creating one.

That responsibility should not be underestimated. The decisions made by this first generation of architects will set the precedent for decades: how governments procure future programmes, how investors perceive the industry, and how communities come to understand fusion itself. Architecture is rarely given the chance to define an entirely new building type. Fusion presents exactly that chance.

For much of the 20th century, critical infrastructure was designed to perform a single function, judged on efficiency alone. The most successful infrastructure of this century is expected to do more, attracting world-class talent and earning public confidence while performing technically.

Fusion is no exception. The prototype plants being designed today will become magnets for researchers, manufacturers and universities, drawing in advanced manufacturing and training academies rather than standing as isolated industrial compounds. That changes the architect's task fundamentally, from arranging buildings efficiently across a site to creating environments capable of supporting collaboration and long-term economic growth.

Designing a fusion facilities as civic infrastructure

If fusion is to become a successful industry, the next challenge is not only technical but civic. Public trust will determine whether fusion is understood as a national opportunity or delivered to communities rather than with them, and that confidence is built through transparency and legibility as much as technical data.

This is where architecture becomes critical. A facility that appears impenetrable and defensive reinforces the idea that advanced energy belongs behind fences. A facility that is understandable and, where appropriate, publicly accessible sends a different message: that fusion is part of a shared national future. In an industry that depends on long-term public support, this is not a secondary concern. It is a strategic asset.

The same principle applies digitally. Fusion will be designed, coordinated and operated through increasingly sophisticated digital environments in which building information modelling is only the starting point; the future lies in connected ecosystems integrating design, manufacturing, construction and operations into a continuous flow of information. Digital twins will let designers test scenarios before construction begins, and AI will optimise layouts, flag clashes and automate tasks that currently consume enormous amounts of professional time.

Some see this as a threat to design authorship. I see it as a shift in where human value is created. When machines can produce thousands of technically plausible arrangements, the defining question becomes: which one best serves society? AI can optimise a building. It cannot decide what kind of future a nation should build. That requires judgement: the ability to balance safety with openness, efficiency with dignity, and industrial performance with human experience. These are fundamentally architectural questions.

Fusion is becoming a global movement

The UK is part of a worldwide race to commercialise fusion energy, supporting STEP as a “world-first” prototype fusion plant. The industry is moving faster than most people outside it realise. What was once the domain of a handful of national laboratories is now a global ecosystem of governments, institutions and private companies investing billions.

France: ITER the world's largest fusion experiment

UK: STEP UK Fusion Energy’s prototype fusion power plant at West Burton

Japan: JT-60SA the world's largest operational tokamak [check]

Germany: Wendelstein 7-X the world's leading stellarator experiment looking at how to building a magnetic field using external magnets

China: EAST China's “Artificial Sun”, named for being an Experimental Advanced Superconducting Tokomak, chasing record plasma durations

United States: SPARC (United States) CFS's compact tokamak and National Ignition Facility achieved fusion ignition via inertial confinement and powerful laser beams

South Korea: KSTAR superconducting tokamak for long-duration plasma

Taken together, these programmes show something remarkable: fusion is no longer a distant scientific aspiration, but a global industrial race already under way, and the nations that win it will define the technologies, skills and places that shape one of the most important industries of the century.

A nation-building project

Fusion is not ultimately a power-station project. It is a nation-building one. If commercial fusion succeeds, it will require new factories, new materials, new transport infrastructure and new skills academies, influencing where people work and how industrial capability is distributed across the country.

For too long, many of our most consequential industrial programmes have had architecture added late, if at all, the profession left to handle finishes while others set the strategy. Fusion offers a rare chance to reverse that. The spatial language, public interface and civic identity of this industry are still open questions, and decisions made in the next decade may shape its physical character for the next century.

Architects should not wait to be invited into that discussion. We should be proposing new models of industrial campuses, shaping digital delivery standards, and working with engineers, manufacturers and communities from the very beginning. Design quality is not a luxury added after the real work is done. It is part of the real work.

The industrial transformations that are remembered in history are not only those that generated power. They are the ones that generated confidence, capability and a sense of collective progress. Fusion gives us the chance to help build all three.

Jason Boyle is chief architect for STEP, the UK's prototype fusion power plant programme

LG Energy Solution has completed the establishment of its energy storage system (ESS) production network in North America, accelerating its push to capture growing demand in the rapidly expanding ESS market.

Following the opening ceremony for LG Energy Solution Michigan-Lansing on Aug. 18, the plant is now ramping up operations.

The Lansing plant serves as a combined manufacturing hub for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries for ESS applications and nickel cobalt manganese batteries for electric vehicles (EVs), with an annual battery cell production capacity of more than 35 gigawatt-hours.

The plant began producing pouch-type LFP batteries for ESS applications this year and plans to begin mass production of prismatic LFP batteries next year, marking LG Energy Solution's first prismatic battery production in North America. The company has also secured orders to supply EV batteries to Toyota.

LG Energy Solution Michigan operates two production sites in the state, in Holland and Lansing. LG Energy Solution Michigan President Choi Dae-sik said that operating two plants in different locations is not easy but “there is significant synergy because we can quickly transfer the experience accumulated at the existing plant to the new one.”

He said the company is transferring its production and quality management experience and operational know-how from Holland to Lansing to accelerate the stabilization of the new plant and minimize trial and error. The company plans to connect the workforce, organizations and production experience of the two plants to operate them as a single production system.

With the Lansing plant going into operation, LG Energy Solution now has five ESS manufacturing sites in North America: two in Michigan, NextStar Energy’s plant in Ontario, Canada, and two joint venture plants — L-H Battery Company’s plant in Ohio and Ultium Cells’ plant in Tennessee.

By the end of this year, LG Energy Solution plans to expand its ESS production capacity in North America to 50 gigawatt-hours, accounting for 80 percent of its global ESS production capacity. Based on the improved capacity, the company said it will meet rapidly growing demand in the region.

LG Energy Solution’s ESS order backlog reached 140 gigawatt-hours as of the end of last year, while it secured more than 3 trillion won ($2.17 billion) in new ESS orders in the first half of this year.

LG Energy Solution has signed a series of supply deals with customers including Tesla, Terra-Gen, Excelsior Energy Capital, EG4 Electronics and Hanwha Qcells.

In May, LG Energy Solution signed a 6 gigawatt-hour ESS battery supply deal with DTE Energy, which is involved in Oracle’s artificial intelligence data center project. In July, it agreed to supply up to 2.9 gigawatt-hours of ESS batteries for a Google project with renewable energy independent power producer Cypress Creek Energy.

“The operation at Lansing plant is an important milestone that will accelerate LG Energy Solution’s growth in North America,” LG Energy Solution CEO Kim Dong-myung said. “We will strengthen the U.S. battery ecosystem and expand our local production capabilities by building an advanced battery manufacturing network that supports the future of the U.S. mobility industry and energy infrastructure.” (Advertorial)

text:
Carbon fiber is a key component in automobile manufacturing, aerospace engineering and energy infrastructure, but it mostly relies on petroleum-derived products, which can be expensive and contribute to carbon emissions. But what if carbon fiber was made of a free waste material and was as strong as - or even stronger than - the petrochemical-based products? Engineers at Washington University in St. Louis are unveiling that prospect in research recently published in the journal Matter.

“For the first time, this allows us to create renewable carbon fiber that reaches the high standard of quality used in automobile manufacturing,” said Joshua Yuan, the Lucy & Stanley Lopata Professor and chair of energy, environmental and chemical engineering at WashU McKelvey Engineering. Yuan is also the director of the National Science Foundation (NSF) Carbon Utilization Redesign for Biomanufacturing (CURB) Engineering Research Center at WashU.

Key to the work is making use of a waste material called lignin, the second-most abundant natural biopolymer on earth. Lignin is produced as a byproduct of the paper pulping and biorefining industries, and ordinary disposal methods for lignin result in a substantial environmental footprint.

WashU engineers wanted to see if they could use lignin to improve production methods for carbon fiber. This human-made material is traditionally manufactured using synthetic polyacrylonitrile (PAN), a petroleum-derived product that is mixed with chemicals, spun through tiny jets into fibers, washed and stretched. This type of production process for carbon fiber is called "wet spinning." However, PAN is not cheap, accounting for up to 50% of the total manufacturing cost of carbon fibers, which limits its use to high-end products, Yuan noted.

By adding affordable and abundant lignin to the process, the WashU team found that they could cut the use of PAN by half, reduce production costs by 25% and cut carbon emissions substantially. But the new carbon-fiber product they created still needed to meet automobile industry standards for tensile strength and elastic modulus.

So the researchers also developed another new process that greatly improves performance. That process involves deploying single-walled carbon nanotubes into the polymer matrix, acting almost like rebar in lining up the crystallization chemistry. This innovation revealed a new design principle for carbon material development.

“Crystallization alignment is critical for carbon fiber quality,” Yuan said.

The carbon nanotubes allowed the researchers to make a precursor solution of the lignin and PAN. That solution was then extruded as fiber for the wet spinning process of production, then further heat-treated to strengthen the product.

Weiwei Li, a postdoctoral scholar in Yuan's lab and first author of the research, described their research as an innovation in three steps.

The first step was to create that nanotube template that can mix well with lignin and PAN and allows for high crystallization or orientation, Li said. Step two involves running that precursor solution through a wet spinning and tension-assisted heat treatment. Finally, one round of optimized carbonization fully strengthens the fiber. The three steps together maximized the crystallite content, while the carbon nanotubes guide the crystallite orientation to create rebar effects for outstanding mechanical properties.

“All these together allow us to create lignin-based renewable carbon fiber that has highly aligned crystalline structure,” Yuan said.

The automobile industry is just the entry point for markets of optimized carbon fiber; it's used in many industries, from sports equipment to wind turbines.

“Carbon fiber reinforces plastics and has very broad application,” Yuan said.

text:
Staff Reporter

PRESIDENT Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah has called for a clean energy transition that is measured not only in megawatts and emissions, but in jobs, skills and industrial value created for developing countries.

Speaking in New York on Saturday on the occasion of the United Nations Private Sector Forum hosted by the UN Global Compact under the theme “Advancing a Clean, Just and Secure Energy Future”, the President said energy policy has become inseparable from economic security, climate resilience and human development.

“We meet at a moment when energy policy has become inseparable from economic security, climate resilience and human development. The question before us is no longer whether the global energy system must change, but how we can accelerate that change at the scale and pace required,” Nandi-Ndaitwah said.

Photos: Namibian Presidency

She said for Namibia, the energy debate is not abstract, as reliable and affordable energy determines whether a rural clinic can preserve medicines, whether a small enterprise can expand, and whether a young person can find decent work at home.

“A clean energy transition must therefore be measured not only in megawatts installed or emissions avoided, but in jobs created, communities connected, skills transferred and industries established,” she said.

Nandi-Ndaitwah said Namibia supports the objectives of the Paris Agreement and limiting global temperature increase to 1.5 degrees Celsius, but stressed that the transition must recognise different national circumstances and safeguard the right of developing countries to industrialise, eradicate poverty and secure universal energy access.

“A transition that leaves communities without power, workers without viable alternatives or countries trapped at the bottom of global value chains will neither be durable nor fair,” she warned.

She said Namibia’s approach is anchored in a diversified energy system, expanded domestic generation and stronger regional integration.

At continental level, she said Africa’s energy transition must be an industrialisation strategy that uses clean energy not only to export electricity or unprocessed minerals, but to manufacture, beneficiate, strengthen food systems, modernise transport and create a skilled workforce.

Nandi-Ndaitwah said governments must provide direction, predictability and enabling infrastructure, while business must bring investment, innovation and responsible execution. She called on the UN, development finance institutions and international partners to help align standards, mobilise finance and strengthen cooperation.

“Together, we can build an energy future that is cleaner and more secure; an industrial future that creates value where resources are found; and a transition that is genuinely inclusive and leaves no country, community or worker behind,” she said, adding that young people and women must play a central role.

She invited business leaders to join Namibia in the journey towards a cleaner, healthier and more prosperous world.

The event was attended by UN Secretary-General António Guterres, UN Global Compact CEO Sanda Ojiambo, Heads of State and Government, and private sector leaders.

text:
Market snapshot: Tube Investments of India's electric vehicle subsidiary, Montra Electric, has mapped out an aggressive roadmap to achieve a revenue of $1 billion (approximately ₹9,600 crore) by the year 2030. Under this plan, nearly 70% of the targeted top-line expansion will be driven by electric trucks. This marks a significant strategic pivot toward the commercial heavy and light vehicle segments as the primary engines of long-term growth.

Data Snapshot

Montra Electric is targeting a top-line milestone of ₹9,600 crore by 2030.

Electric trucks are projected to contribute nearly 70% of the target 2030 revenue.

Montra Electric recorded ₹740 crore in consolidated revenue for the previous financial year.

What's Changed

Targeting a ≈13x revenue multiplier to reach ₹9,600 crore by 2030, compared to the recorded revenue of ₹740 crore in the preceding fiscal year (derived: ₹9,600 cr vs ₹740 cr).

Shift in product-mix focus with heavy electric trucks emerging as the primary revenue contributor at 50% of total targets, while three-wheelers shift to a 20% share.

Key Takeaways

Electric trucks will anchor the company's long-term commercial vehicle architecture, projected to bring in nearly ₹6,720 crore of the 2030 revenue target.

Heavy commercial vehicles will generate half of the target revenue, with small commercial vehicles contributing 23-25%.

The brand currently has approximately 21,000 active vehicles on the road across various segments.

Strategic emphasis is moving toward high-capacity battery solutions (350 to 400 kilowatts) to mitigate range limitations on short, predictable shipping routes.

SAHI Perspective

Montra Electric's 2030 roadmap points to a bold move away from lightweight passenger vehicles into capital-intensive electric trucking. Although electric truck penetration in India currently sits below 1% due to massive long-haul infrastructure deficits, the company is targeting predictable, closed-loop freight networks where battery capacity limits are manageable. Backed by its parent Tube Investments of India, which has injected and raised ₹3,000 crore for clean mobility operations, Montra possesses the financial leverage to build local manufacturing scale and battery systems.

Market Implications

Montra's expansion into electric commercial trucks intensifies competition in a high-tonnage vehicle market historically dominated by legacy players. Its focus on localization—exemplified by its 1.7 GWh battery assembly plant in Manesar—helps insulate the company from component supply shocks and enables better unit pricing, accelerating industrial transition timelines.

Trading Signals

Market Bias: Bullish

Tube Investments is well-positioned to benefit from its clean mobility arm's scale-up, backed by a clear ₹9,600 crore 2030 revenue target and high-value fleet partnerships such as the deployment of 57 heavy trucks with TVS Vehicle Mobility Solutions.

Overweight: Electric Vehicles, Auto Components, Commercial Vehicles

Underweight: Traditional ICE Components

Trigger Factors:

Sustained deployment of the Rhino series of heavy electric trucks across industrial routes.

Margin improvement driven by localized battery manufacturing at the Manesar facility.

Favorable policy clarity regarding PM E-Drive scheme scrapping linkages.

Time Horizon: Medium-term (3-12 months)

Industry Context

India's heavy commercial vehicle market is in the early stages of electrification. Because long-haul charging corridors remain limited, early adopters are relying on closed-loop logistics operations. Montra is targeting this specific segment, deploying fixed-battery and battery-swapping configurations to address range constraints and capture commercial fleet demand before highway charging networks fully mature.

Key Risks to Watch

Extremely low domestic market penetration (below 1%) of electric heavy commercial vehicles.

Lack of high-voltage charging networks along primary national transport highways.

Regulatory friction from PM E-Drive, which links purchasing subsidies to the voluntary scrapping of older diesel fleets.

Recent Developments

In August 2026, Montra Electric collaborated with TVS Vehicle Mobility Solutions (TVS VMS) to deploy 57 of its Rhino 5538 heavy electric commercial trucks into active freight services in Chhattisgarh. Concurrently, Montra expanded its operations internationally, entering new electric vehicle markets in Nepal, Tanzania, and West Africa.

Closing Insight

Montra's strategic direction highlights a structured transition from component fabrication to end-to-end commercial EV supply. Success in reaching its ₹9,600 crore revenue target will rest heavily on successfully scaling its localized battery operations and resolving range constraints through dedicated fleet partnerships.

title: N.C. regulators reject Duke Energy $584M turbine request - Business North Carolina
description:
Commissioners Bill Brawley, Tommy Tucker and Donald van der Vaart say the $584 million project is premature, given what they see as unreliable estimates of future power demand.
In a 3-1 decision, they opposed acting on the application before ruling on Duke’s updated Carolinas Resource Plan, the utility’s master plan for power-plant construction.
Van der Vaart said in a separate comment that the commission is under no obligation to green-light the projects in an approved resource plan.
Asserting that the turbine project was the only one Duke could bring on quickly “does not by itself substitute for” the work SB 266 requires, van der Vaart says.
Friday’s decision came out as Duke was asking customers in the Carolinas to “voluntarily reduce electricity usage” from the afternoon into the early evening.
text:
Commissioners Bill Brawley, Tommy Tucker and Donald van der Vaart say the $584 million project is premature, given what they see as unreliable estimates of future power demand. It’s certain that the project will put costs on the back of Duke’s ratepayers and pose “a significant risk that new generation is approved before the need for” it is clear, they said.

In a 3-1 decision, they opposed acting on the application before ruling on Duke’s updated Carolinas Resource Plan, the utility’s master plan for power-plant construction.

Van der Vaart said in a separate comment that the commission is under no obligation to green-light the projects in an approved resource plan.

Permit requests, he says, “must stand on [their] own evidentiary record” and the existence of the Carolinas Resource Plan “should not transform a subsequent [permit review] into a ministerial act.”

He also says 2025’s Senate Bill 266 requires Duke to show the Utilities Commission it has thought about whether it could blunt the need for new power plants through grid upgrades, conservation or power “storage.” The latter takes in battery storage and hydro systems like Duke’s Bad Creek plant in South Carolina.

Asserting that the turbine project was the only one Duke could bring on quickly “does not by itself substitute for” the work SB 266 requires, van der Vaart says.

The Sherwood Smith plant is next to the $10 billion data center Amazon plans in Richmond County.

Duke officials said they are “disappointed” by the ruling and are “assessing potential next steps.” Their studies showed the turbine was “part of a least-cost path to maintain reliable and affordable service for customers as energy demand continues to grow across North Carolina.”

The decision doesn’t tie the new turbine specifically to that project, but says that much of Duke’s power-demand projections are tied to data-center growth. Turbines such as the five at Sherwood Smith are generally peak-load units, not for around-the-clock use.

Friday’s decision came out as Duke was asking customers in the Carolinas to “voluntarily reduce electricity usage” from the afternoon into the early evening. “Above-average heat,” it said, was putting pressure on the grid.

Commissioner Floyd McKissick dissented from the decision, saying the added turbine would “provide critical firm capacity during extreme weather events” and other times “of elevated demand.”

“There is no Plan B,” he said, adding that there had been no opposition to the application.

Will Scott, a leader of the North Carolina branch of the Environmental Defense Fund, praised the ruling. Duke’s gas-plant build-out “is too rapid and too expensive,” and that short-term needs “should not saddle customers with what are, over the long-term, likely to be inefficient, stranded assets.”

Brawley, Tucker and van der Vaart are Republicans, while McKissick is a Democrat.

name: Texas Environment
title: Public meeting set on formosa plastics wastewater permit | Local News - Crossroads Today
description:
The meeting comes as the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality considers Formosa’s application to renew the wastewater permit for its Point Comfort facility.
They are now questioning why the agency has taken a different position on Formosa’s permit.
San Antonio Bay Estuarine Waterkeeper and Environment Texas requested the October public meeting, giving residents an opportunity to raise concerns and provide comments on the proposed permit.
The public meeting begins at 7 p.m. Oct. 19 at the Bauer Community Center, 2300 State Highway 35 North in Port Lavaca.
The meeting will include an informal question-and-answer session with representatives from TCEQ and Formosa, followed by a formal public comment period.
text:
The meeting comes as the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality considers Formosa’s application to renew the wastewater permit for its Point Comfort facility.

Formosa proposed including a zero-discharge limit for plastic pellets, powders and flakes in the permit, consistent with requirements established under a federal court settlement. TCEQ instead proposed permit language that environmental groups say could allow an unspecified amount of plastic material to be discharged into Matagorda Bay.

Texas Surface Water Quality Standards require the state’s surface waters to be “essentially free” of floating debris and suspended solids that could harm aquatic life or interfere with the use and enjoyment of waterways.

Environmental groups say TCEQ previously indicated that the standard provided sufficient justification for zero-discharge requirements for plastics in individual wastewater permits. They are now questioning why the agency has taken a different position on Formosa’s permit.

“You know something’s backwards when the company is asking for a tougher pollution standard and the environmental agency won’t give it to them,” Environment Texas Executive Director Luke Metzger said. “TCEQ needs to explain its about-face and put a clear, enforceable zero-plastic-discharge limit in Formosa’s permit.”

In 2019, Formosa agreed to a $50 million settlement resolving a federal Clean Water Act lawsuit filed by San Antonio Bay Estuarine Waterkeeper and Diane Wilson. The lawsuit involved plastic pellets and other materials discharged from the Point Comfort complex into Cox Creek and Lavaca Bay. The settlement requires Formosa to stop discharging plastic pellets, powders and flakes and provides funding for environmental restoration and community projects.

San Antonio Bay Estuarine Waterkeeper and Environment Texas requested the October public meeting, giving residents an opportunity to raise concerns and provide comments on the proposed permit.

“Now is the time to show up, speak up and send a clear message to TCEQ to stop industrial plastic discharges into our bays and waterways,” San Antonio Bay Estuarine Waterkeeper Executive Director Diane Wilson said.

Wilson said the organization has documented plastic associated with Formosa’s wastewater discharges on 1,016 occasions since 2021.

The public meeting begins at 7 p.m. Oct. 19 at the Bauer Community Center, 2300 State Highway 35 North in Port Lavaca.

The meeting will include an informal question-and-answer session with representatives from TCEQ and Formosa, followed by a formal public comment period. Comments made during the formal portion will become part of TCEQ’s official record.

No final decision on the permit will be made at the meeting. The public comment period will close when the meeting concludes.

The permit application is available at the Port Lavaca Public Library, 200 W. Mahan St. TCEQ’s technical documents are also available online.

text:
LG Energy Solution has established five energy storage system (ESS) production sites across North America, accelerating its efforts to expand its presence in the rapidly growing ESS market. In August, the company held a grand opening ceremony for its new Lansing facility in Michigan with operations officially underway.

The start of production at the Lansing plant marks the completion of LG Energy Solution’s five-site ESS manufacturing network in North America. In response to the EV market slowdown and evolving clean energy policies, the company has strategically rebalanced its global production footprint by converting portions of EV battery production lines to ESS manufacturing. Through these efforts, LG Energy Solution has built one of the battery industry's most diversified manufacturing networks, positioning itself to meet rapidly increasing ESS demand across North America, driven by the expansion of data centers and renewable energy infrastructure.

The Lansing facility serves as a manufacturing hub capable of producing both LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries for ESS applications and NCM (nickel cobalt manganese) batteries for electric vehicles. The plant is expected to achieve an annual battery cell production capacity exceeding 35GWh. Production of ESS pouch cells began this year, while mass production of prismatic LFP batteries is scheduled to start next year. In its EV business, the company has also secured supply for Toyota.

With Lansing now operational, LG Energy Solution now operates five ESS production sites in North America, including three wholly owned facilities in Lansing and Holland, Michigan, and NextStar Energy in Ontario, Canada, as well as two joint venture plants: L-H Battery Company in Ohio and Ultium Cells in Tennessee. All five facilities operate as dual-purpose manufacturing hubs producing both ESS and EV batteries, providing the manufacturing flexibility needed to respond quickly to changing market demand.

This extensive manufacturing footprint is the result of a strategic rebalancing initiative that the company has pursued intensively over the past two and a half years. David Kim, CEO of LG Energy Solution, has outlined the strategy, stating, "We will actively pursue the rebalancing of our global production facilities to expand our business structure beyond EVs into ESS and new businesses, while optimizing production sites and maximizing the utilization of our investment assets." By rapidly adapting production capacity to shifting market conditions, the company has built one of the strongest manufacturing portfolios in the global battery industry.

LG Energy Solution is also building momentum in its EV battery business. LG Energy Solution recently announced the restart of EV cell production at the Ultium Cells facility in Ohio, which had temporarily paused operations earlier this year. Meanwhile, its Queen Creek facility in Arizona is expected to begin mass production of 46-series cylindrical batteries in the fourth quarter, supported by production lines with approximately 50 percent higher equipment efficiency compared with previous configurations.

Building on its strong manufacturing foundation, LG Energy Solution continues to secure new business opportunities. In the ESS sector, the company has signed agreements with major customers including Tesla, Terra-Gen, Excelsior Energy Capital, EG4, and Hanwha Qcells. In May, it signed an ESS battery supply agreement totaling 6GWh with DTE Energy. In July, the company also agreed to collaborate with renewable energy independent power producer Cypress Creek Energy on ESS supply for Google's largest solar-plus-storage project, with potential volumes reaching up to 2.9GWh. In the EV sector, LG Energy Solution continues to expand partnerships with global automakers, including Mercedes-Benz, while broadening its customer base for mid-priced battery products such as LFP and high-voltage mid-nickel batteries, particularly in Europe.

“The launch of the Lansing facility represents an important milestone that will accelerate the growth of LG Energy Solution’s North American business,” said Kim. “By establishing an advanced battery manufacturing network that supports the future of America’s mobility industry and energy infrastructure, we will continue strengthening the U.S. battery ecosystem while expanding our local production capabilities.”

text:
The Central Electricity Authority (CEA) has proposed making battery energy storage systems (BESS) mandatory for all new ground-mounted solar and onshore wind projects commissioned from 1 July 2027, a move that could accelerate the battery industry's shift beyond electric mobility into stationary storage.

Under the draft rules, a 100 MW solar or wind project would need at least 10 MW of storage capacity with a minimum two-hour duration. The requirement would rise to four hours for projects commissioned from July 2029.

The proposal comes as India's need for grid-scale storage is expected to expand sharply. The country added 2,668.54 MW of BESS power capacity, equivalent to 7,785.6 MWh of storage in 2026. Solar capacity stood at 164.59 GW and wind at 58.14 GW as of 31 July.

For battery manufacturers that built their businesses largely around electric two-wheelers, three-wheelers, four-wheelers and light commercial vehicles, the emerging stationary-storage market offers another major source of demand.

A Formalisation, Not A Surprise

The proposed mandate largely formalises a transition that is already visible in procurement. “Buyers have stopped asking for vanilla solar in the last few months — every serious conversation in the last months has been peak-power or solar-plus-storage,” said Sudharman Ezhil, Director & CEO, Natrinai Ventures (NGE Green Energy).

Ezhil said storage makes renewable assets more useful to lenders and offtakers by allowing projects to schedule power, manage deviation settlement and participate in evening demand periods, when time-of-day tariffs and exchange prices can be significantly higher than daytime solar rates. “What CEA has done is set a floor... it's a welcome move,” he said.

Ezhil expects storage to become standard within two to three years, irrespective of the mandate, as buyers look for projects that can provide power beyond solar generation hours. NGE Green, for instance, already treats BESS as a default line item. The system is sized according to the offtaker's load rather than the regulatory minimum.

Beyond Electric Mobility

The emerging BESS market is also allowing lithium-ion battery manufacturers to diversify beyond electric mobility. Pratik Kamdar, Co-founder & CEO, Neuron Energy, said BESS “has the potential to become a significant new market for Indian lithium-ion battery manufacturers”, pointing to India's projected requirement of more than 236 GWh of BESS by 2031-32.

“This creates an opportunity to diversify beyond electric mobility and participate in utility-scale as well as commercial and industrial storage applications,” Kamdar said.

The shift is also beginning to appear in manufacturers' strategies. Amara Raja Energy & Mobility told investors after its FY26 results that it was giving BESS a larger role in its mix. “A major change in our strategy is the introduction of BESS as a larger part of our mix. Earlier, we had largely focused on EVs,” the company's management said.

For manufacturers, the opportunity extends beyond cells and battery packs to areas such as battery management systems, thermal management and monitoring technologies.

Same Cells, Different Engineering

The move into stationary storage, however, is not a straightforward extension of EV battery manufacturing. “BESS cannot be treated as a simple extension of an EV battery platform,” Kamdar said, pointing to differences in operating requirements, including long-duration operation and frequent charge-discharge cycles.

“Battery pack architecture, BMS software, monitoring and thermal-management systems need to be designed around the specific operating profile of stationary storage,” Kamdar added.

At the same time, the underlying expertise developed through EV battery manufacturing remains transferable, giving existing lithium-ion manufacturers a starting point as they move into grid-scale and commercial storage.

Regulatory Gaps Persist

While the market opportunity is expanding, developers point to commercial and regulatory issues that could affect the pace of deployment.

Ezhil said one challenge is the way solar-plus-storage projects are priced. “The industry keeps trying to sell a blended Rs /kWh tariff that folds battery costs into solar energy. That structure fails bankability,” he said.

Ezhil argued that solar and storage need separate capacity and energy charges, or that batteries should be deployed behind the meter, to better reflect the different functions and costs of the two assets.

State-level rules also remain inconsistent, particularly around banking and surcharge provisions for commercial and industrial storage projects, Ezhil said.

Tamil Nadu's resource adequacy plan, for instance, projects a need for more than 11 GW of additional storage by 2035 and flags evening-hour power shortages between October and April. “The regulatory framework should be pulling private storage into that gap, and we are waiting eagerly for the new policy to get going,” Ezhil said.

The CEA has invited comments on its draft proposal until 4 October 2026, before the regulations are finalised.

For India's battery manufacturers, the proposed mandate could provide further impetus for stationary storage to develop from a supplementary market into a significant part of the country's power infrastructure.
