Donate Now

Practical Shortcomings

If China recycled an additional 1,400 metric tons from its power sector, its recycling rate would increase from roughly 30 percent to approximately 90 percent. This would bring its recycling to a level comparable with the United States, where reuse is voluntary but strongly encouraged, said Ottinger, the former EPA analyst. In Europe, recycling is mandatory. The rate there should be 100 percent; however, precise figures are unavailable, said Cornelia Elsner, a policy adviser with the German Environment Agency.

A study published in 2023 in theProceedings of the Chinese Society for Electrical Engineering noted that SF6 recovery and purification technology in China still has considerable room for development with “several practical shortcomings.”

The study found that the high construction costs of centralized SF6 recycling centers in China resulted in a limited number of facilities concentrated in provincial capitals that cannot easily cover all regions, particularly remote areas.

In 2024, the China Electricity Council published non-binding guidance recommending utilities recycle the gas, and do so on-site. In December, MEE went a step further, incentivizing utilities to recycle SF6 by allowing them to sell carbon credits when they recycle more than 90 percent of their waste gas.

Jin Yana, an assistant professor of environmental economics at Peking University, said the program’s assumption of a high level of recycling is smart policy. It ensures “that the market only issues carbon credits for exceptional, above-and-beyond efforts rather than rewarding standard industry practices,” Jin said.

However, incentives alone may not be enough. Stronger regulations may be needed to address SF6 emissions, a 2024 report on fluorinated greenhouse gases by the Beijing-based Institute for Global Decarbonization Progress concluded.

Next Steps

State Grid and China Southern recently began using alternative electric insulating gases including SF6 mixed with nitrogen gas as more climate-friendly options in low-to-medium-voltage electrical equipment. However, alternatives for high-voltage equipment will need 10 to 20 years to fully mature in China, according to a 2022 assessment compiled by the Administrative Center for China’s Agenda 21, a government agency.

In July, government officials called for the development of projects with the capacity to reduce emissions of SF6 and other “non-CO2” greenhouse gases such as nitrous oxide and hydrofluorocarbons by a total of 30 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent by 2030. The new policy was included in the country’s National Climate Change Response Plan jointly released by MEE and 18 other government departments.

It’s the first time the government has called for an SF6 management plan, said Ma Yue, an assistant analyst at the Institute for Global Decarbonization Progress and author of the 2024 fluorinated gas report. This “sends a positive policy signal for advancing SF6 emissions reductions in the power sector,” Ma said.

China’s utilities could receive assistance in emission reduction efforts from the German government’s international development agency, which is seeking to build a “coalition of the willing” among emerging and developing countries to reduce SF6 emissions.

“It’s really one greenhouse gas where not much has happened yet, and actually, a lot can happen,” said Philippe Lempp, who oversees the German initiative and held a workshop with government officials and industry executives in Beijing in 2024 to discuss potential reduction efforts.

Hu Jianxin, a professor at Peking University’s College of Environmental Sciences and Engineering, said SF6 is difficult to replace in cold climates but is less necessary elsewhere.

“I think the direction first of all is to block its use in non-essential places,” Hu said. “We do not use SF6 anymore in such places and we just keep allowing less and less essential use.”

Kraehling, who was part of the 1990s efforts to rein in this climate super-pollutant, said a similar reduction could happen in China today.

“If you are able to bring together all these stakeholders, you not only have a good chance for success, but you also have a good chance for acceptance,” Kraehling said.

Rudy Lu and Peter Aldhous contributed reporting.

text:
A couple of moves by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) this week get slammed by environmentalists and deliver wins for power plants known to contribute to pollution.

The EPA got rid of rules adopted during the Biden administration that forced power plants run by coal and natural gas to cut greenhouse gas emissions or utilize carbon capture technology. It’s direct opposition to the Clean Air Act. The agency claims it doesn’t have the authority to oversee greenhouse gases related to climate change. The EPA says it will save power plants $310 billion.

The EPA also proposes eliminating every other greenhouse gas rule that’s on the books for the energy industry, claiming that would save $370 million more in compliance costs. There is now a 45-day window open for public comment on that proposal. Conservation was once a big principal of conservatism in the Republican party. What should be the takeaway from these decisions? Host Jim Niedelman got into the issues with Scott County Democratic party chair Kay Pence and former Rock Island County Republican party chair Bill Bloom.

“I think it’s extreme shortsighted, and it will increase local opposition to having power plants,” Pence said. “It will slow the progress toward transitioning to cleaner energy.”

“I think if you look at coal used to be a major employer across the Midwest, particularly across the river to our friends in Illinois,” Bloom said. “I think what he’s trying to do, he’s trying to keep coal as a viable industry in the United States.”

title: New York is getting 700 curbside EV chargers so drivers can ditch window extension cords
description:
Here's what to know The city plans to install 700 Level 2 curbside chargers.
While parts of Europe have already made curbside charging common, most large American cities still have relatively few options.
That shortage can be a major obstacle in dense neighborhoods where drivers lack driveway or garage access.
More background The city already has some experience with curbside charging.
For Gordon, that demand is especially significant for the city's 80,000 rideshare drivers.
text:
For New Yorkers who rely on street parking, charging an electric vehicle has often been more hassle than habit, but a major change is underway.

New York City selected Brooklyn startup It's Electric to spearhead a broad curbside charging expansion, which will make it far easier for apartment residents, rideshare drivers, and other motorists without private garages to switch to cleaner cars, according to InsideEVs.

Here's what to know

The city plans to install 700 Level 2 curbside chargers.

The rollout will reach every borough, with extra attention on neighborhoods that have high concentrations of Uber, Lyft, and taxi drivers.

While parts of Europe have already made curbside charging common, most large American cities still have relatively few options. That shortage can be a major obstacle in dense neighborhoods where drivers lack driveway or garage access.

Tiya Gordon, It's Electric co-founder and chief operating officer, described the regional divide in comments to InsideEVs.

"Once you leave L.A. and you go to Boston, you go to New York, you go to San Francisco, you go to D.C., you go to Philadelphia, you go to New York, it's a desert," Gordon explained.

The city is also linking the charger rollout to a broader transportation goal: transitioning all rideshare vehicles to electric by 2030.

More background

The city already has some experience with curbside charging.

Officials said a pilot program installed 88 curbside Flo chargers, called them "immensely popular with EV owners," and expects to replace them with It's Electric equipment.

City Department of Transportation data indicated heavy use at those locations: EVs occupied the sites 70% of the time overall, some stations reached 99% occupancy, and power was being delivered during 85% of the time the spaces were occupied.

For Gordon, that demand is especially significant for the city's 80,000 rideshare drivers.

"Without curbside charging in neighborhoods like Jackson Heights or Flushing or the Bronx, [drivers] are being forced to drive to a limited amount of fast charging stations, wait in long lines … pay 50 cents per kilowatt hour, and then drive two hours back into Manhattan," she stated.

For everyday drivers, more neighborhood chargers means less wasted time, lower fueling costs than gas, and an easier path to owning a vehicle that produces no tailpipe pollution.

What's being done?

It's Electric said the chargers were built for crowded city streets.

The stainless steel posts have no dangling charging cords, screens, or credit card readers, which the company says reduces sidewalk clutter and better matches city design standards.

Rather than depending on a separate utility hookup, the chargers use power from nearby apartment buildings, which It's Electric said lowers installation costs and speeds up deployment.

Gordon said there will be no more than two chargers on a single block, and the units will be made in Queens.

The company is also growing beyond New York. Alongside the city announcement, It's Electric said a funding round brought its total funding to $15 million.

Gordon told InsideEVs the startup now has 50 chargers in operation and 700 customers, and has also landed contracts in Boston, Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Philadelphia.

"By putting chargers in the neighborhoods where these rideshare drivers just park overnight and go to sleep, they're waking up and they have that full battery," she said.

Where can I learn more?

These articles dig into apartment charging access, highway build-outs, vandalism, theft, and wireless charging roads.

• Texas is adding 50 new charging stations along major highway corridors.

• In Los Angeles, copper theft at chargers is driving up repair costs and outages.

• Detroit is testing roads that can charge electric vehicles while they drive.

As more Americans make the switch from gas-powered vehicles to EVs, charging infrastructure is slowly but surely rising to meet that increasing demand.

Nearly all wind energy projects in the United States are still on pause almost a month after a federal judge ruled that the Trump administration’s freeze on vertical height clearances for wind turbines was likely illegal. The administration has control over airspace higher than 200 feet, and therefore has control over wind projects on both private and public land, writes Jael Holzman for Heatmap.

On Sept. 17, the Trump administration provided its first update to the federal court since the ruling. Heatmap reports:

The administration claimed that “as a matter of policy” it had “resumed processing wind energy project applications,” but it only described a single instance where a company had heard from the military about moving forward. In addition, that company as well as all others affected by the freeze would still face a “new analytical methodology” for federal agencies reviewing height clearances for all projects, which appears to fly in the face of the ruling. The Justice Department did not provide any more detail about the methodology in its status update to the court.

According to the Department of Justice, at least 110 wind energy projects were in active discussion with the federal government before the injunction, and none have heard from officials since. Another 50 projects are awaiting initial meetings with the federal government.

title: California's gas plants once ruled the grid like a backup generator nobody could live without ...
description:
A peak day that looks nothing like it used to On August 26, 2026, California’s grid hit its yearly peak at 5:55 p.m. — 46,015 megawatts.
The supply picture on that 2026 peak day was equally striking.
Twelve years of decline — and an accelerating retreat The 2026 peak day didn’t come out of nowhere.
“The key story here is batteries,” said Ed Smeloff, a longtime energy analyst who has tracked California’s grid closely.
Rooftop solar and home battery systems have compounded the effect by reducing overall demand and shrinking the peak that gas plants once had to cover.
text:
California’s gas plants are losing ground to solar and batteries faster than predicted

On a sweltering August afternoon in 2026, California’s electricity grid hit its yearly peak demand — the kind of moment that, not long ago, would have sent grid operators scrambling to fire up natural gas plants across the state.

Something different happened instead.

Researcher Jonathan Koomey says the displacement of gas by solar and batteries has become “pretty obvious” to people who study energy systems closely.

The shift had been building for over a decade, quietly reshaping how California keeps its lights on. But in recent years it has moved faster than nearly anyone in the energy industry anticipated — and the numbers behind it are hard to ignore.

A peak day that looks nothing like it used to

On August 26, 2026, California’s grid hit its yearly peak at 5:55 p.m. — 46,015 megawatts. That sounds like a lot. But compare it to September 6, 2022, when the all-time record reached 52,061 megawatts, and the gap tells its own story. The grid is serving a hot, growing state with notably less strain than it did just four years ago.

The supply picture on that 2026 peak day was equally striking. On the CAISO grid, the line for renewable energy towered above natural gas for most of the day. Batteries — shown charging below zero through the midday solar surplus — swung sharply upward just after sunset, covering the evening demand spike that once belonged almost exclusively to gas peakers.

At certain moments, California actually exported more power than it consumed. A state that used to lean heavily on imports during heat emergencies was, briefly, a net supplier to the region.

Twelve years of decline — and an accelerating retreat

The 2026 peak day didn’t come out of nowhere. California’s gas-fired electricity generation reached its high point in 2014 and has declined in eight of the eleven years since. The retreat has been uneven but persistent — and recently it picked up speed in a way that surprised even close observers.

Gas use fell 15% in 2025 compared to 2024. Then, in the first half of 2026, it dropped another 26% compared to the same period in 2025, according to U.S. Energy Information Administration data. Those aren’t incremental numbers. California’s share of total U.S. gas consumption for electricity generation fell from 10% in 2014 to just 4% in 2025 — moving in the opposite direction from the broader national trend. Coal has already faded to near zero in California’s electricity mix, and gas is following a similar trajectory, just stretched across a longer timeline.

How solar and batteries replaced the peaker plant

The mechanism behind this shift is fairly straightforward, even if the scale of it isn’t. California built an enormous amount of utility-scale solar over the past decade, creating a reliable midday surplus of cheap power, then layered in battery storage to capture that surplus and dispatch it later — right when demand peaks in the early evening.

“The key story here is batteries,” said Ed Smeloff, a longtime energy analyst who has tracked California’s grid closely. Batteries essentially do what peaker plants used to do, but without burning anything.

Peaker plants are the primary casualty. Designed to run only a few hours during demand spikes, they’re the least efficient and most expensive gas units on the grid. As batteries take over that role, peakers run less and less. Rooftop solar and home battery systems have compounded the effect by reducing overall demand and shrinking the peak that gas plants once had to cover.

Policy, regional grids, and a wind farm in New Mexico

None of this happened by market forces alone. California’s carbon-reduction laws provided the policy framework that made investment in solar and storage financially viable. The overall direction, as Smeloff put it, has been clear even when specific rules created friction — rooftop solar net metering policies, for instance, have at times hurt the very industry they were meant to support.

Regional grid coordination has also improved. Hydropower from Oregon and Washington is now more accessible as Western grid operators have gotten better at sharing resources across state lines. Then there’s the SunZia wind project in New Mexico — the largest wind farm in the United States — whose output flows into California via a dedicated transmission line under a firm contract, adding yet another layer of clean supply.

A model for other states — and a national counterpoint

Researcher Jonathan Koomey says the displacement of gas by solar and batteries has become “pretty obvious” to people who study energy systems closely. The public, he suggests, hasn’t yet grasped the scale of what’s happened in California.

Texas offers a parallel. Smeloff points to it as another state where the same solar-and-battery formula is already reducing reliance on dirtier power sources. The national picture, though, cuts the other way — the Trump administration has moved to expand natural gas production, and new gas peaker plants are in various stages of planning or construction across the country.

text:
NextEra Energy, Inc. (NYSE:NEE) announced on September 8 that it had secured a loan of up to $1.9 billion from the U.S. Department of Energy to support the restart of a shuttered nuclear power plant in Iowa. The Duane Arnold Energy Center ceased operations in 2020 after 45 years of service. The plant is now expected to resume operations in early 2029, pending regulatory approvals.

The federal funding is intended to help restore the facility and add reliable generation capacity as the US electricity demand soars to record levels amid the AI boom. To help meet the growing demand, President Trump is making efforts to accelerate the expansion of nuclear energy. He has signed an executive order to get 10 large conventional reactors under construction by 2030 and has also called for federal funding to support the restart of shuttered nuclear plants.

John Ketchum, Chairman, President, and CEO of NextEra Energy, commented:

"Restarting Duane Arnold is about delivering new power to meet new demand while generating billions of dollars in economic value for Iowans. Just as importantly, it shows how America can support rapid economic growth and rising electricity demand while helping keep power affordable for existing customers. By bringing new generation online to serve new demand, we can strengthen the grid, create hundreds of good-paying jobs and help ensure Iowa families and businesses are not asked to bear the costs of growth. We appreciate the Administration's leadership in advancing America's nuclear renaissance and share its commitment to an all-of-the-above energy strategy that expands supply, strengthens energy security and keeps America competitive."

Photo by Frédéric Paulussen on Unsplash

NextEra's Nuclear Bet Taps the AI Boom:

Nuclear Energy has garnered significant attention from technology giants, as it can provide reliable and clean electricity to power their data centers. A number of hyperscalers have already signed power purchase agreements with utilities to ensure that they have enough energy available to compete in the ongoing AI race. These contracts typically range from 15 to 20 years, providing long-term revenue visibility.

Additionally, the extension and expansion of existing nuclear facilities will allow utilities to continue capitalizing on the ongoing AI boom without relying exclusively on the lengthy and costly construction of new nuclear plants.

NextEra Energy has also taken a similar step to reduce Duane Arnold's commercial risk. Last year, it signed a 25-year agreement with Google to buy power from the nuclear power plant, providing a long-term customer for its 615 MW of output. Therefore, the latest DoE financing provides substantial financial support for a project that already has a long-term customer and a clear strategic rationale.

Another major growth catalyst for NextEra is its proposed merger with Dominion Energy, which will create the world's largest regulated electric utility business by market capitalization. The $66.8 billion deal will expose NextEra to the largest data center cluster in the world in Northern Virginia, while also providing it deep and direct access to the PJM Interconnection grid region.

NextEra's Nuclear Revival Still Faces Major Hurdles:

Despite the encouraging financing announcement, the project remains several years away from generating meaningful earnings and cash flows and still faces regulatory and execution risks. The restart requires approval from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, and it needs mentioning that no previously shuttered nuclear power plant has yet successfully completed a restart in the United States.

NextEra's broader expansion strategy also faces the risk of a potential AI bubble, since a major part of its investment thesis is based on the rapidly growing power demand from data centers. While hyperscalers are currently committing hundreds of billions of dollars to expand their data center infrastructure, the eventual economic returns from these enormous investments remain uncertain. Any meaningful slowdown in AI adoption, weaker-than-expected returns, or a subsequent pullback in capital spending could significantly reduce the projected power demand.

Conclusion:

The $1.9 billion federal loan provides important financial support for NextEra Energy's planned restart of the Duane Arnold Energy Center, reducing funding pressure on the nuclear project. Combined with the 25-year PPA with Google and rising AI-power demand, the plant offers significant long-term potential. However, regulatory approvals, execution challenges, and uncertainty surrounding AI spending could limit the upside.

title: Opinion: Let's talk CT energy costs with actual numbers, not assumptions - Hartford Courant
description:
A recent report issued by the Boston-based Fiscal Alliance Foundation report argues that New England’s shift from natural gas to renewables is driving up electric bills.
Connecticut Powers New England,” examines what has driven energy costs over the past 25 years.
In 2012, Connecticut launched an initiative to expand natural gas, promising lower costs and a cleaner environment.
Natural gas used for electricity generation rose 87% between 2014 and 2024.
Let’s use the same yardstick for both sides: measurable rates, measurable infrastructure spending, and measurable projects already coming online.
text:
A recent report issued by the Boston-based Fiscal Alliance Foundation report argues that New England’s shift from natural gas to renewables is driving up electric bills. It’s a tidy story that fits the fossil fuel industry’s storyline, but it’s also missing most of the data explaining why Connecticut ratepayers pay some of the highest electric rates in the country.

That is why the Connecticut League of Conservation Voters commissioned the University of Connecticut’s Center for Economic Analysis (CCEA) to conduct this research. The resulting report, “How Did We Get Here? Connecticut Powers New England,” examines what has driven energy costs over the past 25 years. Its findings point not to wind turbines or solar panels, but to the natural gas buildout and the infrastructure transporting gas-fired electricity across the region, including exports from Connecticut. Energy policy debates should be grounded in measurable data.

In 2012, Connecticut launched an initiative to expand natural gas, promising lower costs and a cleaner environment. Natural gas used for electricity generation rose 87% between 2014 and 2024. By 2024, Connecticut generated nearly 45% of all electricity produced in New England, more than any other state. In plain terms, Connecticut had to build the gas plants and therefore absorbed the emissions and the construction costs, and shipped most of the electricity to other states.

What did Connecticut get for hosting all that generation? Not lower rates. Connecticut’s residential electric rate climbed to 30.3 cents by January 2026, with commercial rates now third highest nationally. For a typical household: that means well over $100 more annually for the same usage.

Those dollars are being spent on poles and wires. Delivery charges, the cost of building and maintaining the lines that carry power to your house, make up most of a Connecticut residential bill today. Connecticut ratepayers are also carrying a growing share of regional transmission costs. These costs have grown 72% since 2015 and now account for 10 to 11% of a typical monthly bill.

Let’s look at where markets are heading.

The energy market is already telling us where the future is headed. The amount of new power generation proposed for New England nearly tripled between 2017 and 2025, but what investors want to build has changed dramatically. In 2017, nearly half of proposed generation was natural gas. Today, gas accounts for less than 1%, while wind, solar, and battery storage make up virtually all proposed capacity. The question is no longer whether our energy system will change. It’s what we want that future to look like—and whether Connecticut will be ready for it.

For instance, Revolution Wind began delivering electricity to New England this year and is over 95% complete: the project is projected to save regional ratepayers $400 to $500 million annually once fully online.

This is the debate we’re seeking: what technology or investments can be made that will save taxpayer dollars.

To be clear, while we know gas makes up a large percentage of our energy mix today, we question the economic benefits in its proposed expansion and raise the discussion about where our future investments will be made. The region will need substantially more electricity, and should be centered on whether we can build a diverse enough system of clean generation, storage, transmission, imports and demand flexibility to provide reliable power that is not dependent upon global politics, economic disruption and even the weather.

Let’s use the same yardstick for both sides: measurable rates, measurable infrastructure spending, and measurable projects already coming online. Before Connecticut policymakers make further policy or financial commitments to natural gas, it is necessary to determine whether existing gas infrastructure can meet future power demand while taking advantage of renewable energy that markets already favor.

With those questions in mind, our data shows that doubling down on natural gas is the more expensive bet, in addition to not being the most reliable one.

text:
The $528 million expansion project in Copiah County will increase the company’s production capacity and expand the range of small power transformers manufactured domestically, while creating over 650 jobs.

Governor Tate Reeves and the Mississippi Development Authority announced Tuesday that Hitachi Energy is investing $528 million to expand its operations in Copiah County.

The governor made the announcement from the G20 energy summit in Houston, Texas, alongside Energy Secretary Chris Wright, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin and other federal energy leaders.

The announced expansion project is Hitachi Energy’s largest investment to date in the U.S., officials said.

Calling it “a massive win for Mississippi and the United States,” Reeves said the company plans to create 654 jobs in its expanded Mississippi transformer manufacturing factory.

“Hitachi Energy could’ve made its largest investment in America anywhere in the country – but the company chose Mississippi,” the governor said. “Mississippi’s momentum is growing stronger every day, and it is our people who are building the future of American energy infrastructure.”

Reeves added that Mississippi is proud to play a leading role in powering America’s future.

Hitachi Energy was incorporated in June 2021, but its founding dates back over a century from predecessor companies ABB and its parent company, Hitachi Ltd. Hitachi Energy is now a global leader in electrification that manufactures transformers and other equipment to help power homes, businesses and communities.

The company’s current facility in Copiah County produces small power transformers and employs 475 people.

Andreas Schierenbeck, CEO, Hitachi Energy, said demand for electricity is growing rapidly, and the grid must grow with it.

“This investment in Mississippi, our largest ever in the U.S., reflects our long-term commitment to American manufacturing and building the grid infrastructure that will help power America’s growth for decades to come,” Schierenbeck said. “We are pleased to work with the Trump administration and Governor Reeves to support investment in American manufacturing at a pivotal time for U.S. energy security.”

MDA said the expansion project will significantly increase Hitachi Energy’s production capacity and expand the range of small power transformers manufactured domestically, helping meet growing demand across North America while strengthening the domestic supply chain for critical energy infrastructure.

The project includes the purchase of a 45-acre site at the Copiah County Industrial Park in Gallman, the construction of a new facility, new manufacturing equipment and infrastructure improvements. Construction is expected to begin later this year, with transformer production scheduled to start in 2029.

The company is taking advantage of the Mississippi Flexible Tax Incentive, or MFLEX, program, and MDA is also assisting with site development and infrastructure improvements. Copiah County is assisting with the project, as well.

“Reliable energy infrastructure has become one of the most important factors in economic growth, and that starts with the ability to manufacture the equipment that keeps the grid running,” said Mississippi Development Authority Executive Director Bill Cork. “At $528 million, Hitachi Energy’s expansion is a massive addition to the investment taking place in Mississippi and puts Copiah County at the center of an industry that is increasingly critical to economic development.”

title: Trump's Chesapeake Bay order rebuked stormwater fees. Experts say it won't end them.
description:
In an executive order signed Wednesday, Trump repealed Executive Order 13508, signed in 2009 by President Barack Obama.
Josh Shapiro review Chesapeake Bay stormwater mandates, according to a report from the Times Leader.
Cities in Hampton Roads initiated the stormwater fees in the 1990s in compliance with the Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System permit.
“There was a big push towards meeting water quality, stormwater quality, and how to address projects that deal with flood control or water quality,” said Sam Sawan, Chesapeake’s deputy director of public works.
Stormwater management fees are used in some Hampton Roads localities to pay for infrastructure, such as flood protections, as well as system maintenance.
text:
President Donald Trump revoked a 17-year-old Chesapeake Bay protection policy last week, claiming states and localities had improperly relied upon it to impose stormwater management fees on residents and businesses.

In an executive order signed Wednesday, Trump repealed Executive Order 13508, signed in 2009 by President Barack Obama. The move sent shockwaves throughout the environmental community, where advocates believe the decision jeopardizes decades of bay restoration and weakens federal leadership and accountability.

The administration claims the 2009 order contained a lack of clarity causing “harmful economic impacts,” and specifically takes aim at stormwater management fees, which Trump also refers to as a “rain tax.”

But policy and utility experts say ending the fees would be much more complicated than simply revoking Obama’s executive order.

Will stormwater management fees cease to exist?

Trump’s action orders certain federal and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency officials to coordinate with Chesapeake Bay watershed states, including Virginia, to assess stormwater management fee “financial burdens,” and to encourage states and localities to repeal such taxes.

But Alison Hooper Prost, senior vice president for programs at Chesapeake Bay Foundation, said local and state authority give municipalities the ability to implement stormwater fees, not the 2009 executive order. That order does not directly mention or mandate stormwater management fees.

After the order was signed Wednesday, Republican lawmakers in Pennsylvania, a Chesapeake Bay watershed state, requested the state’s environmental department and Gov. Josh Shapiro review Chesapeake Bay stormwater mandates, according to a report from the Times Leader.

It’s unlikely Democrats who hold political control in Virginia state government would request a similar review. Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s office did not respond to questions about the order by publication deadline.

Cities in Hampton Roads initiated the stormwater fees in the 1990s in compliance with the Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System permit. MS4, which requires localities to pay for operating stormwater systems, create stormwater management plans and eliminate stormwater pollutants, was introduced by the EPA after a 1987 Clean Water Act amendment.

“There was a big push towards meeting water quality, stormwater quality, and how to address projects that deal with flood control or water quality,” said Sam Sawan, Chesapeake’s deputy director of public works. “The way to fund these programs was the stormwater (fee) program. It’s nothing new here (or) in the region.”

What are stormwater fees used for?

Stormwater management fees are used in some Hampton Roads localities to pay for infrastructure, such as flood protections, as well as system maintenance.

“They are directed at not just water quality, but when you think about nuisance flooding or as we’re having increased rainstorms, these fees are allowing communities to build resilience,” Prost said. “The (new) executive order pinpoint(s) them as negative, but they are showing results, and it’s at a time that we need more resources and not less.”

Residential households in Chesapeake currently pay about $11.35 a month in stormwater fees, which totals about $27 million annually, according to Sawan. Rates were last increased about five years ago, he said, and most other cities increase on a regular basis.

Homeowners, and property and business owners pay the fees as their “contribution towards the stormwater system” in Chesapeake, he said. The program funds the capital improvement budget, and stormwater operations, engineering and environmental divisions. This includes flood control and stormwater quality projects.

With Hampton Roads and stormwater, Prost said it’s the “perfect example” of climate change, water quality and habitat convergence. Those challenges might be enhanced with this repeal, she said.

“The previous executive order from 2009 took a real holistic approach. It wasn’t just focused on water quality,” Prost said. “In an area like Hampton Roads, the stormwater management is important for water quality, but it’s also important for habitat, resiliency, what it means for the communities.”

Environmental implications

In Trump’s order, the president questioned the level of ecologic benefits stormwater infrastructure provides to the Chesapeake Bay.

Environmental experts disagree with the skepticism. Stormwater is one of the fastest-growing pollution sources to local rivers and streams, according to CBF President and CEO Hilary Harp Falk, which is addressed by “locally identified funding mechanisms.”

“This is where we’re seeing success — by putting in different practices that are improving local rivers and streams,” Falk said.

Ian Blair, policy program director at Norfolk-based nonprofit Wetlands Watch, said the Clean Water Act focuses on point source and non-point source pollution. Point source pollution involves located origins of pollution, while the latter involves pollution such as runoff from yards and streets.

“We’ve got anything that’s been picked up from any rainstorm going directly into the bay, and just sort of settling at the bottom,” Blair said.

The executive order notes significant improvements in Chesapeake Bay water quality, specifically citing a study contributed to by William & Mary’s Batten School of Coastal and Marine Sciences and the Virginia Institute of Marine Science, which projects the annual dead zone to be among the smallest since 1985.

In a statement to The Virginian-Pilot, VIMS said it is reviewing the executive order, and will continue to work with government agencies and other partners to better understand potential impacts.

Congressional response

U.S. Rep. Jen Kiggans said Friday Trump’s order eliminated “outdated, vague regulations that have allowed local officials to hinder economic development” from the former order. But she said she will be involved in oversight.

“While I appreciate the administration shifting its focus to measurable solutions that build on decade-long cleanup efforts, I will be closely monitoring the next steps … to ensure any action taken is done with the economic and recreational opportunities the Bay provides and the complex ecosystem in mind,” the 2nd District Republican said in a statement.

Kiggans noted the order does not repeal the Clean Water Act, or change water pollution standards for the Chesapeake Bay and state and local water quality requirements.

In a joint statement Friday, U.S. Sens. Mark Warner and Tim Kaine said the repeal “dismantles a longstanding framework” for federal coordination, including scientific research expansion, climate change impact assessment and tackling pollution from agricultural runoff and stormwater.

“Rolling back efforts to clean up the Bay is dangerous not just for our environment but for our economy,” the pair of Virginia Democrats said.

text:
The Environmental Protection Agency moved to scrap most of the Biden administration's climate rules for power plants and signaled that it intends to eliminate the rest as well, Utility Dive reported.

The decision will slow efforts to cut pollution from power plants and raises fresh concerns for communities already shouldering the health and economic impacts of a warming planet.

Here's what to know

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin indicated that the agency completed its repeal of most parts of the 2024 carbon-pollution rule for fossil fuel power plants and is separately seeking to rescind the greenhouse gas standards that still apply to the sector.

In explaining the action, the EPA argued that the Clean Air Act does not authorize it to regulate power-plant greenhouse gas emissions to address climate change.

The agency claimed that position was supported by the Trump administration's reversal of the landmark 2009 Endangerment Finding and by the Supreme Court's Loper Bright ruling.

NASA explained that "human activities (primarily the human burning of fossil fuels) have warmed Earth's surface and its ocean basins, which in turn have continued to impact Earth's climate."

The repeal of the 2024 standards will take effect 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

The EPA plans to hold a public hearing and open a 45-day public comment period on its broader proposal.

More background

Power plants remain a major source of climate pollution, and federal limits were intended to advance the sector toward cleaner energy generation over time.

Weakening those standards makes it harder to reduce the emissions that contribute to worsening heat, wildfire conditions, flooding, and other impacts that typically hit families and local governments first.

Supporters of the rollback argued that the previous rules were too costly and unrealistic.

"In regard to EPA's new proposed rule, we strongly believe that regulatory certainty is helpful as we plan for long-term investments that support grid reliability," said Rachael Marsh, chief legal officer at the Edison Electric Institute.

"We will continue partnering with EPA on a durable and achievable regulatory framework that is cost effective for customers and supports the investments needed to meet growing electricity demand."

Jim Matheson, CEO of the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association, called the Biden-era limits "unlawful, unrealistic and unachievable."

Michelle Bloodworth, CEO of America's Power, asserted that the rules effectively gave electricity providers a choice between closing coal plants by 2032 or trying to meet carbon requirements through carbon capture and storage, which she felt was too costly and insufficiently proven.

Opponents, however, warned that those arguments ignored the public costs of increased pollution and delayed climate action.

For communities near fossil fuel infrastructure or already coping with extreme weather, fewer safeguards mean greater risks over time, even if utilities gain short-term flexibility.

What's being done?

Former EPA veterans, environmental groups, and state and local officials are already organizing opposition, and some have indicated they intend to challenge the rollback in court.

"We've fought every one of these reckless rollbacks, and we're ready to sue again now to protect our health and safety," Connecticut Attorney General William Tong vowed.

Climate Mayors Executive Director Kate Wright also criticized the move.

Utilities, regulators, cities, and advocacy groups are now likely to keep battling over what a "durable and achievable" power-sector framework should look like — and who bears the cost when climate protections are removed.

"EPA has a responsibility to work alongside local leaders to protect Americans' health, not eliminate the safeguards that protect families from deadly toxins," Wright noted.

"While mayors continue to advance local initiatives to protect residents, the EPA is moving backwards."

Where can I learn more?

These articles cover court rulings, federal mandates, and regional policies shaping power-plant and energy rules.

• A federal court let Biden's coal-plant emissions rules stay in place while challenges moved forward.

• The Supreme Court declined to block the EPA's new power-plant mandate for coal and gas facilities.

• EPA under Lee Zeldin moved toward repealing coal and oil standards, alarming health advocates.

text:
Congress leader Jairam Ramesh on Sunday (September 20, 2026) alleged that the National Green Tribunal (NGT) has been “emasculated” by the Narendra Modi government over the past decade and cited a study showing that it did not rule in favour of an environmental or public-interest party in a single appeal heard on merits in the first six months of this year.

The former Environment Minister said the NGT should now rediscover the letter and spirit of the NGT Act, 2010.

“A study published by the South Asian Reporter for Environment Laws (SAREL) on 19 September 2026 found that, during the first six months of 2026, the National Green Tribunal (NGT) did not rule in favour of an environmental or public-interest party in a single appeal heard on merits,” Mr. Ramesh said in a post on X.

He said that 119 appeals were filed before the NGT’s five benches between January and June 2026, and 52 were dismissed on procedural grounds. This, in itself, he said, is questionable.

“Of the 67 appeals heard on merits — 51 appeals were filed by industry, project proponents or property owners. They received favourable orders in 30 cases, or around 60% of these appeals. In contrast, environmental or public-interest parties filed 16 appeals seeking environmental justice. All 16 were dismissed, with none receiving a favourable ruling,” Mr. Ramesh said.

The contrast is particularly significant given that the NGT was established in June 2010 through an Act of Parliament to provide effective and expeditious environmental justice to the citizens of the country, the Congress general secretary said.

“Over the past decade it has been emasculated by the Modi government,” Mr. Ramesh said, adding that the tribunal must “recover and rediscover its courage”.

SAREL analysis

The analysis by SAREL examined the 119 appeals filed at the five benches of the NGT between January and June. While environmental or public-interest parties filed 16 of the 119 merit appeals, the project proponent, property owner, or industry side filed 51 such appeals.

More than 50 appeals were dismissed on technicalities or procedural issues and never reached a merits ruling.

“The public-interest side was not given a favourable judgment in all 16 of its matters, winning none. The industry side was dismissed in only about a third of its appeals and secured a favourable order in 59% (30 of the 51 merit appeals were won), with a further 6% preserved at status quo,” the analysis said.

It also highlighted that dismissal on technical grounds was a major filter, as 44% of all appeals were dismissed on limitation, jurisdiction, maintainability or withdrawal without any merits ruling.

text:
Rising trade friction between Washington and Beijing is not stopping CATL from targeting segments of the U.S. vehicle market that remain commercially attractive. The Chinese battery maker says it has developed a new battery design for pick-up trucks and sees potential to supply the market through local manufacturing partnerships.

U.S. pick-up strategy amid tariff pressure

As reported by Financial Times, CATL says it has developed “tall” batteries tailored for the U.S. pick-up truck market, even as Chinese battery and vehicle groups face steep barriers to entering the country. Zhu Lingbo, chief technology officer of CATL’s international business unit, says the batteries have already been tested by U.S. carmakers, although he does not identify the companies.

Zhu says the U.S. market could still become “huge business” for CATL despite what he describes as intense geopolitics. He says the company could license the technology to U.S. groups for production on American soil, following a model similar to existing arrangements with Ford and Tesla for EV battery manufacturing in the U.S.

That strategy comes as direct exports and fresh factory investment remain difficult for Chinese groups because of high tariffs, localisation requirements and the threat of restrictions tied to national security concerns. CATL was designated last year by the Pentagon as having alleged military links, an allegation the company denies.

Policy risks and global expansion plans

CATL’s comments come ahead of meetings between U.S. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng in New York, before an expected summit in Washington between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping next week. The talks are expected to cover AI, access to rare earth supply chains and the November expiry of the current trade war truce.

The company is pursuing the U.S. opportunity as electric vehicle demand there weakens after the end of EV tax credits and the rollback of emissions rules under Trump. Benchmark Mineral Intelligence expects EV and plug-in hybrid penetration in the U.S. to stay below 10 per cent this year, far behind China’s 65 per cent.

Political resistance in the U.S. remains strong. Industry groups representing the U.S. auto sector last week urged Trump to keep policies that block Chinese carmakers and supply chains from America, even after Trump says he would accept Chinese-owned car plants if they employ American workers.

Outside the U.S., CATL continues to expand in Europe through new battery plants in Hungary and Spain alongside its German operation. Zhu says the company is also searching for additional European production sites and building battery-swapping stations for electric lorries, while noting that any further European investment would require Beijing’s approval.

text:
Egypt has signed an agreement with Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL) and Egyptian battery manufacturer BME to establish a battery manufacturing plant in Egypt.

Egyptian Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly witnessed the signing of the agreement between Maged Wahib, Chairman of BME, and Luo Haining, Director of International Investment at CATL.

The planned facility will initially manufacture battery systems for heavy commercial vehicles, with the first phase designed to deliver an annual production capacity of 1 GWh.

Initial investment in the project is expected to exceed EGP 2 billion.

First Phase to Focus on Heavy Commercial Vehicles

The factory is planned as an industrial base for battery system manufacturing in Egypt.

During the first phase, production will focus on battery systems for heavy commercial vehicles. The project is targeting a 40% local content ratio and is intended to supply both the Egyptian and international markets.

The partnership is expected to combine CATL’s battery technology, production equipment and technical expertise with BME’s Egyptian manufacturing and engineering capabilities.

The companies also expect the cooperation to support technology transfer and the development of a local battery manufacturing supply chain.

Expansion to 5 GWh Planned

Under the planned second phase, the facility’s annual production capacity is expected to increase to 5 GWh.

The expansion is intended to broaden the factory’s product range beyond heavy commercial vehicles to include passenger vehicle batteries and energy-storage systems for renewable electricity generated from solar and wind projects.

The second phase therefore represents a planned expansion of both production capacity and application areas, rather than the current production scope of the facility.

Supporting Local Battery Manufacturing

BME was established by Egyptian transport manufacturer MCV and Auto D for Industry, Trade and Supplies.

Through the partnership with CATL, BME plans to manufacture battery systems locally for vehicle manufacturers operating in Egypt.

Local production is expected to reduce Egypt’s reliance on imported battery systems and could reduce some transportation and logistics costs by locating battery production closer to vehicle manufacturing operations.

The project is also intended to strengthen domestic manufacturing capabilities and develop technical skills related to battery production, electric mobility and energy storage.

Government Supports Battery Industry Development

Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly said the government aims to accelerate implementation of the project and move toward the next stages of execution.

The agreement forms part of Egypt’s efforts to develop local battery manufacturing and attract technology and investment into the country’s electric mobility and automotive component sectors.

Industry Minister Khaled Hashem said the facility represents a step toward establishing domestic battery production capabilities as the global automotive industry moves toward electric vehicles and energy-storage technologies.

He also highlighted the importance of automotive component manufacturing within Egypt’s national automotive industry development program.

Project manager Amin Karim Ghobour said the partnership would combine CATL’s technology and technical support with Egyptian manufacturing and engineering capabilities.

The cooperation is also expected to support the development of a local supply chain for battery manufacturing.

Project Summary

✔ Who signed the agreement? BME and CATL. BME is the Egyptian battery manufacturer established by MCV and Auto D for Industry, Trade and Supplies.

✔ Contract value? Initial investment is expected to exceed EGP 2 billion.

✔ End User / Operator? The facility is intended to supply battery systems to vehicle manufacturers in Egypt and international markets.

✔ EPC Contractor? Not specified.

✔ FEED Contractor? Not specified.

✔ When will FEED start? Not specified.

✔ Project Location? Egypt. The specific plant location was not stated in the supplied information.

✔ Project Status / Construction Start? Project agreement signed / development stage. The first phase is planned for 1 GWh/year of battery production. No construction start date was specified.

✔ Flow Control Products Required (Expected Scope): Battery manufacturing facilities can require industrial pumps, valves, actuators, piping, fittings, cooling systems and process instrumentation, depending on the final plant design. Specific equipment requirements have not been disclosed.

text:
Since former Suffolk County Congressman Lee Zeldin was appointed by President Trump to head the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, the EPA’s press office has regularly issued news releases featuring praise for Zeldin and his policies.

For example, one release quoted the Bull Moose Project, a Washington-based organization that describes itself as “dedicated to advocacy for a dominant American future,” declaring: “When historians write about how America was made great again, they’ll list Administrator Zeldin’s accomplishments as KEY.”

Another EPA release cited Grover Norquist, president of Americans for Tax Reform, also based in Washington, saying: “Administrator Zeldin’s bold deregulatory action at EPA will unleash American energy and reduce costs for American families.”

Meanwhile, Zeldin has faced sharply critical coverage in major newspapers and magazines.

The New York Times ran an article headlined, “How Lee Zeldin Shifted the Mission—and the Message—of the EPA.” The article said Zeldin “speaks more about supporting industry and exporting fossil fuels than about protecting the environment.”

The New Yorker published an article by Pulitzer Prize-winning writer Elizabeth Kolbert titled, “Can the EPA Survive Lee Zeldin?” The article noted that Trump has referred to Zeldin as “one of the superstars” of his second administration and as “our secret weapon.” It argued that Zeldin had transformed the EPA from an agency devoted to protecting human health and the environment into one that “more or less openly, sides with polluters.”

Now, as Zeldin approaches two years as EPA administrator, the Sierra Club has published an extensive examination of his tenure in the fall 2026 edition of Sierra magazine, which has a reported circulation of about one million.

The eight-page article, written by journalist Alexander Nazaryan, is prominently featured on the magazine’s cover under the headline: “How an unassuming politician from Long Island helped turn the EPA into a shield for the fossil fuel industry.”

The article states that, “Under the guise of what he calls the Powering the Great American Comeback Initiative—a kind of Project 2025 spin-off—Zeldin has mounted the most dramatic assault on environmental policy in modern U.S. history.”

It says Zeldin’s deregulatory policies “will make it easier for power plants to dispose of coal ash; expose more communities of color to air and water pollution; and, on the whole, make air, water and soil dirtier for all Americans.”

The article also focuses on Zeldin’s February 2026 action eliminating the 2009 EPA Endangerment Finding, which had determined that greenhouse gas emissions including carbon dioxide and methane pose a threat to public health. The EPA describes that action as part of what it calls the largest deregulatory effort in the agency’s history.

The Sierra Club article says the repeal “could result in billions more tons of planet-warming emissions,” citing estimates it attributes to outside sources.

“Zeldin is transforming the EPA in the process—closing offices, canceling grants, and dismissing scientific experts,” the article continues. “He is doing it methodically, without hesitation, and seemingly with the president’s approval.”

“For the past half century,” Nazaryan writes, “Americans have lived with the implicit understanding that the federal government has a responsibility to protect them from environmental harms.”

He describes the creation of the EPA in 1970 and the passage of landmark legislation such as the Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act as part of a period in which the federal government assumed a central role in addressing environmental threats.

“Now, that assumption has been upended, and the stakes could not be higher,” the article says. It argues that the EPA has been reconfigured to defend major polluters, describing that as “a paradox that Trump and Zeldin created together.”

The article details several actions taken by Zeldin and the Trump administration involving fossil-fuel and power-plant regulations.

It says that one of Zeldin’s early actions was attending an event for Trump’s National Energy Dominance Council, where he announced that the EPA would loosen mercury and air-toxics standards for coal-fired power plants.

The article also discusses Zeldin’s actions involving greenhouse-gas standards for power plants and coal ash, a toxic byproduct of coal combustion that can contain contaminants including arsenic, chromium and lead.

The EPA, for its part, says its regulatory changes are intended to reduce costs, increase energy production and provide more reliable and affordable electricity. On Sept. 14, the agency announced the repeal of most of the Biden administration’s greenhouse-gas requirements for power plants and proposed rescinding the remaining greenhouse-gas standards for the power sector. The EPA estimated the finalized action would save $310 billion.

The Sierra Club article also traces Zeldin’s background on Long Island.

Zeldin was raised in Shirley, a hamlet in Suffolk County. The article notes that Long Island’s population density and history of industrial and agricultural activity have contributed to environmental contamination in various parts of the region.

When Zeldin entered Congress in 2015, after four years in the New York State Senate, Nazaryan writes that he appeared aligned with some environmental conservation efforts.

Zeldin became a member of the Climate Solutions Caucus and co-chair of the Long Island Sound Caucus. He also helped introduce legislation that called for a five-year, $65 million-per-year federal commitment to protecting and restoring Long Island Sound.

“Then came Donald Trump’s rise to power,” the article says.

It notes that Zeldin defended Trump following the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol and voted against certifying the 2020 presidential election results. In 2022, Zeldin ran for governor of New York against Democratic incumbent Kathy Hochul, campaigning heavily on crime.

After becoming EPA administrator, the article says, Zeldin declared that he intended to drive “a dagger straight into the heart of the climate change religion.” The article interprets that statement as a rejection of policies supporting renewable energy and an embrace of fossil fuels.

The EPA has described Zeldin’s agenda differently. When he announced his “Powering the Great American Comeback” initiative in February 2025, Zeldin said its goals included clean air, land and water, restoring American energy dominance, permitting reform, expanding artificial intelligence infrastructure and protecting American auto jobs.

The Sierra Club article concludes by pointing to a symbolic change at EPA headquarters in Washington.

“Once there was a small museum at the EPA’s headquarters in Washington, D.C., on Pennsylvania Avenue, to serve as a tribute to its environmental protection legacy. Zeldin closed it,” the article says.

“The space is now empty,” it continues, calling it “an apt symbol of a hollowed-out agency that no longer follows science or conducts meaningful oversight of potential polluters.”

text:
As deputy administrator of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency during former President Joe Biden’s time in office, Janet McCabe helped work to develop a rule for greenhouse gas requirements for power plants.

Now, she watches as President Donald Trump’s EPA works to dismantle it.

“I understand different administrations have different priorities,” McCabe said. “It is super concerning to see this administration so single-mindedly work to not just weaken the rules to make them easier for industry, but to actually attempt to permanently undermine the federal government’s ability to address these public health threats.”

The EPA’s move is just one taken by federal agencies that leaves environmental and utility experts worried about the environmental, health and economic impact on American citizens.

On Sept. 14, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced the repeal of the majority of Biden era greenhouse gas emissions requirements for power plants, according to a news release.

McCabe said the action wasn’t a surprise, especially after earlier repeals of the Greenhouse Gas Endangerment Finding in February. She added that it’s been consistent with actions taken since Trump came into office last year.

Hana Vizcarra, deputy managing attorney for national climate at Earthjustice, also said she wasn’t surprised by the EPA’s recent action, adding that Trump’s first administration had also prioritized coal, despite it being more costly.

“It’s not just that they’re willing to roll back regulations across the board,” Vizcarra said. “They’re rolling back regulations specifically because doing so is favorable to their favorite industry. At the same time, they’re attacking clean energy and other industries that could provide alternatives.”

Vizcarra also added that the power sector is one of the largest greenhouse gas emitters, and repealing requirements could “significantly increase” severe climate impacts nationwide.

The EPA claims its latest action will save $310 billion. The agency also proposed rescinding every remaining greenhouse gas standard for the power sector, alleging it will save $370 million in direct compliance costs.

“For over 15 years, the Obama and Biden administrations implemented a war on coal to destroy reliable and affordable energy. The Trump Administration has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on,” Zeldin said in a news release. “Americans will see a decrease in electricity prices, but this is just the beginning. We are working to go even further so that American energy can be fully unleashed. Realizing the full potential of American energy means more jobs, lower prices, and a more prosperous America.”

Although Zeldin says the move will lead to lower bills, environmental and energy experts say prioritizing coal has costly results for American ratepayers.

“I’ve heard it for 20 years now,” said Kerwin Olson, executive director of the Citizens Action Coalition. “They blame the regulation on the costs of continuing to operate these power plants. That’s such a short-sighted view from our perspective.”

Wind and solar are now the cheapest forms of energy, Olson said, so to make coal cost-competitive with newer and cleaner technologies, agencies need to roll back regulations.

“It doesn’t make sense,” he added. “It shows an extreme disregard for public health and an extreme disregard for the climate and the sustainability of our planet and our very existence.”

Keeping coal plants open will lead to higher utility bills and more pollution for communities, Olson said. He’s worried about what it means for Northwest Indiana, where ratepayers pay the highest utility bills in the state.

“We passed the Clean Air Act and the Clean Water Act and included a mandate that, as we learn more, through science and through technological developments, that we will continue to improve those standards that are designed to protect human health and the environment,” Olson said. “Rolling back that stuff is counterintuitive to those goals, and again, it just shows a blatant disregard for our environment, for our natural resources and for human health.

McCabe also said she’s concerned about what the new power plant deregulations will mean for Northwest Indiana.

“Historically, it has been an area of our state where people are exposed to a lot of pollution from a lot of different things,” she said. “Prolonging the use of coal plants — which produce so much bad pollution in contrast to renewable energy — is very concerning for the health of the people who live in that community.”

Ashley Williams, executive director of Just Transition Northwest Indiana, said in a statement that the EPA is following the same deregulation playbook they’ve been using, adding that the standards were projected to prevent thousands of premature deaths and hundreds of thousands of asthma attacks nationwide.

Williams also added that the repeal “couldn’t have come at a more urgent time” as artificial intelligence data centers are driving a new wave of gas-fired power plants.

“This repeal affects Indiana more than almost anywhere else in the country because the state has already taken away its ability to respond. State policy bars (the Indiana Department of Environmental Management) from adopting any environmental rule stricter than the federal minimum, so when EPA weakens protections, Indiana often feels it first and worst,” Williams said.

“This fight isn’t over. Environmental groups are going to court to challenge the repeal, and EPA’s supplemental proposal to roll back the remaining rules still has to go through a public comment period. We encourage everyone to keep showing up and speaking out.”

State Rep. Earl Harris, D-East Chicago, said in a statement this week that Hoosiers cannot afford any measures that jeopardize health and the environment.

“This decision will hurt Hoosiers across the board but will disproportionally impact Black Hoosiers and low-come Hoosiers,” Harris said. “A 2026 report found that Black Americans are more likely than their white counterparts to live near coal plants. In 2023, the World Resources Institute found that 45% of Americans living within 30 miles of a coal or energy plant are ‘disadvantaged’ economically. There are countless ways to lower utility rates without sacrificing the health of our vulnerable neighbors.”

Federal court ruling could affect Northwest Indiana plant

In December, the U.S. Department of Energy Secretary Chris Wright issued an emergency order that required NIPSCO’s R.M. Schahfer Generating Station to stay open past its retirement date. The agency renewed the executive order several times, and it is up for renewal again Saturday.

Nick Wallace, senior associate attorney at the Environmental Law and Policy Center, said the cost to keep Schahfer open during the first order was more than $400,000 per day. Combined with the cost to keep a Michigan coal plant running, Midwest ratepayers could pay a total of $1 million per day.

“In total, the bill for these plants is over half a billion dollars,” Wallace said, “and the total is still running.”

On Sept. 11, a U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia found that it was unlawful for the DOE to keep Michigan’s J.H. Campbell Coal Plant online, according to the Indiana Capital Chronicle, determining the department had exceeded the emergency authority granted by the Federal Power Act.

Wallace said the DOE issued the order for Campbell about seven months before the Schahfer announcement. Campbell was scheduled to retire in May 2025.

The ELPC challenged both the Campbell and Schahfer orders in a federal court, as well as an order to keep the F.B. Culley plant running in southwest Indiana. Several other cases have been filed, starting at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, about who pays for the plants and what the total bill will be.

“We think the D.C. circuit’s opinion is really clear that what the (DOE) did in the Campbell case was illegal,” Wallace said, “and the (DOE) did the exact same thing in the Schahfer and Culley cases. We want the (DOE) to follow the law and abide by the court’s order and to stop issuing these unlawful orders.”

Olson was pleased with the court’s Campbell ruling, calling it excellent.

“We certainly believe that laid the foundation to void those emergency orders that were issued for the Indiana coal plants,” Olson said. “I think they would find it challenging to renew that order based on that outcome in the courts.”

Sameer Doshi, senior attorney at Earthjustice, said he hopes the DOE considers the court ruling when looking to renew Schahfer’s order. Doshi said Friday morning that he expected to see a renewal regardless of the court’s finding.

State Rep. Randy Novak, D-Michigan City, said in a statement this week that he “would strongly encourage” Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita to challenge the federal order, citing a NIPSCO request to regulators asking for $38 million from ratepayers in return for compliance with the federal order.

“These new deregulation pushes are ludicrous,” Novak said. “Instead of holding utility companies’ feet to the fire, the Trump and (Gov. Mike) Braun administrations are bailing them out and allowing them to cut costs by endangering the environment and our public health. Now is the time to expect more from companies like NIPSCO, not less.”

In a statement to the Post-Tribune Friday, a DOE spokesperson said the emergency orders were essential during a late January winter storm, saying coal generation in impacted regions increased 25% compared to the same time in 2025. The statement also said Campbell operated at more than 650 megawatts each day between Jan. 21 and Feb. 1.

“The Energy Department’s emergency orders, including at Campbell, prevented blackouts and likely saved hundreds of lives during peak capacity events this past year,” the statement said. “Rest assured, the Department of Energy will continue to protect and defend energy security for all Americans.”

The department did not respond to what impact the ruling might have on the renewal of Schahfer’s order or if it was likely to go through.

NIPSCO responded to the federal ruling in a Friday statement to the Post-Tribune.

“We are reviewing the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit’s decision regarding the Department of Energy’s Section 202(c) order for Consumers Energy,” the statement said. “Our focus remains on serving customers safely and reliably while continuing to comply with applicable legal and regulatory requirements.”

text:
While tech oligarchs grandstand about the existential danger AI superintelligence poses to humanity, former Environmental Protection Agency officials say we should be worried about a more immediate threat to our health: the data centers that power those AI models.

The former EPA researchers, now working with the nonprofit Environmental Protection Network, are warning in a new report that since January 2025, Donald Trump’s EPA has embarked on a systematic weakening of pollution safeguards, permitting processes, inspection norms, and other guardrails — at least 30 different actions — that could increase the health risks associated with the data center boom.

There are currently about 3,000 data centers in the United States, and more than 1,500 new centers are in the planning stages. But as developers build out this vast, energy-hungry infrastructure, the country is losing the government regulatory safeguards that are needed to ensure that expansion is done safely, the ex–EPA officials say.

Dan Costa, who spent 35 years at the EPA studying air pollution, noted that for decades the environmental agency, which was established in 1970, had a large and committed cadre of researchers who investigated emerging sources of pollution and new environmental threats.

“Over the decades, toxicologists, chemists, atmospheric scientists, modelers, and engineers worked in concert with academic colleagues on behalf of the American people — not on behalf of industry,” Costa said in a press briefing last week. “We wanted to carry out EPA’s mission of protecting people’s health from industrial air pollution.”

Now, though, that workforce has been gutted. The Trump administration has dismantled EPA’s main research office, and the agency’s priorities have shifted away from strict enforcement of pollution standards. “Transforming the nation’s energy system, while diminishing its scientific capacity to understand what the impacts are going to be, makes no sense,” Costa said.

But that appears to be the direction the country is heading in. President Donald Trump is “positioning America as the global leader in AI,” EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin wrote in a memo last year. The agency is “committed to bolstering” those efforts, Zeldin said, by “cutting heavy-handed regulations to ensure America can build and power the data centers essential to Making America the AI Capital of the World.”

Since Trump returned to the White House, data center developers have seized the opportunity to expand at a rapid pace, helped by the administration’s moves. In some cases, that deregulation has involved keeping old coal-fired plants online past their planned decommissioning times in order to power data centers; other times, it has meant easing regulations on the use of onsite fossil fuel-powered turbines to power hyperscale data centers like xAI’s Colossus.

The agency has proposed a rule change that would let developers begin constructing data centers and their associated power plants before they get air pollution permits. And it has directed the agency’s enforcement staff to avoid any action that could “unduly burden or significantly disrupt” energy production or power generation.

According to one study the former EPA researchers cited in their new report, pollution associated with the AI boom may lead to 1,300 additional deaths per year.

Physician and former EPA administrative official Lynn Goldman said some health impacts of increased data center pollution might be felt quickly — for example, heart attacks or premature births associated with particulate exposure. Others, such as cancer, might take years to emerge. “The AI industry’s race for advantage should not be a matter of life or death,” Goldman said at the press conference. “Families shouldn’t have to pay for the AI boom with their health.”

text:
NAIROBI, Kenya -- Egypt is betting that building wind turbines at home can help it build a renewable-energy industry, positioning it as a template for Africa's push for renewable-energy industrialization.

The country signed a deal with China's SANY Renewable Energy to develop a 2,000-megawatt wind project in the Gulf of Suez alongside Egypt's first wind turbine manufacturing plant. The project is expected to connect to the national grid within 23 months of final agreements, while the factory is intended to supply Egypt and potentially export equipment across Africa and the Middle East.

Even though Egypt's project is still in its early stages, energy experts say its emphasis on scale, local manufacturing and technology transfer could offer lessons for other African countries struggling to turn renewable-energy ambitions into functioning infrastructure.

That includes a project in Nigeria, where a 10-megawatt wind farm took nearly two decades to begin producing electricity. The difference highlights a broader challenge for Africa's renewable-energy push: how to move beyond importing equipment and announcing projects to building the financing, industrial capacity and policy stability needed to deliver them at scale.

"The contrasts are stark," said Fadhel Kaboub, an associate professor of economics at Denison University in Ohio. "We have a project in Nigeria that took two decades to come online, whereas we have this one project in Egypt that looks like it's going to really take off."

Kaboub cautioned that Egypt's deal is not yet proof of success. But its combination of scale, manufacturing and a Chinese technology partner could give it a better chance of attracting investment and coming to fruition quickly, he said.

"For manufacturing anything to be profitable, efficient and successful, you need economies of scale," he said. "The problem with every African country is that our internal markets are too small. We don't have the economies of scale to industrialize one country at a time."

Egypt's plan is part of a broader effort to localize renewable energy technology, increase local content, and leverage the country's trade links to export equipment. The government has said the factory will help reduce reliance on imported equipment while building an industrial base around renewable energy.

That ambition comes with risks.

Kaboub said Egypt needs to ensure that cooperation with SANY results in meaningful technology transfer rather than simply creating another form of dependence on foreign manufacturers.

"If the Chinese partner fully retains control over the technology and there's really no transfer of technology, then we're looking at another cycle of dependence," he said.

Nigeria's experience illustrates how project design can be as important as the technology itself.

The 10-megawatt Lambar Rimi wind farm in Katsina state was contracted to the French wind turbine manufacturer Vergnet in 2010, with completion scheduled for 2012. The project was funded by the Japan International Cooperation Agency and was designed to use 37 turbines rated at 275 kilowatts each.

The project stalled for years before being taken over by the Katsina state government. It was eventually commissioned in September 2025 after the state added 10 megawatts of solar capacity.

Dola Oluteye, founder of the PATNA Initiative and a senior fellow in energy and transport policy at University College London's Bartlett School of Environment, Energy and Resources, said the comparison should not be framed simply as Nigeria's failure versus Egypt's success.

"The useful question is what Egypt has built into its project structure that Nigeria left unresolved for years," Oluteye said. "The cost of capital is the binding constraint, not the resource."

The International Energy Agency says the cost of capital for utility-scale clean-energy projects in Africa is at least two to three times higher than in advanced economies and China. Africa attracts around 2% of global clean-energy spending despite accounting for about one-fifth of the world's population.

Oluteye said Egypt's decision to structure the new wind project in local currency is particularly significant because it reduces the currency mismatch that can undermine African power projects that are financed in dollars but earn revenue in local currencies.

The industrial component could also change the economics and politics of future projects.

"While Nigeria purchased 37 turbines, Egypt is attempting to buy the capability to make them," Oluteye said.

African countries could use their collective market to negotiate better terms from technology providers, including requirements for local manufacturing and technology transfer.

"If we form a negotiating bloc with a joint industrial policy, we can probably get better terms for technology transfer and joint ventures that could transform the continent at scale," Kaboub said.

For Nigeria, the challenge is therefore not simply finding more wind.

"If something is new, especially in Africa, you want to pilot it first," Kaboub said, adding that stronger feasibility studies, affordable financing, clearer project ownership and policy continuity are critical.

"The implementation of policy is what is critical, not the fact that you have 50 policies on your website or in your government documents," he said.
