text:
By Molly Peterson

The burned remains of the Moss Landing Power Plant battery energy storage facility caught fire again Friday morning, prompting Monterey County officials to issue a shelter in place order — less than two years after it became one of the largest battery storage facility fires in history.

Workers for Vistra, the plant’s Texas-based operator, noticed a flare-up early Friday morning against the wall of a building that burned in the initial January 2025 fire. The cause: roughly 1,500 inaccessible battery modules, still charged, spontaneously ignited, said Chief Jess Cortez with the North County Fire Protection District.

“They’re in the smoldering stage right now,” Cortez said at a briefing Friday afternoon, adding that at that point there was no active fire. “The incident is very dynamic. There could be possible flare-ups.”

Local authorities lifted the order to shelter in place later Friday afternoon. Still, the flare-up reignites fears about battery storage facilities — even as California comes to increasingly rely on them. The state now has “the nation’s largest battery energy storage fleet,” the California Energy Commission announced in August.

“If we had only known the worst-case scenarios of how not to build batteries, we wouldn’t have built Moss Landing,” said Dustin Mulvaney, a professor at San Jose State University in the school of planning, policy and environmental studies. “Because it keeps coming back to haunt us.”

The incident also sharpens the tension between Gov. Gavin Newsom’s push to shortcut permitting for energy and other projects, and the communities hosting these facilities.

Fire, rekindled

In January 2025, residents from across the Monterey Bay area watched large plumes of smoke and ash spewing from Vistra’s 300-megawatt battery energy storage facility at the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County.

It was the facility’s fourth safety incident, the third on the Vistra property, since 2019, according to a letter Assemblymember Dawn Addis, a San Luis Obispo Democrat who represents Moss Landing and parts of Santa Cruz County, sent state regulators last year. The fire continued for days before crews could control it, then rekindled briefly a month later.

Newsom called for a state investigation. The California Public Utilities Commission began with a site visit that month.

Nearly two years later, that investigation is ongoing, with a root cause analysis underway in coordination with Vistra and an independent consultant, said Terrie Prosper, a spokesperson with the Public Utilities Commission.

Monterey County Supervisor Glenn Church expressed frustration about the delay.

“Why it takes a year and a half to come up with an answer when everything is just about near the end of being cleaned up, I don’t know,” he said.

Before the state approves any more of these facilities, he said, “it’s a good idea to know what’s causing these fires.”

Safety rules, too late

Unlike facilities built more recently, the Moss Landing site was built in an enclosed, aging building with older battery technologies crammed closely together — allowing fires to spread quickly, Mulvaney said.

Denise Grab, the Clean Energy Law & Leadership project director for the Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, agreed: The site is “one of the earlier battery storage facilities in the state and in the country, even. And the design is not up to par with current safety designs.”

Battery plants still carry less overfall harm than fossil fuel plants, Grab added.

“There are risks from other types of energy generation as well, particularly fossil fuel,” Grab said. “Asthma, premature death, heart attacks, lung disease from fossil fuel plants is significant, and (battery plants pose) a different kind of risk.”

California passed a series of safety laws both before and after the January 2025 fire, including several laws from state Sen. John Laird, a Santa Cruz Democrat, aimed at better planning for — and preventing — fires.

A 2022 law by then-Sen. Ben Hueso required the California Public Utilities Commission to set new standards for battery storage facilities and boost oversight of their emergency plans. But the commission didn’t bring its proposal for implementing Hueso’s law to a vote until after last year’s Vistra fire.

“We should have never built Moss Landing the way we did,” Mulvaney said. “We were too late with coming up with the standards and certifications, which make batteries much safer today.”

Environmental health controversy

Vistra says that the cause of last year’s fire is still unknown. The energy company commissioned a study finding that chemical concentrations in nearby soil or water posed no risk to humans or the environment.

“As a result, no further human health or ecological risk evaluation related to the (Moss Landing fire) event is warranted,” the report read.

But scientists’ findings and resident accounts suggest otherwise. As the fire blazed for days in January 2025, residents reported wheezing, coughing, headaches and eye irritation.

Researchers presented additional findings at a symposium last month, including evidence from one UC Santa Cruz researcher of elevated exposure to battery-related materials in hair samples.

Scientists with the San Jose State University’s Moss Landing Marine Laboratories have found high levels of nickel, manganese and cobalt in soil around the facility. Ivano Aiello, the scientist who led the study, said Vistra’s recent report examined potential contaminants months after the fire was contained.

The long-term health impacts of potential exposure remain unclear, and researchers continue studying the incident.

Richard Stedman, an air pollution control officer with the Monterey Bay Air Resources District, said regulators placed four monitors at the fence line around the Vistra facility, and two more nearby: None detected unhealthy levels of particulate matter as of Friday’s briefing.

Brian Roeder, founder of the community group Never Again Moss Landing, said the public’s trust in regulators and politicians who are meant to protect them continues to erode.

“We’ve had 20 months to prepare for this,” he said. “Here we are again, right back where we were before, knowing this could happen.”

SALISBURY — A statewide program that has certified more than 1,600 environmental educators is finding a new home at Catawba College.

The North Carolina Environmental Education Certification Program will move from the N.C. Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) to Catawba’s Center for the Environment on Oct. 1.

According to a release from the Salisbury-based college, the transition will “preserve the certification program, its staff, and all the programs and resources that connect educators across the state.” That also includes the listserv and calendar.

“We ask our students to consider their stewardship as citizens, about how they can serve others,” said Catawba President David P. Nelson in the release. “We ask the same questions of the college. This program has served our state well, and we are glad to respond to this opportunity to serve the people of North Carolina by carrying on this important work.”

The certification program is part of a broader state environmental education effort that began in the early 1990s. Since the state’s July budget decision, environmental educators, classroom teachers and program partners have expressed support for continuing the work at another institution.

Lee Ball, executive director of the Center for the Environment, and staff from DEQ’s Office of Environmental Education and Public Affairs announced the transition at the 35th annual conference of Environmental Educators of North Carolina, the state’s nonprofit professional association for environmental educators. The announcement drew a standing ovation.

“This transition will extend the center’s work in environmental education and create opportunities for our students to learn from and work with educators serving communities across North Carolina,” Ball said.

DEQ Secretary Reid Wilson added, “The Environmental Education program has been a resounding success for 30 years, awarding Environmental Education Certificates to more than 1,600 people. Educating children about the natural world and their role in protecting it is more essential than ever. The Center for the Environment at Catawba College deserves a huge thanks for taking on the leadership of the program in the wake of the new state budget’s removal of its funding.”

Lisa Tolley, program manager for the environmental education program at DEQ, thanked Ball, the Center, Catawba College, Wilson, the leadership of Environmental Educators of North Carolina and the statewide community of educators for supporting the transition.

“This transition preserves North Carolina’s environmental education legacy and allows an important statewide career-development and community-building resource to continue,” Tolley said.

Marty Wiggins, program consultant for the environmental education program, said the certification program will continue to serve the entire state.

“Our plan is to make a seamless transition to the Center for the Environment,” Wiggins said. “All of the resources that support the program, such as the NCEE listserv and calendar, will continue to be an integral part of the certification program.”

Details of the Oct. 1 transition are still being finalized. Certification participants and educators who use the program’s resources are not expected to experience delays or interruptions in access.

text:
The Environmental Protection Agency moved to scrap most of the Biden administration's climate rules for power plants and signaled that it intends to eliminate the rest as well, Utility Dive reported.

The decision will slow efforts to cut pollution from power plants and raises fresh concerns for communities already shouldering the health and economic impacts of a warming planet.

Here's what to know

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin indicated that the agency completed its repeal of most parts of the 2024 carbon-pollution rule for fossil fuel power plants and is separately seeking to rescind the greenhouse gas standards that still apply to the sector.

In explaining the action, the EPA argued that the Clean Air Act does not authorize it to regulate power-plant greenhouse gas emissions to address climate change.

The agency claimed that position was supported by the Trump administration's reversal of the landmark 2009 Endangerment Finding and by the Supreme Court's Loper Bright ruling.

NASA explained that "human activities (primarily the human burning of fossil fuels) have warmed Earth's surface and its ocean basins, which in turn have continued to impact Earth's climate."

The repeal of the 2024 standards will take effect 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

The EPA plans to hold a public hearing and open a 45-day public comment period on its broader proposal.

More background

Power plants remain a major source of climate pollution, and federal limits were intended to advance the sector toward cleaner energy generation over time.

Weakening those standards makes it harder to reduce the emissions that contribute to worsening heat, wildfire conditions, flooding, and other impacts that typically hit families and local governments first.

Supporters of the rollback argued that the previous rules were too costly and unrealistic.

"In regard to EPA's new proposed rule, we strongly believe that regulatory certainty is helpful as we plan for long-term investments that support grid reliability," said Rachael Marsh, chief legal officer at the Edison Electric Institute.

"We will continue partnering with EPA on a durable and achievable regulatory framework that is cost effective for customers and supports the investments needed to meet growing electricity demand."

Jim Matheson, CEO of the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association, called the Biden-era limits "unlawful, unrealistic and unachievable."

Michelle Bloodworth, CEO of America's Power, asserted that the rules effectively gave electricity providers a choice between closing coal plants by 2032 or trying to meet carbon requirements through carbon capture and storage, which she felt was too costly and insufficiently proven.

Opponents, however, warned that those arguments ignored the public costs of increased pollution and delayed climate action.

For communities near fossil fuel infrastructure or already coping with extreme weather, fewer safeguards mean greater risks over time, even if utilities gain short-term flexibility.

What's being done?

Former EPA veterans, environmental groups, and state and local officials are already organizing opposition, and some have indicated they intend to challenge the rollback in court.

"We've fought every one of these reckless rollbacks, and we're ready to sue again now to protect our health and safety," Connecticut Attorney General William Tong vowed.

Climate Mayors Executive Director Kate Wright also criticized the move.

Utilities, regulators, cities, and advocacy groups are now likely to keep battling over what a "durable and achievable" power-sector framework should look like — and who bears the cost when climate protections are removed.

"EPA has a responsibility to work alongside local leaders to protect Americans' health, not eliminate the safeguards that protect families from deadly toxins," Wright noted.

"While mayors continue to advance local initiatives to protect residents, the EPA is moving backwards."

Where can I learn more?

These articles cover court rulings, federal mandates, and regional policies shaping power-plant and energy rules.

• A federal court let Biden's coal-plant emissions rules stay in place while challenges moved forward.

• The Supreme Court declined to block the EPA's new power-plant mandate for coal and gas facilities.

• EPA under Lee Zeldin moved toward repealing coal and oil standards, alarming health advocates.

text:
WESTFIELD, Mass. (WWLP) – A large majority of respondents to a recent WWLP.com poll said they are concerned about the environmental impact of data centers, reflecting growing public debate as Westfield officials continue reviewing a proposed data center campus.

The poll asked readers, “Are you concerned about the environmental impact of data centers?” Of those who responded, 85% said yes, while 15% said no.

The results generated hundreds of comments on Facebook, where community members shared a wide range of opinions about the benefits and drawbacks of large-scale data center developments.

Many commenters expressed concerns about water consumption, energy use, noise pollution and the potential strain on local infrastructure. Others questioned whether communities fully understand the long-term environmental effects associated with large data facilities.

“Everyone should be concerned,” one commenter wrote, while another argues that data centers could increase utility costs and place additional pressure on local resources.

Several residents pointed to Westfield’s ongoing discussions surrounding a proposed data center development, saying the project has heightened awareness about environmental issued and quality-of-life concerns.

Others defended data centers, arguing that modern facilities use advanced cooling temperatures and that environmental impacts can be mitigated through regulations and engineering solutions.

“Nothing about a data center can’t be mitigated via regulations and good engineering,” commenter Rich DiMascio write.

Supporters also highlighted the economic benefits that data centers can bring, including construction jobs, tax revenue and investment in local communities. Some commenters said data centers are essential infrastructure as demand for artificial intelligence, cloud computing and online services continues to grow,

The discussion comes as the proposed data center campus in Westfield remains under consideration. Earlier this week, the Westfield Planning Board reviewed a request from developer Servistar Realties LLC to extend its special permit for the project.

According to the developer, the facility would use a closed-loop cooling system designed to minimize water use and would operate independently from the Westfield Gas and Electric system. The company has also stated that the project is not intended to function as an artificial intelligence facility.

Meanwhile, members of the Westfield City Council’s Natural Resources Committee have announced plans to host public meetings with experts from Boston University and UMass Amherst to help residents better understand issues related to water usage, air quality, noise pollution and energy consumption.

text:
Gov. Abigail Spanberger on Friday unveiled a package of legislative proposals to rein in the data center industry in Virginia, with goals to tighten environmental regulations, increase cost allocation for the industry, and make the proposal process more transparent by barring non-disclosure agreements between localities and data center developers.

The plan does not include a moratorium on data center development while the details of the plan are refined, a step several environmental and advocacy groups and citizens have demanded in recent weeks.

Dubbed the “Data Center Accountability Framework,” Spanberger’s plan outlines five pillars as key priorities: transparency, environmental protections, lowering energy costs, promoting clean energy, and focusing on local workers.

“The Framework is a thorough plan to end data center secrecy, protect our environment, lower energy costs for families, bolster our clean energy economy, and make sure Virginia workers have the protections and assurances they deserve,” Spanberger said in a press conference to announce the plan at the Virginia State Capitol.

Spanberger also signed Executive Order 22, which will kick-start her plans for clamping down on the industry ahead of the next legislative session that will begin in January 2027.

Transparency

Perhaps the most concrete of the directives is a measure to ban nondisclosure agreements between data centers and executive branch agencies, departments, state boards and commissions. It also bars these agencies from requiring such agreements for data center projects.

The order does not impact the use of nondisclosure agreements by localities, but the governor said she plans to work with the General Assembly to pass a law banning the agreements at the local level.

In the framework package, the governor also proposes eliminating by-right local approvals of data centers that use more than 25 megawatts of power.

Many counties statewide have taken steps towards requiring conditional use permits,which require public hearings and a vote of approval from local leaders.

Additionally, the governor wants to remove data centers from Virginia’s fast-track permitting process that allows permit approvals for the projects to speed up when they are proposed in “business ready” locations.

The fast-track process is a remnant of Gov. GlennYoungkin’s administration, which encouraged and supported the rapid build out of the state’s data center industry as a means to boost Virginia’s business reputation.

Environmental protections

The framework directs lawmakers to develop policies to create standards for energy efficiency, water use and land impacts.

Budget language that passed the General Assembly in June directed the Department of Environmental Quality to identify “water scarcity areas,” data centers’ water use for cooling could put drinking water availability at risk. Data centers located in those areas, mainly east of Interstate-95, will have to reduce their water use.

The framework also outlines a plan to expedite noise regulations that were also in the budget language, but does not state when those regulations will be put into place. Currently, DEQ has until 2029 to research the lowest possible sound levels data centers could operate on and make that the standard across the board.

Lower energy costs

Spanberger’s new data center plan requires utilities to allocate more of the energy infrastructure costs largely spurred by data centers onto the industry.

Dominion Energy has already taken action on this front, after the utility created a new rate class, GS5, which mostly includes data centers and large manufacturers. The State Corporation Commission approved the new rate class last November.

Like the recommendations in the framework from the governor, the G5 rate class includes 14-year contracts, as well as specific cost allocations for energy generation, distribution, and transmission costs.

The SCC also recently directed Dominion to create a new tariff to directly assign the cost of high-voltage transmission lines that are only necessary due to data centers to those customers. Spanberger supported the tariff, which is reflected in her framework.

Tech giant Microsoft has already put the State Supreme Court on notice that it could appeal that order.

Microsoft representatives said in an email last week that the company hopes “any rates ultimately put in place are transparent, fair, and reflect the costs each customer creates.”

But filing notice of appeal, they continued, “Microsoft preserves its ability to challenge any implementation that does not meet these expectations.”

Elevating clean energy, hiring Virginia workers

Another component of Spanberger’s plan looks to limit the amount of power data centers can produce on-site through natural gas generators and other “behind the meter” methods that don’t draw from the electric grid.

The plan also proposes making it easier for data centers to bring clean energy options on-site by reforming utility charges for clean energy investments.

PJM, the regional grid operator for 13 states including Virginia, recently proposed a new rule to direct data centers to pay for their power generation or cover their energy needs by backstop power purchases. This would help bring more power on the grid when it’s strained on very hot and cold days.

Several recent proposals by data centers in the commonwealth show the industry’s growing interest in building its own gas turbines to power data facilities. That method skirts around the Virginia Clean Economy Act, which requires the retirement of carbon emitting power sources by utility companies by 2050.

The framework prioritizes hiring local workers to build data centers and using local businesses for procurement and contractors.

Lawmakers, environmental groups, data centers react

A slate of state legislators spoke up in support of Spanberger’s framework Friday afternoon, sentiments shared by some environmental groups.

“Governor Spanberger’s Data Center Accountability Framework is a step in the right direction,” a statement by the Virginia House Democratic Caucus read. “We look forward to continuing to work with Governor Spanberger in the upcoming 2027 legislative session to develop thoughtful legislation that holds data centers accountable.”

Many of these policies require legislative action from the General Assembly to take effect. Also many of the proposals are prospective, meaning they will apply to new data center applications rather than the more than 600 data centers that are already operating or being built statewide.

“For those that are up and running and already operating, we have the ability and intention to continue to make sure that into the future we are holding them to greater and greater standards,” Spanberger said.

Representatives from the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, Sierra Club, and League of Conservation Voters joined Spanberger for the announcement and called it a strong first step towards enacting legislation to cement the framework’s goals.

Other organizations were critical of the framework because it didn’t include an outright pause on data center development.

“It does not address the continued connection of data centers to the grid, despite inadequate power and the many impacts on air quality, water supply, electric bills, and people and communities,” the Piedmont Environmental Council said in a statement. “Not to mention the hundreds of miles of proposed transmission lines, solely to support data centers.”

“We must stop the madness and issue an immediate pause on approvals until these protections – and more – are fully implemented,” Chesapeake Climate Action Network Director Victoria Higgins said in response to the framework.

The Data Center Coalition, the leading national group that lobbies for the industry, said they are waiting for more details on the plan.

“(We) are ready to engage with policymakers to ensure workable, balanced policies that keep Virginia competitive and honor prior commitments by the Commonwealth and its localities,” coalition representative Nicole Riley said.

Spanberger didn’t answer directly when asked why she did not impose a data center development moratorium while her package is considered before lawmakers. She reiterated that some Virginia localities are considering pausing data center development.

“While (localities are) looking at what’s available to them as a potential option, it is up to our communities… But the state has to show leadership,” Spanberger said. “We are in a place where day by day, community members are demanding action.”

The framework, she added, “is an opportunity for us to take action and ensure that we are moving forward.”

The Allegheny Valley School District has received a $300,000 Solar for Schools grant through Pennsylvania’s state grant program. The funds will support the installation of a new solar energy system at Acmetonia Elementary School.

text:
Charging an EV in the U.S. still involves too much fumbling with QR codes and credit cards. Red E Charge is trying to cut that out. The Detroit-based operator has turned on Plug & Charge at a good chunk of its stalls, so drivers can walk up, plug in, and let the payment sort itself out. It's calling the new service Red E Go.

The catch, as always, is the setup. Drivers complete a one-time configuration in the network's smartphone app, entering vehicle details and a payment method. After that, the phone and the wallet can stay in the car. No app to open, no card to swipe, no code to scan at compatible stations. Red E is calling the feature Red E Go, and it's live at select locations rather than the whole footprint.

That footprint isn't small. The numbers come from the Department of Energy's Alternative Fuels Data Center. Red E runs more than 1,500 sites and about 4,600 ports in 46 states. Of those, 2,159 ports are fast chargers spread across 579 stations, while 600 locations also offer nearly 2,500 Level 2 ports.

The more interesting story is momentum. A Paren report pegged Red E as the No. 4 network for DC fast charging growth nationwide during the second quarter. Its 315 new ports put it behind Tesla, Walmart, and ChargePoint, but ahead of Electrify America, EVgo, and Ionna. For a name most drivers couldn't pick out of a lineup, that's a real result.

Customers reportedly like it, too. Red E ranked fifth in JD Power's latest Electric Vehicle Experience (EVX) Public Charging Study, trailing Ionna, the Mercedes-Benz Charging Network, the Rivian Adventure Network, and Tesla's Supercharger network. Its 628 points on the 1,000-point scale sat just under the 666-point segment average, but still topped Electrify America, EVgo, and ChargePoint.

Stall output ranges from a plodding 10 kW to a genuinely quick 640 kW depending on location and plug type. The network supports J1772, CCS1, NACS, and CHAdeMO, with pricing from $0.40 to $1.15 per kWh, according to DCFC Tracker.

“Battery storage is not an option for Pakistan. It is a core component of our energy security,” Muhammad Imran, Pakistan’s Trade and Investment Counsellor in Guangzhou, told an audience in Shenzhen.

He was delivering a keynote speech titled “Unlocking Opportunities in Pakistan’s Energy Storage Market” at the 2026 New Energy Storage Digital Intelligence, Safety & High-Quality Development Forum, Gwadar Pro reported.

He noted that Pakistan has set a national target to raise the share of clean energy in its electricity mix to 90 percent by 2035.

The forum was a sideline of the 2026 International Digital Energy Exhibition, held at the Shenzhen Convention and Exhibition Center from Sept 15 to 17 and co-launched with the 2026 Energy Green Development Conference.

Spanning more than 50,000 square meters, the event brought together participants from over 50 countries and regions and nearly 400 overseas enterprises, showcasing nearly 100 digital energy innovations.

The counsellor’s message reflects Pakistan’s energy reality. According to Pakistan’s Ministry of Energy, clean energy sources including hydropower, nuclear, wind and solar account for approximately 55 percent of the country’s electricity generation, while nearly 38 gigawatts of distributed solar have been installed through consumer-led investment.

Federal Minister for Energy Sardar Awais Ahmad Khan Leghari has said battery storage is essential to shift surplus daytime solar power to peak hours and reduce reliance on imported fuels.

To support this, Pakistan has proposed the National Lithium-Ion Battery Manufacturing Policy 2026-2031, which sets out phased localization targets, tariff reforms and performance-based incentives to encourage manufacturing and private sector investment.

Pakistan’s cooperation with China is already moving forward, with partnerships taking shape between the two countries.

text:
The state of California has awarded $44 million for 15 projects, including funding for a tribal organization to acquire 80 acres in Lake County for Indigenous-led ecological restoration, cultural programs and job training.

The Tribal EcoRestoration Alliance will acquire the Politsuwi property, located on the ancestral lands of the Robinson Rancheria, Scotts Valley Band of Pomo Indians and Habematolel Pomo of Upper Lake. The property will expand the adjacent EcoCultural Stewardship Training and Demonstration Center and protect oak woodlands, wetlands and wildlife habitat.

The awards, announced by Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office, were made through the California Wildlife Conservation Board and included $32 million from the voter‑approved 2024 Climate Bond. The funded projects span 11 counties and support the state’s goal of conserving 30% of its lands and coastal waters by 2023.

“These investments are about standing with tribes and communities, restoring the ecosystems we all depend on, and protecting the natural heritage of generations to come,” Newsom said in a statement.

Other awards include $11.5 million for The Wildlands Conservancy to acquire about 14,177 acres in Siskiyou County to expand the Beaver Valley Headwaters Preserve and protect salmon and steelhead habitat. The project connects more than 20,000 acres of mountain meadows, rivers, and forest habitat to protect Scott River salmon and steelhead runs, secure streamflow, and provide future wildlife-oriented public access.

The Tahoe Resource Conservation District received $4 million to restore 79 acres of meadow along the Upper Truckee River, Lake Tahoe’s largest tributary. Mojave Desert Land Trust received $7.5 million to acquire about 1,093 acres near Yucca Grove, permanently conserving habitat for the Mojave desert tortoise, Joshua tree woodlands and desert washes.

California says its tribal conservation programs have awarded more than $200 million toward returning more than 100,000 acres to Native American tribes in California.

text:
Gov. Abigail Spanberger, derided during Virginia budget talks earlier this year as a “data center diva” by state Sen. L. Louise Lucas, announced Friday what she called the most comprehensive and aggressive data center accountability effort in the nation.

Spanberger, in a Richmond news conference, said her Data Center Accountability Framework will give communities transparent information and a voice in local approval, protect Virginians from higher energy bills, and enforce the country’s strongest environmental standards for data centers, which have been proposed all around the Fredericksburg area.

The Democratic governor also signed Executive Order 22, which her office said immediately puts many of the framework’s core pieces into action, and created a Virginia AI Task Force to address growing concerns and risks posed by the rise of artificial intelligence.

Spanberger’s plan includes proposed legislation for the 2027 General Assembly session.

She said the legislature has done a lot to raise issues about data centers in the past few months, and that she looks forward to working with them to codify parts of her reforms into Virginia law.

“At the end of the day, we all want the same thing: We want Virginia to be a national leader in data center accountability,” Spanberger said.

The comments seemed to contrast with recent months in Richmond, when the governor’s office, House of Delegates and state Senate clashed over data center tax breaks even though Democrats control all three.

It was during that fight that Lucas, the Senate president pro tempore and Spanberger’s fellow Democrat, called the governor a “data center diva” for pushing to continue tax incentives.

Spanberger said Friday that the data center industry has expanded rapidly without a strong plan to address impacts on Virginians’ electric bills, water, land, air or quality of life.

“These impacts are not hypothetical or far off into the future,” the governor said. “Virginians are feeling them right now, day in and day out — which is why the need for action is urgent, and why the state must lead with a clear, detailed and comprehensive plan.”

She said her reforms are organized around five core requirements: increasing transparency, strengthening environmental protections, lowering energy costs, bolstering the state’s clean energy economy and delivering a better deal for Virginia workers.

In terms of transparency, her plan would ban nondisclosure agreements for commercial projects.The executive order already bars state agencies from signing them. Her plan also would eliminate by-right approval and require local approval for any data center using more than 25 megawatts of power, regardless of prior project approvals.

On environmental protections, Spanberger said her Accountability Framework has several new, higher standards for emissions, water use, noise pollution and land use. It would require existing and future data centers to move to cleaner backup generators, Tier IV or better.

In terms of lowering energy costs, the framework would require utilities to allocate a more equitable share of transmission and generation costs to data centers and other large customers. The executive order also directs the state’s chief energy officer to push utilities, the State Corporation Commission and PJM Interconnection, the nation’s largest grid operator, to shield households from infrastructure costs driven by data centers.

“Virginia families and small businesses should not foot the bill for the data center industry,” Spanberger said. “It is no exaggeration to say a lot of these companies are among the biggest and the wealthiest corporations in the world. And they will pay their fair share.”

Regarding the clean energy economy, Virginia’s chief executive said the state will prioritize grid access for data centers that source clean energy five years sooner than the Virginia Clean Economy Act requires, reduce emissions from their backup generators by 60% and have at most a minimal allowance for on-site natural gas generation. Operators that receive priority access and then fail to comply would pay double the state’s electricity consumption tax, according to the framework.

The framework also would limit the electricity data centers can generate from on-site natural gas to the maximum extent practicable.

Finally, Spanberger said her framework prioritizes the training and hiring of local workers, both for construction and long-term employment.

The state also will stop offering assistance through the Virginia Business Ready Sites Program and expedited permitting programs to new data center projects expected to draw 25 megawatts or more of peak power, according to the executive order.

“This was a loophole,” she said, “and we are changing that policy today.”

The AI Task Force created by Spanberger’s executive order will be led by Dave Wilkinson, Virginia’s chief transformation officer; Matt McGuire, counsel to the governor; and Traci DeShazor, secretary of administration, she said.

It will work to develop policy and legislative proposals to address and regulate several of the risks posed by AI, including workforce displacement, data privacy and cybersecurity.

In a statement Friday afternoon, the Data Center Coalition, the membership association for the data center industry, said it awaits further details about how Spanberger’s policy goals will be implemented.

“The Data Center Coalition and its members share Gov. Spanberger’s goals of ensuring that Virginia can compete for the significant economic opportunities presented by responsible data center development while protecting the interests of residents, communities and ratepayers across the Commonwealth,” Nicole Riley, director of Virginia government affairs for the coalition, said in the statement.

If done right, Riley said, there is a path for continued job creation, responsible investment and clean energy deployment that protects ratepayers and delivers benefits for families and communities.

“However, significant and abrupt policy changes without meaningful stakeholder engagement could prove unworkable and jeopardize the real tangible benefits this industry can create,” she said. “We hope the implementation of this process will be based in fact and evidence, and account for the tens of thousands of jobs and billions of dollars of economic activity connected to digital infrastructure.”

Riley said Virginia’s electric rates are below the national average and other states in the region, and that “numerous studies have found that data centers pay their full cost for electric service without driving up residential bills.”

“The governor, legislature and State Corporation Commission have taken actions and adopted policies to ensure data centers continue to pay their own way and that residential ratepayers continue to be protected moving forward.”

She also said data centers’ water use is about 0.5% of state withdrawals, and that backup generator emissions are only a fraction of what is allowed.

“Data centers take compliance and accountability seriously, building only where and operating only how they are authorized to do so under local, state, and federal rules and regulations,” she said. “Our members will continue to work with communities, local officials and policymakers across Virginia to ensure the sustainable use of water, energy and other natural resources, while promoting the responsible development of this important 21st-century industry.”

At the federal level

Spanberger’s announcement Friday came two days after Rep. Eugene Vindman, D-Va., said he supported recent federal data center legislation.

Vindman, whose 7th Congressional District includes the Fredericksburg area, joined Reps. Kristen McDonald Rivet, D-Mich., and Don Davis, D-N.C., as an original co-sponsor of the Reverse Big Ugly Tax Breaks for Data Centers Act, H.R. 10448, his office said Wednesday.

The bill would bar data centers that draw more than 50 megawatts from claiming bonus depreciation or Opportunity Zone tax benefits on their property, according to its text. Vindman’s office called the breaks unfair and said Republicans expanded them last year in H.R. 1, the federal tax and spending law.

“It is past time we make data centers pay their fair share,” the Democrat said in a prepared statement. “Across Virginia, families and businesses are being forced to foot the bill for massive infrastructure investments needed to power large data centers.”

Vindman also voted Wednesday in favor of H.R. 9340, the Ratepayer Protection Act, legislation he said was aimed at protecting families and businesses from the costs of infrastructure upgrades needed to accommodate the rapidly growing energy demands of large data centers. The bill, sponsored by Rep. Gabe Evans, R-Colo., would have state utility commissions consider standards requiring data centers that draw more than 100 megawatts to pay the full incremental cost of serving them.

title: Ford Recalls Mustang Mach-E Because A Battery Repair Can Make Things Worse
description:
There are few things an EV driver needs to trust more than the little number telling them how much battery is left.
Unfortunately, 86 Ford Mustang Mach-E owners may have discovered an unusually creative way for that number to lie.
Ford is recalling certain 2023-2025 Mustang Mach-Es equipped with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries after discovering an issue involving replacement Battery Energy Control Modules, or BECMs.
Read: Ford Recalls 288,000 Explorers Because The Roof Trim Keeps Flying Off The problem is almost comically simple.
Ford says the incorrect State of Health calculation may increase lithium plating within the battery cells as DC fast-charging cycles accumulate.
text:
There are few things an EV driver needs to trust more than the little number telling them how much battery is left. Unfortunately, 86 Ford Mustang Mach-E owners may have discovered an unusually creative way for that number to lie. Ironically, the problem only exists because their cars were previously repaired.

Ford is recalling certain 2023-2025 Mustang Mach-Es equipped with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries after discovering an issue involving replacement Battery Energy Control Modules, or BECMs. According to the automaker, every one of the 86 vehicles included in the recall is estimated to have the defect.

Read: Ford Recalls 288,000 Explorers Because The Roof Trim Keeps Flying Off

The problem is almost comically simple. When a replacement BECM was installed, it initialized the battery’s State of Health at a fresh-from-the-factory 100 percent instead of inheriting the actual State of Health from the battery already in the vehicle. That’s considerably more consequential than simply being off by a percentage or two.

Since the car believes its battery is healthier than it really is, Ford says it can also display an artificially high State of Charge on the instrument cluster. In other words, the Mach-E can tell its driver that there’s more juice in the tank than there actually is. That discrepancy can eventually cause unexpected power limitation and ultimately a complete loss of motive power. Drivers may see a wrench or turtle warning light as the vehicle begins limiting power.

There is another, potentially more serious concern. Ford says the incorrect State of Health calculation may increase lithium plating within the battery cells as DC fast-charging cycles accumulate. Severe lithium plating can increase the risk of thermal venting and, potentially, a vehicle fire. Thankfully, there’s no indication that things have reached that point. As of its filing, Ford said it wasn’t aware of any crashes, injuries, or fires related to the issue. It also hadn’t identified any field reports specifically tied to the State of Health overestimation problem.

The solution is a simple software update that will allow the BCEM to recognize and then use the actual state of health that the corresponding battery has. It’s an extremely small recall, but also a fascinating reminder of just how much modern EVs rely on software knowing exactly what’s happening inside the battery.

text:
Some companies are talking less about their climate commitments, while others are shifting the goalposts or quietly letting targets lapse.

In President Donald Trump's second term, major American businesses are bending with the political winds and stepping back from environmental commitments in line with what scientists say is required to prevent the worst consequences of human-caused global warming.

Climate Week NYC, which begins Sunday, is an annual jamboree of civil society, governments and companies on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.

"It's probably the biggest year I've had companies saying, 'Well, we haven't got anything to announce, so you know, I'm not sure we'll be on stage,'" Helen Clarkson, CEO of the Climate Group, which organizes the event, told AFP.

"We're seeing 'green hushing' is definitely increasing, and that's a real challenge because I think if we all give in to this idea that the word climate should never be spoken, that is a lost battle."

The explosion of AI data centers looms large over the trend, as U.S. tech companies rush to finance private gas plants to power them.

Earlier this year, Meta left the Climate Group's RE100 -- a voluntary pledge by leading companies to source all their electricity from renewables -- fueling speculation that other tech giants could follow.

It's not just Big Tech, though.

Dylan Tanner, executive director of InfluenceMap, a think tank that tracks corporate climate policy and lobbying, said automakers were among the worst offenders.

"Many car manufacturers with sales in the U.S. have weakened their EV production targets in recent years, no longer putting their push to electrify within clearly defined timeframes," he said.

In January 2021, for example, GM set a target of 100 percent zero-emission vehicle sales by 2035.

While it technically maintains this target, the company this year backed the Trump administration's weakening of a fuel economy rule to a level that would require no further improvement.

"GM believes that the EV transition must account for market and consumer realities... Ultimately the market will determine how quickly the EV transition occurs," the company wrote in a comment supportive of the rule.

First wave, then backlash

Tanner, who has tracked this topic since 2015, said few companies supported climate policy action at first, but momentum grew after the 2015 Paris Agreement and landmark legislation in Europe and in the United States under former president Joe Biden.

A backlash to that first wave of high-ambition commitments began around 2023, with Trump bringing "a tailwind for some of the negative actors," he said.

Pushback came from the fossil fuel sector and companies reliant on it, such as utilities, but also the US Chamber of Commerce, Tanner said.

Just this week, the chamber praised the Trump administration's rule to remove curbs on greenhouse gas emissions from power plants.

In 2020 retail giant Walmart committed to cutting emissions by around a third by 2025 and two-thirds by 2030 from a 2015 baseline. But in a 2024 report it acknowledged it would miss the first target as well as its recycling goals.

Also in 2020, Google pledged to run on carbon-free energy by 2030, in what CEO Sundar Pichai heralded as a "moonshot." But by 2024 it had stopped claiming its operations were carbon neutral, and this year it acknowledged its emissions were still rising.

Beverage giants Coca-Cola and Pepsi have changed the baseline years for their emissions reduction targets and weakened their ambitions.

Even companies whose climate policies have held steady -- as with Apple under InfluenceMap's scoring -- have drastically reduced their public engagement.

Rachel Cleetus of the Union of Concerned Scientists said there was a clear limit to corporate climate action.

"I think it's pretty clear that voluntary commitments and announcements are always going to be insufficient and we actually do need mandatory public policies on the books," she told AFP. "Without those policies... we just get this whiplash effect where companies are just swinging in the wind as politics change."

text:
The countries most vulnerable to climate change are spending nearly 25 times more on repaying debt than on climate action, according to a new ActionAid report released Wednesday.

The report, “Debt Fuels the Climate Crisis: How the Finance Flows,” is “really unpacking the narrative about how the climate and debt crises are supercharging each other,” said Teresa Anderson, one of the authors and global lead on climate justice for ActionAid International, a nonprofit global federation focused on poverty eradication and social justice.

Across 65 highly climate-vulnerable countries analyzed, debt servicing is expected to consume 65 percent of government revenue in 2026. “They are only getting to keep one third of the money that they are actually raising, but that’s for climate, healthcare, education and public services,” said Anderson.

The imbalance comes as many of those countries are already struggling with both mounting debt and intensifying climate impacts. More than 93 percent of the climate-vulnerable countries are either in debt crisis or at significant risk of one, according to the report. “A lot of that debt was taken on very unfair, illegitimate terms and shouldn’t really be part of the economic picture today,” said Anderson.

Compounding the problem, much of the international funding intended to help developing countries address climate change comes in the form of loans. According to the report, two-thirds of the money labeled as climate finance by Global North countries has been provided through loans, potentially adding to countries’ existing debt burdens.

Countries in the Global South have to pay back their external debt in dollars, pounds or euros, which are stronger currencies than their own.

Countries may also pursue exports that are harmful to the environment—including fossil fuels—because they need to earn the foreign currency required to service their debts, Anderson said. In other words, fossil fuel production can become not only an energy issue but a fiscal one: exports provide the foreign currency governments need to repay creditors.

Climate disasters deepen that cycle. In the aftermath of a major flood, drought or other disaster, foreign investors may withdraw capital or become more reluctant to invest, weakening demand for the country’s currency. “When there is a decrease in demand, that makes your currency depreciate more, so you have to come up with much more local currency to pay your debts,” said Kevin Gallagher, director of the Boston University Global Development Policy Center.

Zambia offers a stark example of how that vicious cycle can play out.

Between 2023 and 2024, an El Niño-driven drought devastated crops across the southern African country, affecting more than 9 million people and contributing to severe food and water shortages. Cereal production fell sharply, while drought-driven power shortages disrupted businesses and livelihoods.

As the crisis deepened, some families turned to increasingly desperate ways of coping. “We saw quite a number of barter exchanges happening where, for example, child marriages went up because in Zambia, when you marry a young girl, you get in return some resources,” said Michael Mwansa, ActionAid Zambia’s thematic lead on climate justice.

At the same time, Zambia has little room in its budget to prepare for the next climate shock. According to ActionAid’s analysis, the country is spending more than 60 percent of its government budget on debt repayment this year, while just 0.32 percent is budgeted for climate resilience and adaptation.

The report proposes several ways to break the cycle.

One recommendation is to cancel unpayable or unjust external debts, with the goal of ensuring that no climate-vulnerable country spends more than 10 percent of its national revenue on external debt repayments. “Is it realistic, based on current political will? No. But can you do it? Sure,” said Niranjali Amerasinghe, executive director of ActionAid USA, based in Washington, D.C.

For Zambia, Mwansa said that canceling unpayable or unjust external debts would be a real game changer. “If Zambia’s debt were to be canceled, it would have the capacity not only to respond to the current climate crisis, but also to address other social amenities,” he said. “We are talking about social protection programs, health and education.”

Gallagher cautioned that outright debt cancellation could have unintended consequences. “The majority of their debt is from multilateral development banks, such as the Asian Development Bank or the World Bank. The problem is if you just cancel that debt outright the banks will get their credit ratings downgraded and then they won’t be able to lend affordably—which might make further debt distress inevitable,” he said.

Instead, Gallagher pointed to another option, also cited in the report: renegotiating the terms of existing debt. That could include reducing the amount countries owe without eliminating the debt entirely.

The report argues that today’s crisis calls for a deep relief, exceeding the scale of the major debt-cancellation initiatives of the late 1990s and 2000s. The goal, Amerasinghe said, is to “ensure that countries are in a place where they can balance debt repayment in fair terms with what they need to spend on.”

Overall, the burden is greatest in sub-Saharan Africa, which is the region hardest hit by the cycle of climate shocks and debt distress.

text:
esla’s proposed $10.1 billion solar cell and module manufacturing facility in Texas has cleared a major local regulatory hurdle following a unanimous vote by a Houston-area school board.

The board of trustees for the Lamar Consolidated Independent School District (Lamar CISD) voted 7-0 to approve a property tax incentive agreement for the clean energy project. Code-named Project Crystal Sun, the application outlines a 1,234-hectare factory site near Richmond in Fort Bend County. The filing was prepared by consulting firm Kroll and signed on July 22 before surfacing publicly in early August.

The school district’s approval provides Tesla with a temporary valuation limitation under the state’s Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation (JETI) Act. The agreement provides a 10-year property tax limitation on the taxable value of eligible property for school district maintenance and operations purposes from 2029 through 2038, addressing a key site-selection requirement Tesla outlined in its filings.

If executed as planned, the development would mark the largest single manufacturing investment Tesla has proposed on paper. Public documents filed with the state confirm a $10.1 billion total capital commitment, which includes $1.5 billion in real property alongside $8.6 billion in manufacturing equipment and personal property. Tesla projects that the plant will create 9,712 permanent full-time positions once fully operational, along with 1,147 peak construction jobs.

The filing details a fully vertically integrated solar cell and module production stack. Equipment lists submitted with the application include machinery for ingot pulling, wafer slicing, chemical coating, metallization, printing lines, cleanroom systems, and automated material handling. The $8.6 billion earmarked specifically for manufacturing equipment reflects high-volume automated cell and wafer lines rather than simple downstream module assembly.

While a large portion of historical U.S. solar manufacturing additions have centered on module assembly using imported cells, Project Crystal Sun would bring cell and wafer fabrication directly onto domestic soil. The move aligns with previously stated ambitions by Tesla leadership to establish massive domestic solar supply chain capacity.

Construction is targeted to span from 2026 through 2028, with commercial production scheduled to start in the first quarter of 2029. However, Tesla noted in the paperwork that it is actively evaluating a competing out-of-state site, making the receipt of local tax incentives a key factor in final site selection.

An economic impact analysis attached to the filing estimates that full buildout could contribute $107 billion to Texas gross domestic product and $6.4 billion in state and local tax revenue over a 38-year horizon.

While the tax application for Project Crystal Sun does not specify an exact annual nameplate capacity in gigawatts for the Fort Bend County facility, industry analysts view the $10.1 billion investment as the foundational pillar toward Tesla’s previously stated target of 100 GW of annual domestic solar manufacturing capacity.

For comparison, total U.S. solar module manufacturing capacity across all producers stood at roughly 60 GW as of early 2026, with solar cell manufacturing capacity lagging significantly behind at under 15 GW, though capacity is scaling rapidly.

title: Holtec's Early Work Exemption Is Real Progress | Nuclear Now #21 - Buttondown
description:
Early work exemptions are tightly scoped and common in large infrastructure projects, and the regulator has been explicit that this does not prejudge safety findings for the reactors themselves.
**THE ECONOMICS** Holtec’s Palisades plan is economically interesting because it overlays SMRs on top of an existing nuclear site with grid interconnection, cooling water access, and community familiarity with nuclear operations.
Early site work helps on that front for one specific reason: it lets Holtec start reducing geotechnical unknowns and construction risk now, before the project locks in its final financing structure.
Until now, the only truly de-risked U.S. nuclear projects have been large light water units like Vogtle and the planned restarts backed by hyperscaler PPAs.
If NRC can show that narrowly scoped exemptions for early work do not compromise safety findings but do reduce schedule risk, that pattern can be replicated across multiple sites.
text:
Holtec getting clearance to start early site work at Palisades is not another “vision” announcement, it is the first meaningful sign that a U.S. small modular reactor project tied to a real site, a real grid, and a real customer is stepping off the PowerPoint and into the dirt. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s exemption for early excavation support and site work is narrow on paper, but in project reality it is the difference between an SMR that exists only in investor decks and one that is starting the long, messy process of becoming an operating plant. This is real progress, not noise, with some important caveats.

Holtec plans two SMR units at the existing Palisades Energy Center in Michigan, with roughly 680 megawatts of capacity, and the NRC has now explicitly authorized early excavation and site preparation ahead of a formal Limited Work Authorization. That matters for three reasons. First, it means the developer has done enough engineering and licensing homework that the regulator is comfortable letting them start disturbing soil, installing support structures, and committing real money to the site. Second, it moves Palisades into a different category than most U.S. SMR projects, which are still trapped in design certification, generic design assessment, or feasibility study limbo. Third, it gives the supply chain and local stakeholders a concrete timeline, however preliminary, instead of yet another press release about “advanced clean energy hubs.”

The hype will say this proves SMRs are “here,” which is wrong. Holtec does not yet have full construction authorization, the reactor design still faces the same capital cost and schedule risk that killed NuScale’s first utility project, and the exemption covers site work, not nuclear island construction. The fear will say this is a regulatory shortcut, that NRC is lowering the bar, which is also wrong. Early work exemptions are tightly scoped and common in large infrastructure projects, and the regulator has been explicit that this does not prejudge safety findings for the reactors themselves. What has changed is subtler and more important: a U.S. SMR project that is tied to an existing grid interconnection and a known market is now spending non-trivial capex on physical work, under NRC oversight, at a named site. In a field crowded with speculative thorium accelerators and corporate MoUs that never become projects, that is the signal worth paying attention to.

**THE ECONOMICS** Holtec’s Palisades plan is economically interesting because it overlays SMRs on top of an existing nuclear site with grid interconnection, cooling water access, and community familiarity with nuclear operations. That cuts soft-cost risk immediately. You are not fighting new transmission build, greenfield permitting, or local political learning curves, you are reusing the sunk infrastructure of a shuttered plant. The two SMR units targeting about 680 megawatts imply unit sizes in the 300 to 350 megawatt range, putting them closer to GE Hitachi’s BWRX-300 class than to the microreactors now being marketed to data centers. At a plausible nuclear capacity factor of 90 percent and wholesale prices in the 50 to 70 dollars per megawatt-hour band for firm low carbon power in the Midwest by the early 2030s, annual revenue per unit pencils out in the 120 to 180 million dollar range. The real question is whether all-in overnight costs land below 7,000 dollars per kilowatt, which is roughly the threshold at which these projects stop being science experiments and start being utility assets.

Early site work helps on that front for one specific reason: it lets Holtec start reducing geotechnical unknowns and construction risk now, before the project locks in its final financing structure. Ground conditions and civil works surprises are notorious cost drivers in nuclear builds. By doing excavation support and site prep under an NRC exemption, Holtec can tighten its contingency estimates and give lenders and tax equity partners a sharper view of the cost profile before they commit. That does not magically turn SMRs into cheap technology. The fabrication, module transport, and on site assembly learning curves still have to be earned the hard way. But compared to a factory-first, site-later fantasy, this sequence is more bankable. Over the next twelve to eighteen months, watch for Holtec to translate this early work into a revised cost estimate, a structured financing package leveraging Inflation Reduction Act tax credits, and offtake agreements that price the value of firm zero-carbon power against increasingly volatile gas and renewables-plus-storage stacks.

**WHAT THIS ACCELERATES** This exemption accelerates three overlapping trajectories. First, it pulls Palisades toward the front of the U.S. SMR deployment pack. Until now, the only truly de-risked U.S. nuclear projects have been large light water units like Vogtle and the planned restarts backed by hyperscaler PPAs. Most “advanced” designs are still purely regulatory stories. Holtec’s ability to do physical work on site, even pre-LWA, moves it closer to the restart-and-expand model we are seeing with big tech backed reactors, where existing sites become hubs for new nuclear capacity. Second, it pressures other SMR vendors with real designs, like GE Hitachi with BWRX-300 and X-energy with Xe-100, to demonstrate comparable project maturity on named sites, not just MoUs. Utilities and investors can now benchmark: who has an NRC paper trail that translates into excavators on an approved pad, and who is still talking about generic assessments and “candidate sites.”

Third, it accelerates state level and federal learning on how to sequence approvals for repeatable SMR deployments. If NRC can show that narrowly scoped exemptions for early work do not compromise safety findings but do reduce schedule risk, that pattern can be replicated across multiple sites. The winners here are developers who have done serious site characterization and are willing to put real money into non-recoverable early works. The losers are the concept companies whose “projects” consist of corporate press releases and thin community engagement, they cannot claim comparable progress once the market internalizes that real SMR advancement comes with construction risk and accountable milestones. For countries watching the U.S. to calibrate their own SMR regulatory pathways, Palisades becomes a reference case: this is what it looks like when an advanced reactor project starts moving under a mature regulator without compromising safety rigor.

**WHAT THIS SIGNALS FOR NUCLEAR’S DIRECTION** The most important thing this story tells us is that the center of gravity in the nuclear revival is shifting from abstract technology to project execution at existing sites. Holtec at Palisades is not selling a radically new physics package, it is selling familiar nuclear engineering in a smaller form factor, anchored to a transmission node that already exists. That is exactly where nuclear needs to be if it wants to be part of the AI and clean energy buildout instead of a perpetual R&D line item. Over the next few years, the projects that matter will share three traits: they reuse existing nuclear or fossil sites, they get early regulatory permission for limited physical work to reduce risk, and they secure offtake from buyers who value 24/7 power more than lowest-bid marginal megawatt-hours. Watch which SMR and “advanced” vendors can put shovels into the ground under real regulatory instruments, and which are still announcing design assessments and international roadshows. The industry is moving into a phase where the dividing line is simple. Either you have a site, a regulator, and a backhoe, or you have a slide deck.

Upgrades to Churchill Falls hydroelectric facility

The Government of Canada has announced an agreement to support hydroelectric and wind energy projects worth nearly C$70 billion (US$50.5 billion), calling it the largest clean-energy investment in North American history. The agreement was announced by Prime Minister Mark Carney alongside the Premiers of Québec and Newfoundland and Labrador. It includes up to C$10 billion in federal financial support for projects expected to generate a combined 14 GW of renewable power.

Among the projects covered by the agreement are upgrades to the Churchill Falls hydroelectric facility in Labrador, expected to boost its capacity by up to 2.5 GW, and the construction of a new 2.7 GW hydroelectric facility at Gull Island on the Churchill River, also in Labrador. The deal also supports the development of 2 GW of onshore wind power in Labrador, along with new transmission infrastructure to carry electricity from Churchill Falls and Gull Island to the Quebec border, and from Churchill Falls to Labrador City.

text:
Building on the momentum of last year’s landmark Nuclear Summit event, Southwestern Pennsylvania is set to reinforce its role as the centerpiece of America’s industrial and energy renaissance. Hosted by the Allegheny Conference on Community Development, the upcoming Energy & Industrial Future Summit will convene on Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Wyndham Grand Pittsburgh in Downtown Pittsburgh.

Bringing together senior C-suite executives, site selectors, capital providers, labor leaders, and federal and state policymakers, the summit aims to address a pivotal national opportunity: how the rapid nationwide expansion of power generation opens massive downstream growth for regional manufacturing, robotics, and high-tech supply chains.

Capturing the Downstream Industrial Opportunity

The national push to expand baseline energy infrastructure—spanning commercial power generation, small modular deployment, and military energy systems—is driving unprecedented industrial demand across the United States. While generation facilities power the grid, the broader economic surge lies downstream in the components, hardware, robotics, and advanced machining required to build and sustain these complex systems.

Southwestern Pennsylvania is uniquely positioned to capture this national market by blending its deep industrial foundation with emerging technologies. The Commonwealth’s strategy leverages Southwestern Pennsylvania’s specialized ecosystem of manufacturing anchors, defense suppliers, robotics centers, and allied technical fields. Industry leaders such as Curtiss-Wright Corp. and Westinghouse Electric Co., alongside innovation catalysts like the Advanced Robotics for Manufacturing (ARM) Institute, position the region as a primary operational hub to reshore critical supply chains, build advanced hardware, and deploy automated production for nationwide infrastructure.

“Southwestern Pennsylvania has the skilled workforce, advanced manufacturing expertise and strong industrial base needed to support the growing demands of the nation’s defense and energy markets,” said Josh Brittingham, Vice President and Sr. General Manager of Curtiss-Wright’s Cheswick, PA facility. “The recent $80 million investment in our Cheswick operations reflects our confidence in the region and our commitment to expanding critical manufacturing capacity here in Pennsylvania. This assessment evaluates the domestic legal architecture, international trade exposure and environmental consequences of the Trump administration’s September 2026 repeal of federal greenhouse gas regulations for the United States power sector.

The September 14, 2026, finalization of the repeal of Biden-era power plant greenhouse gas regulations by the Environmental Protection Agency effectively dismantles the federal statutory framework for limiting carbon dioxide emissions from the United States electricity sector, relying heavily on the February 2026 rescission of the 2009 Endangerment Finding and the Supreme Court’s Loper Bright decision to eliminate current limits while proposing the abolition of all remaining standards for coal- and gas-fired plants [EPA Finalizes Repeal of 2024 Power Plant Regulations, Delivering $300+ Billion in Savings — US EPA — Sep 2026]. While the administration projects over $300 billion in compliance savings for the energy industry, this decisive regulatory rollback fractures American alignment with international carbon pricing regimes, thereby exposing domestic energy-intensive exporters to the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism without the benefit of a domestic carbon tax offset [Two Continents, Two Directions: What the EPA Rollback and CBAM Tell Us About Global Climate Policy — LinkedIn / Alex L — Sep 2026]. The principal judgment derived from the available public record is that federal climate regulation of the power sector is now structurally disabled, an action that irrevocably transfers regulatory authority to fragmented state-level regimes and underlying market forces while simultaneously guaranteeing protracted, multi-jurisdictional litigation over the agency’s statutory interpretation of the Clean Air Act [EPA scraps Biden power plant GHG rules, moves to eliminate other standards — Utility Dive — Sep 2026].

The $300 Billion Savings That Costs American Manufacturers $1.2 Billion in Border Tariffs

The Trump administration’s September 14, 2026 repeal of federal greenhouse gas limits on coal- and gas-fired power plants is not deregulation in the classical sense but the unilateral demolition of the only regulatory instrument that could have generated a domestic carbon price recognized under the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, speaking at the G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial in Houston, projected $300 billion in industry savings, yet what the figures omit is that American steel, aluminum, and chemical exporters now face full CBAM tariff exposure estimated at $450 million to $1.2 billion annually because Washington has abolished the very mechanism that would have entitled them to offset deductions. The fiscal arithmetic is inverted: savings accrue to a shrinking fleet of subcritical coal plants; tariffs are paid by the manufacturers who depend on them.

The Endangerment Finding was the price anchor, and Zeldin removed it

The February 12, 2026 rescission of the 2009 Endangerment Finding, announced by President Trump alongside Zeldin as the single largest deregulatory action in US history, did more than repeal a scientific determination because it eliminated the statutory predicate under Section 111(d) of the Clean Air Act that classified carbon dioxide as a pollutant subject to federal regulation. Without that predicate, no future administration can impose carbon compliance costs on existing power plants without first re-establishing the endangerment finding through a multi-year rulemaking process that will be immediately challenged in courts operating under the Loper Bright standard of zero deference to agency expertise, meaning the regulatory architecture required to generate a domestic carbon price has been dismantled at the foundation level rather than merely suspended for a political cycle.

Loper Bright gave the EPA a legal exit but eliminated the economic one

The June 2024 Supreme Court ruling in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, which overturned Chevron deference, provided the legal mechanism, while the 2022 West Virginia v. EPA decision, which invoked the Major Questions Doctrine to prohibit generation shifting beyond individual plant fence lines, provided the doctrinal ceiling that allowed Zeldin’s EPA to argue that the Clean Air Act’s Section 111(d) does not contain explicit congressional authorization for the carbon capture and hydrogen co-firing mandates the Biden-era 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards would have imposed. The legal argument is internally coherent, but the economic consequence is structurally destructive because by eliminating the mandate the administration eliminated the only mechanism that would have forced US power generators to internalize a carbon cost, thereby eliminating the explicit carbon price that foreign border adjustment regimes require as a precondition for tariff deductions.

The $300 billion figure is a counterfactual dressed as a balance sheet

The EPA’s $300 billion savings projection is not a measurement of avoided expenditure but a counterfactual calculation of the amount utilities would have spent on carbon capture retrofits, amine scrubbing systems, and hydrogen blending infrastructure had the 2024 rules survived judicial review, a figure constructed after the agency’s Regulatory Impact Analysis discarded the Social Cost of Carbon metric entirely and reclassified carbon dioxide as a globally dispersed pollutant devoid of localized health externalities. The actual saving is smaller and concentrated in a specific asset class: the 150-plus gigawatts of subcritical coal capacity and the 400-plus gigawatts of natural gas fleet that would have faced capital expenditure mandates, while the EPA’s stated rationale that power plant emissions constitute a small and decreasing part of global emissions contradicts the cumulative impact methodology used by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and provides the European Commission with the evidentiary basis to treat the repeal as a disguised industrial subsidy under WTO Subsidies and Countervailing Measures rules.

CBAM turns American deregulation into a European tariff base

Because the United States has enacted production tax credits and methane waste fees but no national carbon tax or cap-and-trade system, the explicit carbon price paid by American manufacturers for electricity consumption is legally recognized as zero by the European Commission, which triggers the application of punitive default emission values rather than verified facility-level data under CBAM’s definitive phase. US primary steel exports to the EU, approximately $8.5 billion annually, face estimated CBAM liabilities of $450 million to $600 million, while aluminum smelters, nitrogenous fertilizer producers, and advanced chemical manufacturers face combined additional exposure of $1.25 billion to $2.25 billion calculated against EU ETS prices near €85 per tonne with free allowances being phased out, and Washington’s deregulation does not reduce this exposure but guarantees it by eliminating the domestic instrument that would have generated offset deductions.

State cap-and-trade regimes create a two-price electricity market that fragments the grid

The federal vacuum does not produce a uniform national electricity price because the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative in the Northeast and the linked cap-and-trade systems of California and Washington continue to enforce declining mass-based emission caps, creating a bifurcated market where generators in RGGI states face $15 to $20 per short ton CO2 compliance costs while generators in Texas or Florida face zero. Independent power producers operating across multiple Independent System Operators must maintain jurisdiction-specific emissions tracking and allowance surrender protocols, and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s mandate for seamless interstate commerce collides directly with this patchwork, producing divergent wholesale capacity clearing prices that reward relocation of energy-intensive manufacturing to unregulated jurisdictions precisely because those jurisdictions are most exposed to CBAM.

The G20 Houston framing signals petrostate alignment while multinationals bypass the State Department

Zeldin’s decision to announce the repeal at the G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial alongside Interior Secretary Doug Burgum was a deliberate diplomatic signal aligning the United States with OPEC-plus nations prioritizing fossil fuel monetization, while the European Union, Canada, and the United Kingdom responded by accelerating negotiations toward a plurilateral climate club architecture designed to harmonize their respective carbon border mechanisms. The transactional logic leverages bilateral LNG export capacity to discourage allied nations from adopting EU-aligned tariffs, but the structural outcome is isolation because the domestic instrument that would have entitled Washington to a seat at the table has been abolished, forcing US multinational manufacturers to bypass the State Department entirely and negotiate bespoke product-specific carbon intensity benchmarks directly with the European Commission to maintain market access.

Who pays in 2028: the medium-term ledger

Over the next 12 to 24 months the costs distribute asymmetrically: US steel, aluminum, and chemical exporters absorb CBAM liabilities estimated at $1.7 billion to $2.85 billion annually with no offset mechanism available, small and medium manufacturers in unregulated states lose access to the capital required for ISO 14064 verification that multinational competitors negotiate bilaterally, and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission manages capacity markets where artificially suppressed clearing prices driven by zero-carbon-cost legacy bids starve investment in advanced nuclear and long-duration storage. The physical consequence is a hidden reliability deficit in which aging boiler tubes and turbine blades on retained subcritical units face correlated forced-outage risk during extreme weather events that market price signals cannot price in advance, and the WTO dispute settlement body will adjudicate whether the Houston deregulation constitutes an actionable subsidy under the Subsidies and Countervailing Measures Agreement, a ruling that could authorize retaliatory tariffs beyond the CBAM perimeter. The manufacturers pay the tariffs, the grid absorbs the fragility, the subcritical coal fleet collects the savings, and that is the distribution the decision actually made.
