Offshore Wind Is Just For Starters Offshore wind is just part of the plan.
text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

If US President Donald Trump really wants to annex Canada, he’ll have a big problem on his hands. The Canadian province of Nova Scotia is laying plans to begin exploiting its copious offshore wind resources, and if it’s one thing Trump can’t stand, it’s wind turbines, especially offshore turbines. Clearly, Trump is deathly afraid of the things. They haunt his dreams, day and night, with their looming towers and whispering blades. How else to explain why Trump can’t stand to see another wind turbine rise up from the ground on his watch, offshore or on…

Canada & The US Offshore Wind Connection

Trump’s fear of wind turbines has taken on the nature of a religious crusade. Last year he tried, and failed, to stop construction on US offshore wind projects that were already in motion along the Atlantic Coast. He also ordered the Defense of Defense to “review” — meaning, to delay — onshore wind farms in the pipeline.

The courts have agreed that Trump’s actions against offshore wind projects are unlawful, and the onshore reviews are also unlawful. However, as of this writing the onshore projects are still on hold while the Defense Department invents more hoops for developers to jump through.

Meanwhile, this year Trump also doubled down on his war against offshore wind, offering taxpayer-funded payoffs (some say bribes) to get offshore leaseholders to walk away from their plans.

With this in mind, what are energy-hungry coastal states to do? The thirst for reliable, localized power generation is particularly acute among Northeastern states. Massachusetts, for one, has already begun eyeballing an offshore wind partnership with Canada, leveraging the “Wind West” project in Nova Scotia.

Earlier this year, Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey and Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston put their John Hancocks on a new Memorandum of Understanding, pledging to collaborate on offshore wind projects in the North Atlantic that benefit both the US and Canada.

“I look forward to sharing this clean energy with Massachusetts, powering economic opportunities for the New England region, and creating thousands of jobs and billions in investment in Nova Scotia,” Houston enthused in a press statement dated February 5.

More Offshore Wind From Canada

The centerpiece of Nova Scotia’s offshore wind plan is Wind West. It was among 20 investment opportunities showcased by the Government of Nova Scotia at the inaugural Canada Investment Summit in Toronto last week.

If all goes according to plan, Wind West will add offshore wind to Nova Scotia’s existing roster of conventional offshore energy resources. According to the Government, the province hosts annual average offshore wind speeds topping the range of 9-11 meters per second, making it among the strongest wind areas in North America.

“Nova Scotia has the offshore wind potential to power about a quarter of Canada’s electricity needs,” the Government states, referring to an estimated 60+ gigawatts in offshore wind potential.

The plan calls for a 5-gigawatt tranche of offshore wind turbines in Phase I alone, producing 24 terrawatt-hours of electricity per year or about twice the current peak demand in Nova Scotia.

“Wind West will be Canada’s first offshore wind development and will set the scale, direction and trajectory for future growth,” the Government emphasizes, noting that it has identified offshore sites capable of hosting 62 gigawatts, with wind power supporting capacity factors of up to 60%.

Capacity factor refers to the difference between actual electricity generation and the full operating capacity of a power plant. So far this year, for example, coal power plants and high efficiency combined cycle gas power plants in the US have scored capacity factors ranging from the mid-30’s to the low-60’s, depending on the month, with other forms of fossil-fueled power generation scoring far less.

Offshore Wind Is Just For Starters

Offshore wind is just part of the plan. Under the wing of Canada’s new new Eastern Energy Partnership, Nova Scotia and other eastern provinces are eyeballing a gold mine of regional markets for clean power with offshore wind as the centerpiece, as described in the Wind West strategic plan:

Offshore wind from Nova Scotia can provide enormous quantities of clean energy, at stable prices, while diversifying supply, and boosting reliability for customers. And, in addition to Nova Scotia’s offshore wind, the Atlantic Provinces have other enormous resources to offer–in new and expanded hydro, in new nuclear, in onshore wind, geothermal, tidal and others.

The Eastern Energy Partnership is aimed at establishing new transmission resources between Quebec and the Atlantic Canada provinces of New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island, adding an east-west focus to Canada’s longstanding links with US markets to the south.

All else being equal, additional energy production and electricity-sharing among Canadian provinces would also ripple into the US, whether in terms of new electricity infrastructure, new supply chain jobs, or both.

The wheels are already in motion for a ramp-up in US-Canada clean power activity. Despite some hitches, the new 1.25 gigawatt Champlain Hudson Power Express transmission line officially opened for business in June, covering up to 20% of electricity demand in New York City with hydropower from Quebec.

An Offshore Wind Turbine By Any Other Name…

Meanwhile, back here in the US, the Department of Energy may have figured out a way to restart its wind power programs even while Trump is still in office. Instead of using “wind turbines” to describe, well, wind turbines, DOE has come up with something called “aeromechanical energy systems.”

In support of the verbal gymnastics, DOE also mashed up the former offices of Solar Energy Technologies and Wind Energy Technologies into the new “Integrated Energy Systems Office,” thus avoiding the awkwardness of maintaining an office with “wind” in its title.

The IESO landing page is still bare-boned, but the office does make it clear that the reference to “aeromechanical” means wind turbines and not, say, aero mechanical conveyor belts.

“IESO addresses challenges to the long-term reliability and performance of wind energy systems and promotes the recycling of end-of-life wind energy components.”

The leap from “addressing” to “funding” is a rather long one for wind power nowadays, so don’t hold your breath for IESO to kick in with federal funding for new wind programs, onshore or off.

On the brighter side, while the nation’s copious offshore wind resources are on hold for the time being, coastal states are not taking Trump’s offshore lease buyout/payoff/bribery scheme lying down.

On the Atlantic coast, a group of attorneys general representing New York, Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Rhode Island has sued the US Department of the Interior over its billion-dolar deal with TotalEnergies. In California, Attorney General Rob Bonta and the California Energy Commission have also taken the Trump administration to court over its buyout of the Golden State Wind lease.

Regardless of what the courts decide, Trump has effectively kneecapped states all across the country for the time being, choking off access to an abundant, accessible, and economical energy resource even as conventional fuel costs are flying through the roof. Who voted for this guy, anyways?

text:
After years of delays and plateaued development timelines, it might finally be time for the small nuclear revolution. In a brand new report, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has once again increased its long-term nuclear power forecast, projecting that the world’s nuclear power generation capacity will fully triple by 2060. The Agency expects a whole lot of that increased capacity to come from a strong wave of small modular nuclear reactors connecting to power grids around the world, at long last.

For years, small modular reactors (SMRs) have been touted as a game-changer for clean energy, with the potential to offer round-the-clock, emissions-free electricity at a fraction of the up-front cost of traditional nuclear power plants. Typically, nuclear power plants are huge, bespoke operations with enormous up-front costs and long timelines for approval, construction, and connection. By contrast, SMRs would be factory-made and mass-produced to the same specifications, and then set up on-site. A bigger site would use more of them, and a smaller one would use less. Simple as that.

But these visions have been slow to materialize thanks to regulatory hurdles, funding gaps, and nuclear fuel supply chain issues, among other snags. The primary issue is that while these models are cheaper than traditional nuclear energy, that doesn’t mean that they’re cheap. While the nascent technology will likely continue to get cheaper over time, it is not yet genuinely competitive with other clean alternatives like large-scale hydropower and offshore wind projects.

“A key argument from SMR proponents is that the new reactors will be economically competitive,” says David Schlissel, IEEFA director of resource planning analysis. “But the on-the-ground experience with the initial SMRs that have been built or that are currently under construction shows that this simply is not true.”

While many of the world’s biggest economies – including The United States, the United Kingdom, China, and Russia – have all been investing heavily in the development of SMRs, Russia and China remain the only two nations in the world to have operational, grid connected models. The United States has approved a single patent for an SMR design, with an expected commercial deployment date slated for 2028.

But it would seem that the long slog toward commercial reality is finally picking up speed. The IAEA’s high growth scenario anticipates that 28 percent of all new nuclear capacity added by 2060 will come from SMRs. In the lowest nuclear power growth case, SMRs represent 23 percent of new capacity. In either case, their role is considerable, and both of these numbers represent a huge uptick in confidence compared to the Agency's previous projections, in which SMRs represented 24 percent of new capacity in the high case and just 5 percent in the low case.

The IAEA report also includes a regional breakdown of where they expect to see this development occur by 2060. The Agency anticipates “particularly strong uptake in North America where about 60% of new nuclear capacity could come from SMRs.” Strong regional growth is also expected in South-Eastern Asia and in Latin America and the Caribbean, at 40 percent each in both high and low growth scenarios.

The wheels are already turning in the United States, where just this week the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission approved a fast-tracked plan for the construction of two planned SMRs at the Palisades Energy Center in Michigan. The plant will be allowed to break ground on the project early, before a Limited Work Authorization is issued. Together, the two will produce a projected 680 megawatts of electricity.

In the United States and beyond, the SMR revolution is increasingly seen as a vital piece of the artificial intelligence energy puzzle. With a single hyperscale AI data center able to consume as much electricity as 50,000 homes, scalable, baseload, and low-emissions energy capacity additions are needed as quickly as possible. At present, the AI boom is leading to a massive natural gas boom, but the tech sector is also throwing money behind next-gen technologies like SMRs to more sustainably power its insatiable energy needs in the future. In that sense, the future can’t come fast enough.

By Haley Zaremba for Oilprice.com

title: Joby Autonomous Cessna Caravan Crosses the US | MiGFlug
description:
The aircraft is older than the software flying it The J208 is a converted Cessna 208B Grand Caravan wearing the US registration N101XW.
That is not an accident, and it is not a compromise.
Phoenix is the leg that matters Flying a straight line across empty desert under an autopilot is a party trick.
Joby’s own film of the tour shows the ground station: a pilot commanding the mission with a keyboard, a mouse and a microphone.
The honest summary is that a 33-year-old freight turboprop just flew itself across a continent, and the only thing standing between that and a commercial service is a regulator’s signature and a date nobody has published.
text:
A single-engine turboprop flew from California to the Atlantic this month, taxied itself, took itself off, found its own way around thunderstorms, slotted into one of the busiest general aviation airports in America without ever having been there, and landed on the Outer Banks. The pilot sitting in the cockpit touched nothing for 3,199 miles.

Joby Aviation announced the crossing on 18 September 2026 and called it the first fully autonomous flight across the United States. The aircraft finished the eastbound leg a few miles from the spot where the Wright brothers got a heavier-than-air machine off the ground in 1903, then flew a low pass past the First Flight Monument on the way in. Subtle, it was not.

What Joby flew, though, is the genuinely interesting part. It was not the electric air taxi that the company’s share price rides on. It was a Cessna Caravan built in the 1990s.

The aircraft is older than the software flying it

The J208 is a converted Cessna 208B Grand Caravan wearing the US registration N101XW. DroneXL, reading the FAA registry, records it as a 1993 airframe, serial 208B0382, registered to Joby Aero in July 2024 and carrying an experimental airworthiness certificate for research and development. The Caravan type certificate behind it dates to 1984.

That is not an accident, and it is not a compromise. It is the strategy. Joby’s stated logic is that bolting an autonomous system onto an airframe the FAA has already approved gives it a route into air logistics that does not require a new type certificate, a new production line, or a decade of flight test to prove a novel configuration. The Caravan has been hauling freight into small fields since the mid-1980s. The mechanics, the spares chain and the operator pool already exist. Everything new on this aircraft is software and sensors.

Two pilots, no flying

“Pilotless” is the wrong word for what happened, and Joby has not used it. There were two pilots involved in this flight. Neither of them flew the aeroplane.

A remote pilot on the ground acted as pilot in command, managing flight-plan updates and handling air traffic control on the aircraft’s radios. A safety pilot sat in the cockpit with the authority to take over at any second. Joby’s claim is narrow and specific: that safety pilot made zero control inputs from California to North Carolina. The aircraft handled taxi, takeoff, navigation and landing itself, supervised from Joby’s Autonomy Headquarters in California and from Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina, at ranges of up to 2,323 miles.

The route ran Concord, California (KCCR) to Phoenix Deer Valley (KDVT), then Fort Worth Alliance (KAFW), Shaw Air Force Base (KSSC) and finally Dare County Regional Airport (KMQI). Each leg was a demonstration for somebody: dual-use autonomy in Arizona, freight at one of America’s big industrial logistics hubs in Texas, military flight operations in South Carolina.

Phoenix is the leg that matters

Flying a straight line across empty desert under an autopilot is a party trick. Deer Valley is not empty. It is one of the busiest general aviation airports in the United States, the radio never stops, and the circuit is full of student pilots doing student pilot things. Joby says the aircraft integrated into that traffic with no prior familiarity with the field, and rerouted around severe weather and thunderstorms in real time on the way there.

That is the engineering claim buried in a press release otherwise full of ribbon-cutting. Deviating around live convective weather into an unfamiliar, saturated airport is the actual problem in autonomous flight. Everything else is cruise.

Joby’s own film of the tour shows the ground station: a pilot commanding the mission with a keyboard, a mouse and a microphone. It looks less like a cockpit than like air traffic control, which is roughly the point.

The military has already been buying this

The autonomy stack came from Xwing, whose autonomy division Joby acquired in 2024, built around a Caravan that was already flying itself. Joby now counts more than 400 flights and over 800 automated flight hours behind the system, in both controlled and uncontrolled airspace.

It has also been through three US military exercises. In the Air Force readiness exercise Agile Flag, Joby says the aircraft carried replacement parts that got other aircraft back into service about 24 hours sooner than conventional delivery would have managed. In REFORPAC, aircraft in Hawaii were operated by people sitting in Guam, nearly 4,000 miles away. Those are not proofs of concept. Those are budgets.

On the civil side the flights are tied to state programmes rather than marketing: North Carolina’s eLIFT-NC healthcare logistics initiative, and the multi-state uFLY coalition led by Utah’s transport department, which is evaluating high-altitude and extreme-environment airspace integration on the FAA’s behalf.

Now it turns around

The J208 heads west again through Raleigh (KRDU), Fredericksburg and Washington DC (KRMN), Louisville (KSDF), Wichita (KICT), Oklahoma City (KOKC), Salt Lake City (KSLC) and Portland (KPDX). One of those stops is an easy drive from the Pentagon and Capitol Hill, which is unlikely to be a coincidence.

The honest summary is that a 33-year-old freight turboprop just flew itself across a continent, and the only thing standing between that and a commercial service is a regulator’s signature and a date nobody has published. The Wright brothers took 12 seconds and 120 feet. This one took a fortnight and 3,199 miles, and the pilot was the passenger.

Sources: Joby Aviation press release, 18 September 2026; AeroTime; FLYING Magazine; DroneXL.

title: Q+A: Wahleah Johns on a $100M fund to close tribal energy's predevelopment gap
description:
“I’ve always seen tribal communities facing major energy economies without getting to participate in them,” Johns said.
Johns spoke with Tribal Business News about her work at Four Directions, and what makes the pre-development gap such a challenge for tribal energy.
What is the Four Directions Energy Fund, and what gap in the market are you trying to fill?
We want to establish it so it can be focused here in the US but also with other countries that have tribal communities.
What do you see happening globally and what does it mean for tribal energy sovereignty?
text:
Wahleah Johns (Navajo) recalls growing up near a massive coal mine in northern Arizona. Coal from the mine helped power much of the western United States — while tribal members just miles away went without electricity.

People would be carrying water to and from homes “just over the hill” from the mine, Johns said, an experience she says shaped her view of the relationship Native communities often have with their energy resources.

“I’ve always seen tribal communities facing major energy economies without getting to participate in them,” Johns said. “That experience showed me how extractive industries can operate without caring for the communities around them. It also shaped my belief that tribes should design energy projects that benefit their people directly.”

Johns served as director for the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Indian Energy Policy and Programs under the Biden administration, which made historic investments in renewable energy, particularly solar and wind. However, the Trump administration has since pivoted away from those technologies and back toward extractive energy like coal and oil.

Regardless of the level of federal support, Johns said a persistent gap exists: Tribes often lack the funding to move projects through early development, but can’t get investment without having shovels in the ground.

It’s a catch-22 that has become an increasingly sharp focus in Indian Country energy, Tribal Business News reports — and the kind of challenge Johns wants to address at the Berkeley, Calif.-based Four Directions Fund, LLC, where she now serves as director, she says.

The fund is in its early days: the organization is sketching out its eventual structure, targeting $100 million in fundraising to begin supporting those early pre-development costs, such as grid connectivity, feasibility studies and environmental reviews.

Johns spoke with Tribal Business News about her work at Four Directions, and what makes the pre-development gap such a challenge for tribal energy.

This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

What is the Four Directions Energy Fund, and what gap in the market are you trying to fill?

We have seen less than 2,300 megawatts of clean energy out there in the US on tribal lands, which is a very low number, and that was surprising to me. That came out of the Office of Indian Energy access report that was released in 2023.

Editor’s note: DOE's Tribal Electricity Access and Reliability report identified more than 2,250 MW of known large-scale renewable energy generation on tribal lands, while noting its list was not exhaustive.

Historically many of the ideas [for solving this issue] have come from outside energy companies or developers and not really within the nations themselves. Tribes themselves need to be seeding these big visions of how they want to participate in the energy economy.

There could be so many energy assets positioned on tribal lands and controlled by tribal governments. Tribes could be looking at land as an economic development opportunity, to utilize renewable energy technology to generate revenues. The fund’s goal is to position tribes in a place where they can leverage these opportunities for more royalties and more equity stake in projects designed and planned by and for them.

It is about being proactive and creating space for tribes to decide what type of projects they want in their communities and their nations, how they want to participate, and putting them in a position of power.

That has been the area I have been most focused on. We are in the early stages of setting up the fund structure. The idea is to have a fund that will support this pre-development work that is needed in Indian Country and tribal communities globally.

Where does the fund stand, and who are you hoping to serve or support?

We want to establish it so it can be focused here in the US but also with other countries that have tribal communities. Our goal is to raise $100 million to start. Discussions around fund structuring and talking with investors have been exciting.

Your website refers to the Four Directions Fund as the “first global Indigenous fund.” Why the global focus?

Indigenous peoples across the world have a connection to land that is unique and beautiful. We want to offer support and guidance if they want to use their land assets for development. We want to support a different approach than what we’ve seen historically, where it is always the outside interest coming into our homelands and proposing something.

Many times communities are in a defensive mode because of history when it comes to energy deals that leave out communities. We hope this approach changes the way business is developed in our nations and our communities.

What challenges do tribal nations face in energy development?

Pre-development funds are hard to find. When I was in the Office of Indian Energy, we understood the gaps that exist. Many projects did not have predevelopment funds to get into the interconnection queue. The interconnection queue can be multi-million dollars to do. Seeing tribes not have access to that type of funding makes it hard for them to participate.

There are costs associated with feasibility studies, engineering studies, and permitting. Some of these areas take time and approval from the federal government or whatever land jurisdiction they are on. Developers will not pay those costs. Tribes are left in a hard place where they cannot have access to capital or it is hard to find the capital to pay for that, and that holds up project development.

How does predevelopment funding change tribal leverage?

Tribes need capital, and to get that capital they need to be able to get projects started. The fund will support predevelopment costs so it lines up their project in a good place. Once it’s up and going and in development, tribes could have the option to sell the project to a developer or continue to develop it all the way through themselves, but they need to get it started to build that equity piece in the first place.

They can negotiate royalty rates, higher royalty rates, utilization of their lands, or sell the project and buy into a long-term contract of being a co-owner or ownership stake of the project. It is about positioning tribes and Indigenous communities in a place where they have more leverage to negotiate better terms.

So it’s about building partnerships from stronger positions?

This will take people helping to do the negotiations and deal structuring that best benefits the tribes who are participating. It will take working with developers on finding the right partners who want to work with tribes, and then helping those developers understand and respect tribal sovereignty.

We are trying to make sure developers understand how important the sovereignty piece is. They have misconceptions about tribes, and that is an area that could be overcome with patience and partnership.

What kind of projects should tribes be pursuing?

With tribes continuing to do their energy planning, I would advocate that they keep doing those planning processes to design systems that support durability, self-sufficiency and emergency backup power. Solar technology is time tested, offers the lowest cost of power, and is well suited for the American West with its 300-plus days of sunlight.

What do you see happening globally and what does it mean for tribal energy sovereignty?

Outside of the US there’s a lot of clean energy projects happening in Indigenous communities already. It is incredible. Adoption of EV mobility is increasing. There is a lot of activity happening outside of the US in emerging markets when it comes to clean energy and technology.

text:
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger on Friday unveiled a framework for regulating data centers amid bipartisan calls within the commonwealth and across the U.S. for greater oversight of the rapidly growing industry.

“Day by day, community members are demanding action,” she said. “Virginia should be leading the nation in setting the highest standards for this industry. And now, I believe we are doing just that.”

The Data Center Accountability Framework sets out limits on data center developers and operators, including required community benefit agreements, limits on the use of on-site power plants and a prohibition of nondisclosure agreements between corporations and local governments.

“The goal here is to actually give power back to our local communities by banning NDAs, ensuring that there can be clear, transparent conversations and that communities have the ability to weigh in,” Spanberger said during a news conference.

The framework elements also include strengthening environmental policies and Virginia’s clean energy economy, lowering energy costs and prioritizing the hiring and training of Virginia workers in data center projects

Spanberger signed an executive order implementing many of the framework’s directives to agencies. The order also creates a task force that’s to monitor developments in AI for risks such as workforce displacement and AI-led attacks on consumer and business data privacy, and address those issues through executive and legislative action.

Many of the policies Spanberger introduced would have to be codified through legislation, and the governor said her office was working with members of the General Assembly.

“The policies put forth in this framework are the highest standards in America,” Spanberger said.

Boys and men in Virginia are falling behind education and workforce progress targets, a state panel said as it looks for ways address the gap between the genders. According to a report released Thursday by the Virginia Boys and Men Advisory Commission, data show boys are falling behind in multiple educational metrics starting from an early age. The commission, after two formal study meetings in Richmond to evaluate challenges and "construct actional policy solutions," concluded that the declines continue into adulthood, with data showing disengagement by men in the workforce. "Proposing targeted policy interventions that help young men strengthens the Commonwealth as a whole, yielding outcomes that benefit men and women, boys and girls alike," the report said. The commission's first study meeting focused on education received data and testimony from the American Institute for Boys and Men, which showed since 2024 only 48% percent of boys in the commonwealth met kindergarten readiness benchmarks compared with 56% of girls. Meanwhile, fourth grade boys' reading scores stagnated until 2019-2022, when they saw a 13.5-point drop, a steep decline compared with a 2.4 drop nationally.

BILLERICA, Mass., Aug. 31, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — AM Batteries, a leader in dry battery-electrode (DBE) manufacturing technology, announced today its role as a core subrecipient of a $50 million award from the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Manufacturing Deployment Office (MDO) under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.

The project, led by Coreshell Technologies, aims to build out approximately 2 gigawatt-hours of electrode manufacturing capacity and 1.5 gigawatt-hours of cell assembly capacity here in the United States. The initiative will establish a resilient domestic battery supply chain while creating more than 100 domestic jobs across production, technical, and administrative roles.

AM Batteries is contributing its dry-coating process for cathode manufacturing, eliminating energy-intensive solvent-based wet coating and toxic solvent-recovery infrastructure. By combining AM Batteries’ dry Powder to Electrode™ platform with advanced material integration, the partnership significantly reduces capital and operational costs while enabling higher-performance, lower-cost cells for domestic electric vehicle and defense applications.

Hieu Duong, CTO of AM Batteries, said:

This project is about proving that a 100% domestically produced high-performance battery cell can be cost-competitive with mass-market cells from Asia.

“The U.S. will not win by simply replicating existing technologies or the status quo; we must create fundamental advantages in manufacturing and materials. By combining AMB’s platform with Coreshell’s MGS anode technology, we can lower cost, improve performance, and help build a globally competitive battery industry in the West.”

Traditional lithium-ion battery manufacturing relies heavily on wet-slurry casting, which requires massive drying ovens and toxic solvents. AM Batteries’ dry-electrode process eliminates these steps entirely, cutting electrode manufacturing CAPEX by up to 40%, reducing OPEX by over 50%, and significantly lowering the carbon footprint of battery plants.

text:
SAN ANTONIO, Texas — A dynamic cross-border manufacturing corridor stretching from San Antonio through South Texas and deep into Northern Mexico is rapidly emerging as North America's next industrial superpower, according to regional economic experts and trade leaders speaking on a recent broadcast of KLRN TV’s Business of Business.

Hosted by former San Antonio Mayor and U.S. Housing and Urban Development Secretary Henry Cisneros, the discussion highlighted how the region — dubbed the Texas-Mexico Automotive Supercluster — is leveraging geographical proximity, integrated supply chains, and massive capital investments to redefine international trade and advanced manufacturing.

Joining Cisneros for the panel were David Marquez, former executive director of economic and community development for Bexar County, and Jorge Torres, president and CEO of McAllen-based Interlink Trade Services.

Beyond the Austin-San Antonio Corridor

While significant attention has focused on the explosive population growth between Austin and San Antonio, Cisneros emphasized that the true long-term economic engine extends south to the U.S.-Mexico border.

"This explosive corridor actually continues beyond San Antonio to the south — the region from San Antonio to the Rio Grande Valley, the borderlands, and then into Mexico is the next superpower," Cisneros said.

The region spans a series of rapidly growing economic centers:

The Rio Grande Valley: Home to 1.5 million residents, seeing massive technology and energy sector investments, including SpaceX’s Starbase facility at Boca Chica, defense technology firm Saronic, and multi-billion-dollar liquefied natural gas (LNG) export projects at the Port of Brownsville.

Laredo: The single largest land crossing point by cargo value in the world, serving as the central artery for U.S.-Mexico cross-border freight.

Eagle Pass: Developing new international bridge infrastructure under the Puerto Verde project.

Northern Mexico: An industrial powerhouse encompassing Monterrey (a metropolitan area of 5 million people), Saltillo, Torreón, Guanajuato, Querétaro, and San Luis Potosí.

David Marquez, former executive director of economic and community development for Bexar County.

The 400-Mile Logistics Radius

Marquez, who authored the original blueprint for Bexar County's automotive cluster strategy following Toyota's arrival in San Antonio in 2003, explained that modern automotive assembly is driven strictly by logistics.

"Logistics drives the costs that you can most manage," Marquez noted. "And if you look at all of the components that make up a vehicle, something like 80 percent or more come within 400 miles of that final assembly facility."

When drawn from San Antonio, that 400-mile radius encompasses South Texas, the Rio Grande Valley, and key Northern Mexico manufacturing hubs like Monterrey and Saltillo. Today, Toyota's San Antonio plant hosts 25 on-site Tier-1 suppliers, a unique setup that feeds components directly into the main assembly line via overhead conveyors.

As Tier-1 suppliers expand, they require secondary (Tier-2) suppliers within close proximity to manage risk and transit times, driving investment across South Texas border communities.

Rio Grande Valley Lands Key Tier-1 Supplier

In the Rio Grande Valley, the industrial footprint is shifting from traditional maquiladora operations to high-tech automotive component manufacturing.

Torres highlighted a major milestone for McAllen, which recently landed French automotive supplier Valeo.

"In McAllen, Texas, we just landed our first Tier-1 manufacturer, Valeo," Torres revealed. "They're going to open up a plant that's going to hire about 500 people. They're going to be making the new generation computer module brain for GM."

Torres noted that while trade policies and USMCA negotiations create temporary market uncertainties, Mexican exports continue to expand rapidly. Beyond automotive manufacturing, advanced trade along the border is seeing significant growth in semiconductors, telecommunications, medical devices, and aerospace components.

Breaking the Cycle of Poverty Through Workforce Training

Both Marquez and Cisneros emphasized that the growth of advanced manufacturing is more than an economic indicator — it is a vital tool for community elevation.

"Advanced manufacturing, I think, perhaps more than any other industry that we have, has the ability to break the cycle of poverty in our community," Marquez said. "It creates at scale the largest number of jobs that can lead to the middle class that meet our population where they are in terms of their job experience, their education level, and their aspirations."

Regional organizations, including the Council for South Texas Economic Progress (COSTEP), are actively working with cross-border automotive clusters to market South Texas as the premier location for tier-supplier expansion.

Addressing concerns regarding border friction, cartels, and political rhetoric, the panel concluded that economic prosperity and cross-border integration remain the most effective defenses against regional instability.

"This region benefits the whole of the United States and North America so much," Marquez stated. "Ensuring that both sides of the border find that prosperity is perhaps our best defense."

text:
Now that the Moss Landing power plant caught fire again, community members are raising new questions about the safety of battery storage facilities in the Central Valley, including those in Kings County.

Battery fires can be especially difficult to fight because water is not always effective and the fires can reignite, according to Kings County Fire Marshall John Wilson.

“We are looking at all that to ensure that this is as safe as possible,” Wilson said.

Lithium-ion batteries are commonly found in household devices such as laptops, phones and portable chargers. But when exposed to heat, they can trigger a chain reaction known as thermal runaway.

“When that happens, our water is not effective on extinguishing or putting out that chemical process going on within the battery itself,” Wilson said.

With multiple battery storage facilities in Kings County, officials said they focus heavily on planning and permitting to help ensure facilities are built safely and located away from sensitive areas.

“We're putting our facilities in Kings County in areas that are not directly next to a home or a school,” Wilson said. “So when we do that there's a lot of time spent on the front end, whether it's wind patterns, pre planning,, things like that."

He also said they maintain fire roads, grass heights and do training drills with the company employees.

Even with those steps, Wilson said the rapid pace of change in battery technology can outstrip regulations.

“A challenge that we have with this is our fire code and if he codes our code cycles in general, generally have a hard time keeping up with the how often these battery systems of all the new products are trying to be more efficient,” Wilson said.

Another concern raised by Kings County neighbors is whether local fire resources could be stretched thin during a major battery fire, potentially leaving fewer crews available for other emergencies.

Wilson said the county is working to secure more resources, and one county supervisor has proposed asking battery storage facility owners to provide upfront funding for fire resources.

In January 2025, the 300 Battery Energy Storage System in Moss Landing burned for several days, and neighbors have continued pushing to learn more about lasting effects.

Fire officials said the fire that prompted this morning’s shelter-in-place was not as large as last year’s incident. The shelter-in-place order has since been lifted.

They also said there are no active flames now, but crews will continue monitoring the scene because these types of fires can reignite easily.

But it was the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1989 that really spelled the end for the plant, which was decommissioned three years later before ever having become operational.
Francisco Pérez, who like Vargas once worked at the plant, recalled the day Castro came to tell them the news.

text:
In Cuba, blackouts like the one that happened this Friday are nothing new. In fact, they have been a feature of life here for decades — even if US President Donald Trump’s ban on oil sales to Havana has deepened the crisis.

With its limited domestic oil production and reliance on foreign exports, Cuba has long searched for alternative forms of energy to help it keep the lights on.

Perhaps its most ambitious attempt was when, in the early 1980s, Fidel Castro embarked on plans to build a nuclear power plant in Juraguá, Cienfuegos province, to be built and financed with the help of the Soviet Union.

It was hoped that the plant, envisioned as the first of three, would provide 15% of the island’s electricity needs and usher in a new era of energy security for the communist nation.

But that dream was never to be.

A dream in ruins

US opposition, the Chernobyl nuclear disaster, and the collapse of the Soviet Union all helped to doom the project, whose long-abandoned concrete shell stands today as a ruin that people can walk around freely.

A short stroll down the road is Nuclear City, the town built to house the thousands of workers the project would have needed and which today is — like the plant — a shadow of its former self.

There, Luis Vargas, an electrician who was part of the project, tells CNN he feels “a deep sorrow inside” when viewing the structure in its current state.

“It’s a shame that it was left the way it is, because unfortunately millions were invested there and it could not be completed,” he says.

Soviet collapse

During the Cold War, Havana bet everything on remaining within the Soviet Union’s sphere of influence and on its assistance with ambitious projects such as the Juraguá nuclear power plant.

Perhaps inevitably, the project soon ran into opposition from the United States which — despite having operated its own Turkey Point nuclear power plant in Homestead, near Miami, since 1972 — objected on safety grounds due to Juraguá’s proximity to the US.

Those US objections only grew when the worst nuclear disaster in history happened in 1986 at Chernobyl, Ukraine — then part of the USSR — and persisted despite the Nuclear Regulatory Commission telling Congress that year that, despite its reservations about the project, Juraguá was more similar in design to Western nuclear power plants than it was to the one in Chernobyl.

But it was the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1989 that really spelled the end for the plant, which was decommissioned three years later before ever having become operational.

Francisco Pérez, who like Vargas once worked at the plant, recalled the day Castro came to tell them the news.

“He told us the truth; he told us what the situation was and what the problem was there, and that the plant had to be shut down.”

While throughout the 1990s there were multiple attempts by Russia and Cuba to revive the project, Washington’s ongoing objections — coupled with the financial difficulties both countries were experiencing — meant none of these came to fruition.

“We have long had doubts about the quality of the plant’s construction and about Cuba’s ability to operate it safely. I would only add that we have conveyed these views to all the governments involved, including Russia’s,” then-US State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told a press conference in 1995.

Five years later, Castro reportedly told Russia he was no longer interested in completing the plant.

Left behind

While Cuba’s nuclear power dream now lies in the ruins of Juraguá, the decades since Castro announced the project have seen this form of energy flourish across the Americas.

Today, according to the IAEA, the United States has 94 operating nuclear power reactors that produce 18-20% of its annual electricity needs; Canada has 17 reactors that produce 13%; Argentina has 3 that produce 7%; and Mexico has two that generate 4-5%.

The two reactors operated by Brazil at its Angra plant have the capacity to generate around 2,000 megawatts — just shy of the deficit Cuba’s Electric Union reported on September 16.

The unfortunate reality for Cuba is that while its nuclear dream collapsed, it still faces the same problem it has for decades: a growing demand for electricity and a lack of capacity to produce it.

On the façade of the giant concrete structure that was once intended to solve that problem, a sign written in Russian and Spanish remains visible despite the passing years.

“Let the atom be a worker, not a soldier!” it says.

In Juraguá, it was neither.

text:
The U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Environmental Management (EM) released on Friday an expression of interest (EOI) seeking input from American industry on the potential transfer of surplus critical minerals, rare earth elements and other materials located at five EM cleanup sites across the country.

The materials identified in the EOI are the result of past nuclear weapons production and government-sponsored energy research. No longer needed for planned activities, they may be valuable to private industry, including advanced technology and manufacturing, alternative energy and national defense, the DOE said.

The critical minerals and rare earth materials subject to this EOI are aluminum, cesium-137, chloride, copper, fluorine, lead, lithium hydride, platinum, selenium, silver, tungsten and vanadium.

“EM is transforming the legacy of America’s nuclear mission into opportunity,” EM Infrastructure, Disposition and Regulatory Policy Director Rob Seifert said in a news release.

“The surplus materials at our sites could help put American resources to work for American industry by supporting jobs, strengthening our industrial base and advancing the administration’s energy and national security priorities,” Seifert said. “This EOI is the first step in that conversation with the private sector.”

Five geographically diverse EM cleanup sites — Paducah in Kentucky, Portsmouth in Ohio, Oak Ridge in Tennessee, the Nevada National Security Site, and Moab in Utah — are participating in the initiative.

The EOI includes site-specific information about the valuable materials, including their type, quantities and locations. EM will host a virtual Industry Day on Sept. 30 to explain the EOI process, answer questions and learn more about market demand and the industrial capabilities available to process, recover or otherwise use the materials.

The initiative supports priorities of strengthening domestic supply chains, advancing American energy independence and maintaining the nation’s competitive edge in critical minerals and advanced manufacturing.

Interested parties must provide their own equipment and expertise for any material relocation or extraction. DOE will evaluate responses based on demonstrated technical knowledge and the quality of proposed use plans.

EM has led the nation’s nuclear cleanup mission for more than 37 years, addressing the environmental legacy of Cold War-era nuclear weapons production at sites across the country. This initiative represents the next chapter in that mission, DOE said.

By Dan Spalding

News Now Warsaw

WARSAW — Slate Auto’s transformation of the old RR Donnelley printing plant in Warsaw into a high tech automotive production facility continues on schedule, according to the company which offered a glimpse on Friday into the changes.

Local media on Friday took a tour of part of the 1.3 million square foot property including the production area that was gutted and brought back to life over the past year.

The start-up automotive company seeks to shake up the market with a stripped-down “Blank Slate” vehicle with a price of $24,950.

More than 180,000 people previously placed a refundable $50 reservation and more than 10,000 have now placed $300 down payments.

“We’re really excited that we have the reservations to prove this is the truck that America wants,” said Jeff Jablansky, Slate’s head of public relations and communications.

Dan Tasiemski, Slate’s head of manufacturing engineering, said they remain on schedule to begin production in the fourth quarter.

Friday’s tour focused on part of the production area, which looks like a new plant, already busy with employees and contractors moving across newly installed heavy duty cement flooring.

Jablansky said the factory is essentially “full and basically ready to start building.”

The tour on golf carts included a stop in the body shop where robots could be seen moving behind what looked like wire cages, moving quietly and efficiently.

The tour also took reporters over a stretch of outdoor pavement that felt like an intense and lengthy rumble strip. The company calls it the BSR, (short for buzz, squeak, rattle) that is part of quality control.

Slate also highlighted how work stations on the assembly line can moves up and down for better ergonomics.

Construction of a 133,000 square-foot extension of the production building is currently under way.

Slate has headquarters in Michigan and other offices in California, and has already hired 575 people for the Warsaw facility. Eventually, the company plans to employ around 2,000 and continues to hire aggressively.

The company is currently hiring, with an emphasis on attracting local workers.

“We need and we want those local candidates … to be a part of this team,” said Stacy Burk, head of plant human resources, “My goal, and I think a lot of the leadership’s goal here is to create a generational place.”

Workers, she said, will need “a willingness to be part of something fun. I tell them, ‘You know, if you want to come to a company that’s got a great culture, come here. You will want to be a part of this. You’ll want to come to work every day.’ ”

text:
It happened yet again.

Another plume of smoke rose from Vistra’s Moss Landing battery plant Friday morning, a year and a half after a catastrophic fire wrecked the grid storage facility in Northern California.

Vistra built Moss Landing on the California coast, south of Santa Cruz, to supply grid capacity to the greater Silicon Valley region. It was the world’s most powerful grid battery when it came online in 2020, with 300 megawatts/1,200 megawatt-hours packed into a former gas turbine hall. That unique design — which is out of step with current energy-storage best practices — came back to haunt Vistra when those batteries turned into fuel for a January 2025 fire, which had been preceded by multiple smaller safety incidents.

Now, like an overdone horror franchise that resurrects its villain ad nauseum, Moss Landing is on fire again.

Vistra has been working on demolishing the site, which entails laboriously removing the intact batteries still in the building, de-energizing them, and shipping them for recycling or disposal. Workers have already extracted 34,000 battery modules, and hoped to finish extracting the last 5,000 modules later this year — those batteries may carry some residual charge.

A statement from Monterey County said the new fire ​“involves batteries that were previously damaged” in the January 2025 blaze, but stressed that it is ​“not comparable” in size. Officials anticipate the fire may burn out ​“over the next 24 hours,” per the statement.

Vistra did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Utility Pacific Gas & Electric operates grid infrastructure next door to Vistra’s Moss Landing site. A spokesperson confirmed that the fire did not start on, or spread to, PG&E property. The utility took its adjacent Elkhorn battery plant offline after the 2025 Vistra fire to assess damage and plans to resume service there on July 1, 2027.

Authorities have issued shelter-in-place orders for the surrounding area — a seaside community that gives way to strawberry fields and other farmland farther inland. For locals, who are drawn to the area’s frolicking sea otters and cavorting whales, fires at Moss Landing have become a surprisingly regular occurrence.

“It seemed like once a year there’d be some smoldering going on,” said David Robinson, who witnessed the latest plume from his boat in the nearby harbor. ​“Then of course the big fire last year pretty much shut everything down. … Now it’s like, man, when is this going to end?”

The January 2025 conflagration stoked concern nationwide about the safety of batteries. Developers looking to build batteries elsewhere commonly have to address fears that these installations will bring a Moss Landing–style fate to their neighbors.

That said, Moss Landing’s fire vulnerabilities are rooted in designs that have fallen out of use by battery developers. Vistra used a less-stable battery chemistry than today’s installations, and it was designed in a way that is not up to current safety standards.

Whereas Vistra opted to reuse the former turbine structure, which it owned, storage developers today build large batteries using modular containers that are carefully spaced out in a field. They are designed to fail safely, so that if one container catches fire, it cannot propagate to the rest of the facility.

Battery chemistries have evolved, too. Moss Landing used the potent nickel-manganese-cobalt lithium-ion recipe that was handed down from the electric vehicle industry. Since then, the stationary grid-storage industry has become a large enough buyer that manufacturers have built dedicated factory lines for cells optimized for that use. The industry has by and large switched to lithium ferrous phosphate, a safer chemistry that gives up some of the energy density valued for automotive batteries.

Energy storage is the fastest-growing source for on-demand electricity capacity in the country. Battery growth is particularly rapid in California and Texas, where the technology helps bank low-cost solar energy during sunny hours for use once the evening comes around. This combustion-free electricity pushes down power prices, and has helped avoid shortages during record heat waves.

The latest fire does not reveal anything new about the safety of modern battery installations — but it rekindles old problems that the industry will have to continue answering for.

text:
As fuel costs rise amid the U.S.-Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars, Americans in the Northeast may have to pay significantly more to heat their homes this winter.

With the price of diesel, in particular, increasing, so too will the cost of a home heating fuel known as heating oil or fuel oil that is commonly used in Northeast states.

Nearly 5 million U.S. households used heating oil as their primary heat source in the winter of 2023 through 2024, 82 percent of them located in the northeastern part of the country.

William O’Neil, principal research analyst at S&P Global, said that heating oil and diesel prices tend to move together, so when diesel prices go up, heating oil usually does, too.

“The price of diesel historically has a pretty strong relationship to the price of heating oil because they’re effectively chemically identical. They just have different additives, different treatments,” O’Neil said.

He said that those Americans could end up paying nearly 50 percent more this year to heat their homes than they were last year.

“It would not shock me if Americans or specifically New Englanders are paying something like $2 more per gallon than they were last winter,” O’Neil said. “Residential heating oil prices last winter were something like $3.75 to $4 a gallon, so an additional $2 per gallon on top of that, you’re talking about something in the range of 50 percent higher.”

The National Energy Assistance Directors Association, which represents state-level officials seeking federal funding to help people pay for energy, released its own analysis last week projecting that heating oil could cost 31 percent more this winter than last.

It estimated that the relevant households spent an average of $1,749 on heating oil last winter and projected they could spend $2,297 this winter.

Mark Wolfe, the group’s executive director, said that as diesel costs have risen further, prices may go even higher.

While heating oil saw the most dramatic increase in the group’s analysis, the organization projected that in general, Americans could spend an overall average of 8.7 percent more to heat their homes this winter.

It projected that natural gas could cost 5.8 percent more, electricity could cost 9 percent more and propane could cost 8.7 percent more.

Wolfe noted that higher fuel costs could have significant economic impacts for lower- and middle-income Americans.

“When you have budgets where there’s very little discretionary income, you have to cut back on groceries. You cut back on medicine. Any discretionary activities you don’t do. If you have to, you borrow from payday lenders. Some people fall behind in the utility bills and get shut off from power. It’s a spiraling effect,” he said.

He noted that this comes on top of high gasoline prices that are also straining Americans’ budgets. As of Friday, the national average gasoline price was about $4.47 per gallon, according to AAA. Diesel, meanwhile, was averaging $6.45 per gallon.

For heating oil specifically, Wolfe said that Americans typically buy the fuel by the beginning of October, meaning the increase could be felt before the midterm elections.

While it’s not entirely clear how this may play out politically, it comes as Maine and New Hampshire face competitive Senate races.

Wolfe said that he wants Congress to increase funding for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) to offset the high energy cost for the poorest families, saying the situation is “rapidly becoming a crisis in affordability.”

Costs of diesel, gasoline and heating oil are all going up because of both the U.S.-Iran conflict and the Russia-Ukraine war.

More specifically, both the price of crude oil and attacks on refineries that produce the oil are playing major roles.

Tom Kloza, chief oil analyst at Gulf Oil, said that the price of crude was high because of disruptions in the Red Sea.

“The Houthis were always a wildcard, and now the Houthis are very, very active,” Kloza said.

O’Neil, with S&P Global, also said that for oil, uncertainties about the future of the Strait of Hormuz are a factor, even as there is some movement in the crucial waterway.

“Earlier on in the war, there was there was this working up towards” a ceasefire, he said. “Now we’re in kind of a point where, with the Houthis getting involved, with the strikes on Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, which was a vital conduit for oil to be exported out of the Middle East without having to pass through the Strait of Hormuz … It adds it adds a shroud of additional doubt that this war and its oil market implications are going to be resolved really anytime soon.”

On the refining side, Kloza pointed to Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries.

“The biggest problem for the world right now is that we are about 7 million barrels a day of refining capacity on the sideline and that means that you know refined products prices: gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel, are going to be sky high,” he said.

description:

Rare earth elements and other critical minerals are important for electronics, clean-energy technologies, transportation, and national security.
The goal is not only to release rare earth elements and other critical minerals trapped inside the material, but also to convert the silica itself into useful products.

text:
A research team led by Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI) has received a $3.3 million award from the National Science Foundation's Growing Convergence Research program to investigate whether biological strategies used by diatoms, sea sponges, and plants could help recover those resources with less energy and fewer harsh chemicals.

The five-year, two-phase effort is being led by Mingjiang Tao, associate professor in the WPI Department of Civil, Environmental, and Architectural Engineering. Professors Carrick Eggleston and Yan Wang are serving as co-principal investigators. Researchers from George Mason University, the University of California San Diego, the University of Massachusetts Amherst, and the University at Buffalo will also contribute.

"Recovering critical minerals is only part of the opportunity," Tao said. "We want to develop a process that uses as much of each waste stream as possible, separating strategically important elements while converting the remaining material into useful products. That whole-material approach could fundamentally change how industries manage waste and obtain essential resources."

Valuable Minerals Hidden in Waste

The project is designed to tackle two related problems.

Many silicon-derived materials used in concrete, glass, ceramics, semiconductors, and silicones require high temperatures, large amounts of energy, and intensive chemical processing to produce. At the same time, industry generates vast quantities of silicon-rich waste, including coal ash residue, red mud, mine tailings, concrete debris, waste glass, and metallurgical slag.

Much of this material ends up in landfills, ponds, impoundments, and large waste piles, even though it can contain useful silicon, critical minerals, and rare earth elements (REE).

One estimate suggests that 11 million tons of REEs trapped in U.S. coal ash landfills is worth $8.4 billion -- nearly eight times the nation's current raw domestic reserves. Rare earth elements and other critical minerals are important for electronics, clean-energy technologies, transportation, and national security.

Looking to Nature for a Cleaner Approach

To find a better way to recover these materials, the researchers are turning to biology.

Diatoms, sea sponges, and certain plants use biological molecules and organic scaffolds to collect dissolved silicon and build complex silica structures under relatively mild conditions. The team hopes to adapt those natural processes to create lower-energy methods for breaking down silica-rich industrial waste.

The goal is not only to release rare earth elements and other critical minerals trapped inside the material, but also to convert the silica itself into useful products.

AI and Biomolecules Could Speed Discovery

The project combines expertise from biology, geochemistry, materials science, metallurgy, engineering, computational chemistry, and artificial intelligence.

Researchers plan to use advanced computational modeling and artificial intelligence to design specialized biomolecules and predict how they will interact with silicon-rich waste. These tools could help the team identify promising approaches for mineral recovery and materials manufacturing more quickly.

As lead principal investigator, Tao will manage and coordinate the overall project while also directing research on biosilicification, the process through which organisms form silica materials, and bio-enabled metallurgy for recovering rare earth elements from silicon-rich wastes.

Eggleston, a professor in the Department of Civil, Environmental, and Architectural Engineering with expertise in geochemistry, will lead work focused on understanding and optimizing the chemical reactions involved in breaking down and rebuilding silicate materials.

His research will examine reaction pathways and rates associated with silicate dissolution, repolymerization, carbonation, glass formation, and silicone synthesis.

Wang, the William B. Smith Professor of Mechanical and Materials Engineering and a widely recognized pioneer in battery recycling and sustainable manufacturing, will lead the development of bioengineered methods for recovering rare earth elements and other critical minerals.

Turning Industrial Waste Into Marketable Products

The researchers will also study whether the technologies can be scaled economically and practically for industrial use.

If the approach proves successful, it could open new ways to convert large volumes of industrial waste into marketable products. That could reduce dependence on newly mined resources, lower the environmental footprint of materials production, and strengthen domestic supplies of critical minerals and rare earth elements.

WPI graduate and undergraduate students will take part in the multiyear project through the university's immersive STEM experience.

The effort brings together sustainability, biotechnology, materials science, data science, and artificial intelligence. It also aims to help build a broader bioengineered, silicon-based materials ecosystem by connecting researchers, industry partners, policymakers, educators, and future innovators across multiple disciplines and sectors.

Imran said he expected stronger industrial coordination between Pakistan and China in energy storage. He also highlighted opportunities for technological innovation and global deployment.

title: Five things Scotland can do to prevent the next energy crisis and best use its renewables windfall
description:
When First Minister John Swinney set out his Programme for Government he promised a Scotland reshaped around prevention rather than crisis management.
The falling amounts of oil and gas produced there disappear into volatile international markets and do nothing to lower domestic energy prices.
Meanwhile, the opposite problem is happening on the renewables side: we have more in Scotland than we can currently use.
Last year, Scotland’s flagship Warmer Homes Scotland scheme, which gives fully funded home upgrades to homes in fuel poverty, still installed three times more fossil fuel heating systems than clean, electrified heating systems.
Asserting leverage in UK collaboration Scotland finds itself in the advantageous position of being a two-time beneficiary of an energy windfall: once in the fossil fuel era and once again for renewable energy.
text:
When First Minister John Swinney set out his Programme for Government he promised a Scotland reshaped around prevention rather than crisis management. This winter, the Scottish Government will have to manage an ongoing energy crisis - as heating oil prices remain high and gas prices, moderated so far by the energy price cap, climb higher.

A strategy centred on prevention, must also try to prevent the next energy crisis - and by far the best way to do that is to fund electrification, helping Scottish consumers embrace electricity in many more aspects of their lives. Yet, as new ministers in Holyrood and Westminster settle into a new parliamentary term, the energy debate continues to be dominated by supply and North Sea drilling.

The reality is that the North Sea is a declining, high-cost basin - there is no getting away from that. The falling amounts of oil and gas produced there disappear into volatile international markets and do nothing to lower domestic energy prices. Meanwhile, the opposite problem is happening on the renewables side: we have more in Scotland than we can currently use. In 2024, Scotland generated twice the amount of electricity that we consumed, over 70% of it from renewables, with most of the surplus sent south. And we could have generated much more electricity: with the grid currently unable to carry more electricity into England, in 2025 57% of the time there was a windfarm somewhere in Scotland being paid to turn off. The costs of paying these Scottish windfarms to turn off costs the UK hundreds of millions of pounds every year. Yet at the same time, over 85% of households remain dependent on gas or oil for their heating, the main chunk of home energy usage.

To deliver a preventative approach to future global energy price shocks, the Scottish Government should focus on five critical reforms:

1. Set an ambitious home decarbonisation target

Heat pumps are the best technology for decarbonising heat because they are three to four times more efficient than traditional gas boilers, converting every unit of electricity into significantly more heat output. At present Scotland’s installation ambition is too modest and overly delayed. Nesta has calculated that over this Parliament there need to be 110,000 heat pump installations to achieve effective residential electrification. Setting this target and being publicly ambitious about installation provides policy certainty for industry to build supply chain capacity and ensure the heating engineering sector can scale to meet this demand.

2. Acknowledge that insulation is not enough

Perhaps understandably, given our drafty homes and chilly climate, there is often a focus on insulation and taking a fabric-first approach to decarbonisation. The idea is we can reduce our energy demand through insulation as a route to decarbonisation. However the reality is that the Climate Change Committee have made clear that enhancements to building fabric and insulation would only deliver 14% of residential emission cuts advised by 2035. Insulation is important but not sufficient to meet the challenge.

3. Provide legislative certainty

The Programme for Government announced a heat in buildings bill due in the first year of the Parliamentary term. This Bill, which was delayed in the previous session, presents a significant opportunity for this Parliament to introduce tangible legislative mandates. There remain a number of options that the Government could consider to phase out the installation of gas boilers that go beyond the current draft bill. However, all would likely create political difficulty, and it is crucial that the Government builds broad political consensus and fosters deep public engagement to secure support for the shift to electrification. This legislation must also address the complexities of Scotland's diverse housing stock, including tenement reform, to facilitate neighbourhood-scale electrification rather than relying on isolated individual actions.

4. Prioritise electrification across fuel poverty schemes

While Scotland’s fuel poverty programmes might currently take the edge of energy costs for homes with a new boiler or insulation, they all-too-often keep homes locked in to an international fossil-fuel cost rollercoaster. Last year, Scotland’s flagship Warmer Homes Scotland scheme, which gives fully funded home upgrades to homes in fuel poverty, still installed three times more fossil fuel heating systems than clean, electrified heating systems. Reforming this national fuel poverty scheme, and local-authority led programmes, to focus on providing these homes with high-quality electrified systems - heat pumps, batteries and solar - will ensure that public funds are driving the transition to an electrostate and giving homes greater energy independence.

5. Asserting leverage in UK collaboration

Scotland finds itself in the advantageous position of being a two-time beneficiary of an energy windfall: once in the fossil fuel era and once again for renewable energy. But those two energy systems are at two very different life stages.

text:
COLUMBIA FALLS — A new subdivision is under development within the boundaries of a federal Superfund site, the first use of the Columbia Falls Aluminium Company plant property since the plant closed in 2009.

The 78-acre development by Mick Ruis will bring more than 400 housing units, and eventually commercial development, to the site, and on Thursday, Gov. Greg Gianforte and Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin praised it as part of a successful future for the blighted area.

“One of the most exciting steps of the Superfund process is being able to delist a project at the end of it, to be able to get an important vision not just started, but completed,” Zeldin said during a press conference. “Fortunately, we are at a very important milestone moment here in Columbia Falls, where there is just so much incredible progress imminently ahead on this project.”

The Columbia Falls Aluminum Company, known as CFAC, began operation in the 1950s, importing alumina and converting it into aluminum, supporting thousands of jobs in the Flathead Valley, but creating hazardous waste byproducts from the smelting process.

In 2016, the site received official Superfund designation from the federal Environmental Protection Agency, and this year a $57 million cleanup agreement was reached between CFAC, owned by the Swiss commodities firm Glencore, Ltd., and the federal government.

Touring the property on Thursday, Zeldin and Gianforte both complimented the work by Ruis, a major developer in the Valley, who purchased a huge swath of the property that has been controversial among local residents.

Residents and city officials have raised issues of having a major development in a wildlife corridor, straining city services, and whether there are additional health and safety concerns due to the proximity to a federal Superfund site.

But the development has been approved by the city and both the EPA and Montana Department of Environmental Quality have said the site does not require cleanup and is cleared for development, according to local reporting.

During the plant’s productive years, hazardous waste materials like cyanide, fluoride and arsenic were deposited in repositories around the CFAC site, which can be picked up by groundwater as it moves towards the Flathead River.

A major part of the cleanup process includes constructing a slurry wall that will be injected below the repository site to prevent further groundwater contamination.

Constructing the slurry wall is expected to be completed in 2029.

The cleanup will also include lining a nearby overflow ditch, adding a landfill to contain contaminants without having to transport them off site, and long-term monitoring of the remedy’s effectiveness.

“Our main goal with cleanup is to protect the Flathead River and cut off that clean groundwater from encountering the waste source,” said plant Superfund Project Manager Allie Archer.

In his comments to the press, Gianforte echoed Archer’s sentiment and highlighted the agreement signed between the EPA and Montana Department of Environmental Quality detailing what the cleanup plan would be, an agreement that followed years of scrutiny by watchdog groups.

“This is going to address the contamination, hazardous materials, and eliminate exposure to prevent contamination of groundwater and the Flathead River, which is right over here, near and dear to my heart,” Gianforte said, adding that he and First Lady Susan Gianforte recently camped on the banks of the Flathead River. “It’s great to see the cleanup efforts underway today to address the hazardous contaminants and return the site to productive use.”

Montana has nearly 20 federal Superfund sites, and DEQ administrator Sonja Nowakowski said the state is seeing progress at “nearly all of them right now.”
