text:
Planet Detroit originally published this story. Sign up for their weekly newsletter here.

By Brian Allnutt, Planet Detroit

Democrat Eli Savit pledges to continue challenging utilities on rate hikes and data center costs, while Republican Doug Lloyd has not detailed his utility oversight positions.

Outgoing Attorney General Dana Nessel pushed back on utility profits, data center contracts, executive perks, and coal plant operations.

Nessel has continued to appeal the MPSC’s approval of DTE’s power supply contracts for the 1.4-gigawatt Oracle and OpenAI data center in Saline Township.

Michigan voters will pick their next attorney general in November as Dana Nessel, a vocal intervenor in utility rate hike cases, concludes eight term-limited years in office.

Michigan voters will pick their next attorney general in November as Dana Nessel, a vocal intervenor in utility rate hike cases, concludes eight years in office.

Washtenaw County Prosecuting Attorney Eli Savit, a Democrat, faces Eaton County Prosecutor Doug Lloyd, a Republican, on the ballot. The winner will choose whether to continue Nessel’s work challenging Michigan utilities — and the federal government.

Nessel, a Democrat, pushed back on data center contracts; the size and frequency of utility rate hikes; sued the Trump administration over issues like the emergency orders forcing the continued operation of West Michigan’s J.H. Campbell coal plant.

The attorney general plays a key role in the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC) process as the only intervenor with the constitutional and statutory authority to represent residents in utility rate hike cases and other proceedings.

Other intervenors, like environmental and business groups, represent subsets of Michiganders, filing testimony in cases before the MPSC, which regulates investor-owned utilities like DTE Energy and Consumers Energy.

Savit’s campaign told Planet Detroit he will take on violent crime and protect public safety, as well as ensure ratepayer and environmental protections.

Savit is “unbought by corporate PACs” and “committed to using the AG’s authority to prevent corporations from ripping people off (and) stop polluters from poisoning our air and water, and to protect every Michigander’s rights,” his campaign said in a statement.

Lloyd’s campaign did not agree to an interview with Planet Detroit or reply to questions sent by email. The candidate touched on ratepayer advocacy in an interview on the WDIV-TV program “Flashpoint,” where he said he would talk to legislators about Michigan utilities’ ability to ask for rate hikes every year.

“It’s the consumers that are feeling the pain right now and I really believe that we need to have our utilities understand that that is a concern for all of Michigan,” Lloyd said.

Nessel set high standard for ratepayer advocacy, expert says

Michiganders should look for an attorney general who will continue Nessel’s work, Karlee Weinmann, research and communications manager for the Energy and Policy Institute, a utility watchdog group, told Planet Detroit.

“She’s absolutely among the leading attorneys general across the country in terms of advocating for the public interest and for ratepayers in utility regulation … at a time when public trust in the utilities and in utility regulation has plummeted,” Weinmann said.

An Ipsos poll, commissioned by consumer advocacy group PowerLines, found 77% of Americans are concerned their utility bills will continue to rise, and 76% want the government to perform stronger utility oversight.

Weinmann praised Nessel’s efforts to challenge things like private jet travel for company executives that was included in a DTE rate hike request and investor-owned utilities’ returns on equity, or the profit passed on to shareholders.

Return on equity is a costly line item in any utility rate case, Weinmann said: “It’s very important to see attorneys general focusing on that area and being as aggressive as they need to be to right-size utility profits.”

The MPSC granted DTE and Consumers 9.9% returns on equity as part of the utilities’ most recent electric rate hikes. A 2025 study from the nonprofit American Economic Liberties Project has criticized such returns for utility stocks that exceed stock market returns that average 6% to 7%, when accounting for inflation. High utility returns add $300 annually to the average customer’s power bills, according to the study.

Michigan House Democrats introduced legislation in March to expand the MPSC from three to five members, limit terms to 12 years, and require commission members to be elected.

The MPSC released policy recommendations for Michigan legislators in July, requesting authority to set multiyear rate plans, require utilities to show how they’re maximizing use of existing grid infrastructure, cut bonuses for utilities that buy power from third parties, and codify into law commission rules against shifting data center costs onto other ratepayers, among other provisions.

Utility power supply contracts for data centers will also likely require sustained involvement by the attorney general as proposals for the facilities continue to emerge in Michigan, and utilities seek to fast track approvals, Weinmann said.

Nessel, who cannot run again because of term limits, has continued to challenge the MPSC’s approval of DTE’s power supply contracts for the 1.4-gigawatt Oracle and OpenAI data center in Saline Township, which moved forward without a contested case in which Nessel and other intervenors would have submitted formal testimony.

Savit pledges to continue with MPSC intervention

One of the attorney general’s most important duties is to forcefully intervene at the MPSC, Savit told Planet Detroit in an interview, saying this role dates to long-serving Michigan Attorney General Frank Kelly, who robustly intervened at the commission.

“Rates should be geared toward ensuring reliability and should be no more than is necessary to do that,” Savit said. He also challenged the rate of return utilities have received and the inclusion of expenses like travel and lobbying in rate cases.

Protecting ratepayers from bearing the costs of bringing data centers online is non-negotiable, Savit said.

“The wealthiest companies in the world are seeking to build these things,” he said. “To my mind, it’s unconscionable to think that we would be forced to bear the cost of electricity use.”

Savit pledged to continue Nessel’s work to fight the Trump administration’s orders keeping Consumers Energy’s Campbell coal plan open, adding that it is adversely impacting ratepayers and public health.

Nessel said in an Aug. 17 statement that keeping the aging coal plant online cost Consumers Energy $295 million between May 2025 and June 30, 2026.

In August, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission approved Consumers’ request to spread the costs of operating the plant across the Midcontinent Independent System Operator’s northern and central regions, Utility Dive reported.

This area includes Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota, North Dakota and parts of Kentucky, Indiana, Illinois, Missouri, South Dakota, Montana, and Manitoba.

Savit said he supports efforts to remove corporate money from politics, including the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics ballot effort, which would ban monopoly utilities and companies with more than $250,000 in government contracts from making political contributions in the state.

This spending erodes public confidence in government, and it’s particularly important for the attorney general to avoid corporate donations, Savit said.

“The state attorney general’s most important client is the people of the state of Michigan, and there are a whole host of circumstances where the state AG is going to be called upon to potentially go up against corporate interests,” he said.

Savit signed the Michigan League of Conservation Voters’ “no utility money challenge,” promising to not knowingly accept more than $200 in total contributions from monopoly utility political action committees (PACs) and lobbyists, executives, employee PACs, and other groups aligned with utility interests.

Lloyd has not signed the pledge.

Public safety is the priority, Lloyd says

Lloyd has emphasized the attorney general’s law enforcement responsibilities in media appearances, and said on “Flashpoint” in April that the “one main focus of government should be public safety.”

In July, he told Petoskey’s WMKT radio: “It comes down to: Are you looking for social justice or public safety?”

Lloyd didn’t comment on the Trump administration’s orders keeping the J.H. Campbell plant open in a July interview with CBS News Detroit, but did challenge Nessel’s lawsuits against the federal government, saying she is politicizing the office.

“Day one, I’m going in, I’m looking at those past lawsuits,” Lloyd said. “There’s been like 50 lawsuits that have gone against the federal government and my question is: Are those lawsuits actually benefiting the citizens of Michigan?”

title: House Republicans push bill to protect fossil fuel industry from climate lawsuits
description:
House Republicans are moving legislation that would sharply limit efforts to make fossil fuel companies pay for climate-related damage.
The bill would block many liability claims involving businesses across the energy supply chain, a step that could protect oil and gas companies from lawsuits over climate damage, Inside Climate News reported.
The push comes as legal challenges against oil and gas companies continue to grow.
Oil companies, meanwhile, argue that pollution from non-renewable energy should be addressed under federal law rather than through state-level cases.
These stories look at efforts to make oil companies pay for damages, regulate pollution, and preserve clean energy incentives.
text:
House Republicans are moving legislation that would sharply limit efforts to make fossil fuel companies pay for climate-related damage.

Here's what to know

The House Judiciary Committee plans to debate and vote on the "Stop Climate Shakedowns Act of 2026," introduced in April by Wyoming Rep. Harriet Hageman. The bill would block many liability claims involving businesses across the energy supply chain, a step that could protect oil and gas companies from lawsuits over climate damage, Inside Climate News reported.

A Senate version from Texas Sen. Ted Cruz and three other Republicans would pursue the same goal. The proposal also claims there is no scientifically credible connection between pollution from burning non-renewable energy sources like gas, oil, and coal and climate disasters, despite decades of research showing that heat-trapping pollution contributes significantly to more destructive weather and extreme heat.

Hageman defended the proposal in a statement, saying, "Energy security is national security. America's energy producers should be protected from the dangerous legal precedent that would be set by the retroactive punishment of lawful activity."

The push comes as legal challenges against oil and gas companies continue to grow. Mike Meno, communications director for the Center for Climate Integrity, said that 11 states, Washington, D.C., two tribal governments, and dozens of cities and counties have sued the industry over alleged deception about climate impacts.

More background

When cities and counties are forced to spend more on wildfire preparedness, heat protections, and other climate adaptation efforts, taxpayers are often left to carry the burden.

One major case drawing close attention, Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, will be heard by the Supreme Court on Oct. 5, according to ICN. Boulder sued ExxonMobil and Suncor in 2018, seeking damages to help pay for adapting to extreme heat and wildfires. Oil companies, meanwhile, argue that pollution from non-renewable energy should be addressed under federal law rather than through state-level cases.

That argument is playing out as the federal government also pulls back climate protections. The Trump administration's Environmental Protection Agency repealed the Biden-era 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards covering current coal plants and new gas facilities and has also proposed narrowing its future authority over power plant pollution.

What's being done?

For now, the bill still has a long road to travel before it could become law. Even so, parts of it could end up in other must-pass legislation.

Local and state lawsuits remain among the biggest active efforts to force accountability. Those cases aim not only to test what companies knew and when, but also to secure funding for communities facing mounting damage from climate-fueled extremes.

Maggie Coulter, an attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity's Climate Law Institute, said the broader strategy would strip states of power at the same time federal protections are weakening.

"This is one piece of the bigger picture," Coulter said, according to ICN. "The federal government's backing off regulations. This kind of Big Oil immunity would take the power away from states to go after companies for their deceptive practices."

As Meno put it, "More than one in four Americans live in a community that is fighting to put big oil companies on trial to hold them accountable for their climate deception and make them pay for the harm that deception has caused."

Where can I learn more?

These stories look at efforts to make oil companies pay for damages, regulate pollution, and preserve clean energy incentives.

• In New York, lawmakers advanced legislation to make polluters pay for environmental damages.

• In Guyana, officials proposed new rules to address pollution problems in the oil industry.

• In Washington, five Republican senators are pushing to preserve clean energy tax credits despite repeal efforts.

Funding will help build a key processing facility in Northwestern Ontario, creating hundreds of jobs, attracting investment and strengthening Ontario's critical minerals supply chain.

TORONTO, Ontario, September 18, 2026 – Invest Ontario is providing up to $11 million in conditional loan support through Ontario's Critical Minerals Processing Fund (CMPF) to help Generation Mining Limited build its wholly owned Copper-Palladium Processing Facility at the Marathon Project in Northwestern Ontario.

The facility accounts for approximately $410 million of the Marathon Project's total $992 million capital investment and represents a major addition to Ontario's critical minerals sector. Once operational, the project is expected to create more than 450 direct jobs, including over 100 positions at the processing facility and approximately 350 mining jobs. Construction is also expected to support about 800 additional jobs. Together, these opportunities will create good-paying careers, support local businesses and contractors, and drive economic growth across Northwestern Ontario.

Invest Ontario's support will help move the fully permitted, construction-ready project toward development. In addition to financial support, Invest Ontario has worked with Generation Mining to connect the company with strategic partners as the project progressed.

The Copper-Palladium Processing Facility will strengthen Ontario's critical minerals value chain by processing minerals mined in the province into materials used by manufacturers in Canada and around the world. Demand for copper and palladium continues to grow as industries invest in electrification, advanced manufacturing and defence.

Copper plays a critical role in electric vehicles, power transmission systems and clean energy infrastructure. Palladium supports emissions-reduction technologies and a range of industrial applications. By expanding Ontario's processing capacity, the facility will help secure a reliable supply of critical minerals for manufacturers, strengthen domestic supply chains and capture more economic value within the province.

The project is also expected to generate opportunities for local businesses, contractors and Indigenous-owned companies throughout Northwestern Ontario. Generation Mining has established agreements with neighbouring Indigenous communities and continues to prioritize Indigenous participation in the project's development. This approach will help ensure economic benefits remain in the region while creating long-term employment and skills-development opportunities for local communities.

Ontario's abundant critical mineral resources, highly skilled workforce and competitive mining sector continue to attract investment from around the world. Projects such as Marathon help bring private capital into the province, create jobs and secure the materials needed to support Ontario's growing manufacturing, clean technology and industrial sectors.

As one of the most mineral-rich regions in the world, Northern Ontario plays a critical role in supporting the economic objectives and industrial capabilities of Canada and its allies. By supporting Generation Mining’s Marathon Project, our government is protecting the resilience and self-reliance of the province’s critical mineral supply chain and delivering on its commitment to keep minerals mined in Ontario processed and refined in Ontario, by our world-class workers.

Hon. Vic Fedeli

Minister of Economic Development, Job Creation and Trade

I want to thank the Government of Ontario for standing behind the Marathon Project. Minister Lecce, Minister Fedeli and their teams, together with Invest Ontario, have been true partners through this process, and their support helps carry Marathon from permits and plans into construction. Ontario has been clear about its ambition to lead on critical minerals, and we are proud to help deliver on it. We look forward to working with the Province and with Canada to build the next critical minerals mine in this country.

Jamie Levy

President and Chief Executive Officer, Generation Mining Limited

Ontario's competitive advantage in critical minerals goes beyond the resources in the ground. It comes from our ability to help companies move strategic projects forward. We're proud to support Generation Mining's investment in Marathon, which will create jobs, strengthen supply chains and reinforce Ontario's role as a reliable source of the materials needed by global manufacturers. This is exactly the type of investment that helps build a stronger, more resilient economy for Ontario.

Khawar Nasim

Chief Executive Officer, Invest Ontario

title: Why one U.S. automaker's truck of the year winning streak is over | Idaho Statesman
authors: Jamie L. LaReau, Detroit Free Press
description:

Jamie L. LaReau is the senior autos writer for USA TODAY Co. who covers Ford Motor Co. for the Detroit Free Press.
This article originally appeared on Detroit Free Press: Why one U.S. automaker's truck of the year winning streak is over Reporting by Jamie L. LaReau, Detroit Free Press / Detroit Free Press USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect Copyright Reuters or USA Today Network via Reuters Connect
text:
For the past six years Ford Motor has had bragging rights when it came to winning the North American Truck of the Year award – but this year it will not.

The North American Car, Truck and Utility Vehicle of the Year (NACTOY) jurors released the list of "Best of 2027" vehicles this week. Not one of the 25 vehicles – which will undergo strict judging scrutiny for the rest of the year before three win at the Detroit Auto Show in January – was a Ford vehicle.

It is shocking considering that in January 2026, Ford won truck of the year with the Maverick Lobo, in 2025 Ford won with the Ranger midsize pickup, in 2024 with the Super Duty, 2023 with the F-150 Lightning, 2022 with the Maverick and 2021 with the F-150, according to NACTOY website. Ford has won in other categories, too, during those years such as North American Utility of the Year in 2022 with Bronco and in that same category in 2021 with Mustang Mach-E SUV.

NACTOY jurors explained Ford's absence from the list as basically bad timing in its product cycle. That's because, to be considered for a NACTOY award, a vehicle must be either all-new or significantly redesigned and Ford lacked cars that met either of those requirements.

"Ford canceled a lot of electric vehicles that were supposed to be on the road by now and those cancelations left holes in its lineup. It's fair to say that's why they don't have more vehicles competing for these honors this year," said Detroit Free Press auto critic Mark Phelan, who is a NACTOY juror and board member.

Phelan noted the NACTOY jurors did consider two Mustang derivatives that had enough changes to their design to be evaluated. But the vehicles did not get enough votes to make the cut to the "best of" 25 contenders.

"They just fell short in terms of how much changes they had this year and how that compares to other vehicles that are new and significantly updated," Phelan said of the Mustangs.

Wall Street seems to understand and forgive Ford's absence from the list – for now.

"Ford is going through a transition period and has a lull in new vehicles hitting the market," Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at New York-based investment banking firm Yorkville Ives, told the Detroit Free Press, part of the USA TODAY Network. "Not being on this list is not a good look for Ford, but (CEO Jim) Farley is focused on driving growth and innovation the next few years. If they are not on this list next year it would be a black eye moment."

'Ford took its eye off the ball'

When asked for a comment for this article, Ford spokesman Mike Levine sent an emailed statement: "We have a winning lineup of vehicles that customers love, and we're proud to have earned NACTOY ‘Truck of the Year' the last six years in a row."

So what happened this year? Industry experts said Ford's business overhaul left product holes in its lineup that will cost it a NACTOY award.

In December 2025, Ford announced it was restructuring its business to the tune of $19.5 billion to shift focus from what was to be a future featuring all-electric vehicles to one, in the near-term at least, that offers more hybrids and gasoline powertrains.

As part of that shift, Ford discontinued the Ford Escape and Lincoln Corsair small SUVs in December. Both had been built at Ford's Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky. Ford is retooling that plant to start making an all-electric midsize pickup called Fathom on its new UEV platform there early next year to be followed by a family of EVs.

Phelan said Ford's overhaul likely disrupted its product planning companywide, eventhough other automakers such as General Motors and Stellantis have also changed product plans and have vehicles on the NACTOY list.

"An automaker has to be able walk and chew gum. It has to do two things at the same time: develop a line of electric vehicles and at the same time keep its gasoline and hybrid vehicles new and competitive. Ford did not do that as well as some of its competitors," Phelan said. "Ford took its eye off the ball."

Maybe next year for Ford

The 25 vehicles NACTOY listed – which include pickups such as the Chevrolet Silverado 1500, GMC Sierra 1500, Ram 1500 TRX SRT, and other vehicles, such as the Chevrolet Bolt and Jeep Cherokee, to name a few – were chosen by 46 automotive journalists who work in Canada, Mexico and the United States. Those 25 vehicles were selected from 56 new cars, trucks and SUVs already on sale, or expected to hit the market before the end of this year. The list includes vehicles with electric, hybrid and gasoline-powered drivetrains.

Phelan said the 25 "best of" vehicles will be narrowed down to nine finalists in three categories – best car, truck and utility – which will be announced in November at the Los Angeles Auto Show. The winner in each category will be announced Jan. 14 at Detroit Auto Show.

NACTOY juror and auto reporter for radio's WWJ (AM-950) Jeff Gilbert described Ford as "a perennial winner" of a NACTOY award that just fell prey to product cadence this time around.

"It has nothing to do with any of the quality issues at Ford, it's strictly product timetable for them," Gilbert said.

Ford leads the industry in recalls this year and has struggled with its quality over the past few years. But the quality of Ford's newer products is improving. The carmaker was ranked first by JD Power in an Intial Quality Survey this year among mainstream brands for the top quality in the first 90 days of vehicle ownership.

"They have a lot of stuff in the pipeline that we'll see," Gilbert said. "I imagine we'll see them in a big way (for NACTOY consideration) next year."

Ford will launch its new all-electric midsize pickup, Fathom, off its new UEV plaform next year.

As the Detroit Free Press reported last month, sources said Ford intends to bring to market several new vehicles in the next few years, which Ford has not publicly confirmed and the vehicle plans are subject to change based on market conditions. But sources said Ford is considering a four-door Mustang, a Ford small SUV to replace the Escape, for Lincoln an all-new SUV based on the Bronco design, and possibly five new all-electric vehicles based off the new UEV platform.

How much does winning matter?

Phelan said winning the North American vehicle of the year award is a huge marketing boon.

"These awards are used extensively in marketing and automakers invest millions of dollars in advertising to tout it when they win an award like this," Phelan said. "They have got ads ready to run the moment the award is announced."

That may be so, but industry observers also note that its impact on sales is fairly negligible.

"Automakers ... like getting earned media. It's free! Some automakers even offer bonuses to execs whose programs win awards," said John McElroy, industry expert and host of "Autoline After Hours," in an email to the Detroit Free Press. "Third-party endorsements are always nice because they're more credible to the public. But there is no correlation to car of the year awards and sales. In fact, just the opposite. Some of the past winners have turned out to be total sales duds."

McElroy listed the 2026 Dodge Charger, 2025 VW ID Buzz, 2024 Kia EV9 and 2023 Ford Lightinng and Kia EV6 as examples of winners on the stage, but disappointing in the showroom.

Mobility Global data does not indicate what impact awards have had on sales, but some data does show that the age of an automaker's portfolio can have an impact, Stephanie Brinley, associate director at Mobility Global, a leading provider of auto industry data, intelligence and forecasting, said in an email.

"Typically, an automaker does see sales improve with fresh products, and products tend to see sales slow in the later years of a lifecycle," Brinley told the Detroit Free Press. "In that way, the overall age of Ford's portfolio can have an impact on sales."

But it is a big point of pride. Phelan recalls at the January 2026 auto show a Ford executive approached him with elation over the fact that it was the sixth year in a row Ford had won the truck of the year category.

But some are blase to the whole affair. Morningstar autos analyst David Whiston said Ford's NACTOY winning streak "had to end at some point."

"I don't think Wall Street cares a ton about this, but you do want to see them winning it from time to time to show they are a leader," Whiston told the Detroit Free Press. "Every year is not essential. What matters to the stock is how much free cash flow is generated and how consistent will that generation be and are results better or worse than expected each quarter."

Jamie L. LaReau is the senior autos writer for USA TODAY Co. who covers Ford Motor Co. for the Detroit Free Press. Contact Jamie at jlareau@freepress.com. Follow her on Twitter @jlareauan. To sign up for our autos newsletter. Become a subscriber.

text:
The Trump administration illegally terminated a $7 billion Solar for All program intended to make solar power accessible to more than 900,000 lower-income Americans, a federal judge in Rhode Island ruled Friday.

The Environmental Protection Agency rescinded the Solar for All funds in August 2025 after President Donald Trump’s massive tax and spending law passed in Congress a month earlier, with Administrator Lee Zeldin calling the Biden-era grant program a “boondoggle.”

District Judge Mary McElroy wrote in the ruling that Congress clearly intended the EPA to continue administering the Solar for All grants that were already obligated. The EPA acted contrary to this intent and without any other statutory authority when it terminated the program, McElroy wrote. She vacated the termination.

The EPA did not immediately respond to a request for comment Friday.

The lawsuit filed in Rhode Island by the Rhode Island AFL-CIO labor organization and others — including the public interest law center Rhode Island Center for Justice and the nonprofit Solar United Neighbors — highlighted the importance of the program for local workforces and lower-income communities seeking access to clean-energy project funding.

Patrick Crowley, president of the Rhode Island AFL-CIO, called the decision “a big victory” for states across the country.

“If and when the program does get up and running, there will be thousands and thousands of union jobs created across the United States,” he said Friday. “We were proud to be the lead plaintiff.”

Clean, affordable power like solar shouldn’t be a luxury, said Alex St. Pierre, vice president for environmental justice at Conservation Law Foundation, one of the nonprofit legal advocacy groups representing the plaintiffs.

“Communities have waited long enough,” St. Pierre said in a statement. “Nearly every family is looking for ways to cut their energy bill. These dollars should go where Congress intended: toward lower energy bills, less climate pollution, good jobs and cleaner air.”

In May, for the first time, solar supplied more of the nation’s electricity than coal.

The Trump administration has targeted a host of programs and policies dedicated to clean energy. The $7 billion Solar for All program was part of the $27 billion “green bank,” formally known as the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund. It was established in the Democratic-backed climate law passed in 2022 under former President Joe Biden. The attorneys general of more than a dozen states also sued over the canceled solar program funding. A federal judge in Washington dismissed the case for lack of jurisdiction in June. The plaintiffs have appealed.

The other $20 billion, also canceled by the Trump administration, was slated for eight community development banks and nonprofit organizations for tens of thousands of projects to combat the effects of climate change, such as residential energy efficiency projects to larger-scale investments such as community cooling. A divided federal appeals court said last month that the Trump administration improperly terminated the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, handing a win to a coalition of nonprofits picked to run the effort.

text:
SPRINGFIELD, Ill. (Capitol News Illinois) — Illinois has made substantial progress in reducing greenhouse gas emissions in recent years, but it is not yet on track to meet its goal of reaching net-zero emissions by 2050.

That’s the conclusion of a new Comprehensive Climate Action Plan released this month by the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency.

To reach that goal, the report suggests Illinois will need to enact significant changes across virtually every sector of its economy, including transportation, building construction, manufacturing, agriculture and waste disposal.

“Illinoisans are seeing the extreme heat and storms climate change has brought to our doorstep this summer,” Illinois Climate Advisor JC Kibbey said in a statement announcing the report. “We are feeling the high, unpredictable costs of fossil fuel every time we reach for our wallets. This plan shows the great progress we’ve made on climate and clean energy — and how much more we have left to do.”

In 2024, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency awarded Illinois a $430 million grant to implement programs to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. That money came through the federal Climate Pollution Reduction Grant program, which was an element of then-President Joe Biden’s signature Inflation Reduction Act.

The Comprehensive Climate Action Plan is intended to provide a roadmap for Illinois to reduce its carbon footprint to as little as 72% below its 2005 baseline. It also outlines two scenarios under which Illinois could virtually eliminate all carbon emissions.

Those would involve a combination of incentive packages and regulatory changes that would affect nearly every sector of the economy. But doing so, the report suggests, would produce $21 billion a year in net economic benefits.

Current policies

According to the document, Illinois cut its net greenhouse gas emissions by 32% from 2005 to 2023. That was due mainly to a shift in electric generation toward natural gas and renewable sources such as wind and solar power.

The transportation industry also saw significant reductions due to improved fuel efficiency standards and the gradual adoption of electric vehicles.

Those trends are expected to continue into the future as long, the report states, as Illinois adheres to its current policies such as the 2021 Climate and Equitable Jobs Act, which calls for the complete elimination of carbon-emitting power production by 2050, and the state’s Electric Vehicle Rebate Program, which offers incentives for lower-income consumers to switch to electric vehicles.

But they will not be enough to reach the goal of net-zero emissions by 2050, according to the report. At best, without any additional policy changes, the report estimates net carbon emissions will only fall to 133 million metric tons by 2050, a 53% reduction below the 2005 baseline.

Path to further reductions

The document outlines a laundry list of additional actions Illinois could take to reduce its carbon footprint even further, starting with providing rebates and other incentives to convert all forms of commercial vehicles, including medium- and heavy-duty vehicles, to electric.

It also proposes new regulations on residential and commercial buildings. Those include adopting clean heat standards that would require a 22% reduction in emissions from natural gas by 2035, offering subsidies to install heat pumps in residential homes, adopting all-electric construction codes for new construction and phasing out gasoline-powered lawn and landscaping equipment by 2035.

It also proposes additional regulations for industrial activities such as requiring net zero emissions from cement production by 2050 and requiring reductions in emissions intensity of cement, glass, iron and steel used in public construction.

The plan also proposes stronger methane monitoring and abatement regulations for landfills and additional incentives for farmers to adopt practices that reduce carbon dioxide emissions.

The report estimates that adopting all the measures outlined in the plan would reduce the state’s carbon footprint to 79 million metric tons, or 72% below 2024 levels.

The document also outlines two scenarios for achieving a complete “net zero” footprint by 2050, both requiring high levels of energy efficiency and replacing fossil fuels with electrification or other kinds of renewable fuels.

One plan, called the “moderate efficiency and flexibility” scenario, assumes full electrification of buildings by 2050 with 32% of households using hybrid heat pumps. It also assumes a rapid expansion of electric vehicles.

The “high efficiency and flexibility” scenario places greater emphasis on reducing energy demand. It calls for shifting the focus of new residential development to multifamily buildings instead of single-family homes to reduce heating and cooling loads. It also calls for higher density development and increased reliance on public transportation to reduce the overall number of vehicle miles traveled on roads.

Costs and benefits

The report acknowledges that adopting the policies it outlines would require substantial new investments from the state, private industry and consumers. Those include costs for new infrastructure, vehicles, heat pumps and alternative fuels, to name a few.

But the report says those investments will also yield long-term cost savings from reduced fossil fuel consumption, greater efficiencies, reduced greenhouse gas emissions and improved health and air quality benefits.

It estimates the improvements in air quality alone would lead to between 392 and 631 fewer premature deaths per year. That translates to between $8.8 and $13.8 billion in avoided healthcare costs and increased worker productivity.

“Including the monetized benefits of reduced (greenhouse gas) emissions and health benefits, the total annual net benefit of the Increased State Action scenario reaches $21 billion by 2050,” the report concludes.

“Since adoption of the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act, Illinois has been a national leader in addressing carbon emissions, particularly from the energy and transportation sectors,” Illinois EPA Director James Jennings said in a statement. “The (Comprehensive Climate Action Plan) builds on these past successes by identifying a path for Illinois to achieve significant reductions in climate change-causing greenhouse gases and meet the state’s long term climate goals.”

(Reporting by Peter Hancock, Capitol News Illinois)

Capitol News Illinois is a nonprofit, nonpartisan news service that distributes state government coverage to hundreds of news outlets statewide. It is funded primarily by the Illinois Press Foundation and the Robert R. McCormick Foundation.

text:
A new patent published September 17, 2026, adds the latest chapter to a quietly growing body of Stellantis intellectual property built around an unusual idea: replacing the conventional piston-engine range extender with a compact gas turbine. Filed by FCA US LLC under PCT/FR2026/000028 and published as WO2026190425, the application describes a stand-alone turbogenerator system for energy transformation.

Taken alone, the filing could be dismissed as speculative IP housekeeping. But it isn't alone. Stellantis and its subsidiary brands have returned to this technology repeatedly across multiple filings spanning 2024 through 2026, each one patenting a different piece of a sophisticated gas-turbine electrical-generation system. Together, they tell a more deliberate story — one that connects directly to the company's September 2025 decision to walk away from full-size battery-electric trucks entirely.

A Patent Trail That Spans Multiple Years and Filings

The clearest link between Stellantis' turbine research and electric vehicles appears in WO2025083344A1, an international application filed in September 2024 and published in April 2025. Its title leaves little room for interpretation: "Electric Motor Vehicle Comprising A Range Extender Device Comprising A Gas Turbine." The filing describes an EV whose traction battery and electric motor draw energy from a fuel-powered turbogenerator — the architecture Stellantis calls an IRReGT, or Intercooled Recuperative Reheat Gas Turbine.

A related French patent, FR3154438A1, assigned jointly to PSA Automobiles and FCA US and published in April 2025, goes further in describing the system's design. It details low- and high-pressure compressor and turbine stages, intercooling, exhaust-heat recuperation, and additional waste-heat recovery loops. Some embodiments incorporate an Organic Rankine Cycle or steam Rankine Cycle to convert otherwise wasted thermal energy into additional electricity.

The activity continued into 2026. A filing published in May of that year, WO2026099551A1, focuses on vaporizing fuel inside a recuperating heat exchanger before it reaches the combustion chamber — a refinement aimed at efficiency and packaging rather than a broad conceptual claim. A separate January 2026 application describes a multi-stage turbomachine with multiple generators, combustion chambers, an intercooler, a recuperator, and control logic tied to generator speed, pressure, and airflow. The newest filing, WO2026190425, extends the series further. This is not one patent protecting one idea — it is a sustained, iterative engineering program.

Why a Turbine Makes Engineering Sense Here

In a range-extended EV, the combustion unit has a fundamentally different job than in a conventional car. The electric motors drive the wheels; the combustion system exists primarily to generate electricity. That distinction matters for turbines, which generally perform better under stable, relatively high-load conditions than when constantly accelerating and decelerating with driver inputs.

A 2020 study published in Applied Thermal Engineering experimentally investigated a micro-gas-turbine EV range extender and reported a power-to-weight ratio of roughly 0.48 to 0.8 kW/kg, with calculated thermal efficiency of approximately 35% for one recuperated configuration under specified design conditions. The researchers concluded that microturbines were technically feasible in this role.

The same body of research, however, flags real limitations. A 2021 Applied Thermal Engineering study found that while a microturbine range extender could achieve low regulated emissions, its specific fuel consumption was considerably higher than a comparable piston engine at similar power output. Rapidly changing power demands also required more sophisticated control strategies than a turbine naturally accommodates.

That context makes Stellantis' engineering choices look deliberate. The recuperation, intercooling, reheating, and waste-heat recovery systems detailed across the patent series address precisely the efficiency weaknesses that have historically kept microturbines out of production vehicles.

The Business Context Behind the R&D

Stellantis' turbine patent work does not exist in a vacuum. In September 2025, the company abandoned its full-size battery-electric Ram pickup program as demand for large BEV trucks slowed. Simultaneously, it renamed the range-extended pickup previously known as the Ramcharger as the Ram 1500 REV, signaling a clearer commitment to the range-extender path for its truck lineup.

The patents stop short of confirming what powertrain will ultimately reach production, and the filings themselves make no claims about launch timing or specific vehicle programs. What they do reveal is that Stellantis has invested engineering resources in turbine range-extender technology across multiple years and multiple distinct technical problems — efficiency, fuel delivery, thermal management, and control systems. For a company that has publicly pivoted toward range-extended powertrains for its largest vehicles, that pattern of R&D is worth watching closely.

text:
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass convene 2026 Urban 20 Summit, with leaders of 35 cities from around the world

Cities will show how climate action can improve lives by delivering more affordable and resilient homes, cutting energy costs, creating good jobs and protecting communities from extreme weather

U20 kicks off Climate Week NYC, with C40 mayors advancing action on extreme heat and resilience, responsible data center growth, clean air and sustainable housing

New York, USA (19 September 2026) – Mayor Zohran Mamdani will welcome mayors from across the United States and around the world to New York this weekend, as city leaders unite for practical action on climate, housing, and migration, as well as making communities safer, healthier and more resilient for newcomers and long-term residents.

New York City and Los Angeles are Co-Chairs of the 2026 Urban 20 (U20). The U20 Mayors Summit, taking place from 19–21 September and convened by C40 Cities and United Cities and Local Governments (UCLG), in partnership with the Mayors Migration Council (MMC), is expected to bring together more than 35 cities from across the G20 countries, represented by 25 mayors alongside deputy mayors and senior city leaders.

US cities including Atlanta, Chicago, Denver, Miami, Phoenix, San Diego and Seattle will be represented, alongside cities from across Canada, Europe, Africa, Latin America and Asia. Their presence demonstrates continued US city leadership and the determination of mayors to work across borders and political divides at a moment when international cooperation is under increasing strain.

The summit will focus on three interconnected challenges facing cities and their residents: housing, climate change, and migration.

Mayors will argue that these challenges – alongside the affordability crisis being felt by many city residents around the world – cannot be tackled in isolation. Climate impacts are increasing pressure on household finances and public services, whilst also contributing to driving people from their homes and putting city residents in danger from extreme weather.

Dependence on fossil fuels leaves families and economies exposed to volatile energy costs while contributing to pollution and extreme weather that undermines the health and safety of daily life. At the same time, cities are welcoming newcomers driven by economic opportunity, labour demand, and climate-driven displacement. These are realities that, met well, can strengthen rather than strain local communities.

City leaders will also show how climate action can improve people’s lives now: delivering healthier, more affordable and resilient homes, lowering energy costs, creating good jobs, cleaning up the air, and protecting communities from extreme heat, flooding and other increasingly severe climate impacts.

Mayors will discuss measures cities are already taking to build more affordable housing, protect tenants and make homes and neighborhoods more resilient. On migration, they will examine how cities can welcome newcomers while maintaining strong public services and social cohesion for all residents. Leaders will also focus on accelerating the clean energy transition while ensuring residents benefit through lower costs, greater energy security, good jobs and healthier communities.

Across all three areas, mayors will make the case that cities are ready to deliver, but need the powers, finance and partnerships to match their responsibilities and ambitions.

The summit will conclude on Sunday with the ratification of a communique setting out a shared city agenda for action. Representatives from the United Nations and other international organisations will then be invited to respond.

Cities at Climate Week NYC

The U20 Summit kicks off a major week of city climate leadership in New York, as C40 mayors join leaders from government, business and civil society groups at Climate Week NYC, one of the world’s largest annual gatherings focused on climate action.

Extreme heat and urban resilience will be at the heart of C40’s work throughout the week, with mayors advancing solutions to protect residents as temperatures rise and pushing for greater investment in adaptation and preparedness. The need for these actions has been shown around the world this year, with Europe experiencing record heat and dozens of countries preparing for the impact of the predicted ‘Super El Nino’.

C40 mayors will also advance efforts to create sustainable data centers, building on the principles of the Global Urban Data Centers Pact launched at London Climate Action Week in June. The pact brings together nearly fifty mayors from six continents around a common approach to ensure that the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure supports economic growth without driving up residents’ energy costs or placing unsustainable pressure on electricity grids, water supplies, land, and the environment.

The week will also provide an important staging point towards COP31, where mayors will continue to show that they can work with world leaders to accelerate climate ambition and ensure the experience of cities helps shape the next phase of international co-operation.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York City said: “This weekend, New York City is welcoming mayors from across the United States and around the world, united by a shared belief that the people who keep our cities running should be able to afford to live in them.

“We are proud to co-chair the Urban 20 with Los Angeles and to welcome leaders who refuse to leave working families to face rising rents, soaring energy bills, and deadly heat waves alone, regardless of where they were born or their immigration status.

“At a time of division and retreat, our cities are choosing cooperation and showing what is possible when we work together to build a better future for all.”

Mayor Karen Bass of Los Angeles said: “Cities are on the front lines of the climate crisis, but we are also where solutions are being put into action every day. From building more resilient homes and neighborhoods to creating good jobs, cleaning our air and protecting Angelenos from extreme heat and other climate impacts, we are delivering real results for our communities.

“Los Angeles is proud to co-chair the Urban 20 with New York City to bring US and global mayors together around a shared agenda to make our cities safer, healthier and more affordable.”

Mayor Yvonne Aki-Sawyerr of Freetown, Co-Chair of C40 Cities, and MMC Founding Leadership Board Member, said: “Whether we lead a city in Africa, Europe, Asia or the Americas, mayors from around the world see many of the same pressures on our residents: rising costs, extreme heat, housing insecurity and displacement.

“But cities are also where solutions are being delivered. We want young people to have real opportunities at home, and we want climate change to never be the reason they have to leave. By working together, sharing what works and investing in a just transition, we can tackle the climate crisis while creating jobs, improving lives and making our communities more resilient.

“The message from mayors in New York will be clear: give cities the tools and resources to act, and we will deliver.”

Mayor Ugur Ibrahim Altay of Konya, President of United Cities and Local Governments (UCLG) said: “The spirit we need to carry forward is one of cooperation over division, solidarity over isolation, and shared responsibility for protecting our communities.

“A stronger multilateral system is needed. It will need to trust cities, work with them, and design solutions that can be delivered through them.

“That is the present we are shaping every day and the future we are committed to delivering.

Kate Johnson, C40 Cities Director for North America, said: “At a time when international cooperation is under enormous strain, US mayors joining counterparts from around the world sends an important message: cities are still working together, and they’re focused on getting things done.”

“Mayors understand those connections because they deal with them every day. They are showing that climate action can mean more affordable and resilient homes, lower energy costs, cleaner air, good jobs and communities better protected from extreme weather.”

Emilia Saiz, Secretary General of UCLG, said: ”Public service delivery is about shaping communities in which people can live with dignity.

“That is precisely why the three priorities of this U20 cycle matter: they speak directly to the conditions that shape people’s daily lives and to the capacity of our cities to protect dignity, opportunity and belonging.”

Vittoria Zanuso, Executive Director of the Mayors Migration Council, said: “Affordability, climate and migration are part of the same story: whether people can build stable, dignified lives in the cities they call home.

“By putting migration at the heart of this year’s U20 agenda, mayors are sending a clear message: cities are not waiting for global debates to catch up – They are already delivering solutions and shaping the conversation.

We’re proud to work with Mayor Mamdani, Mayor Bass, C40 and UCLG to carry that leadership forward and back it up with the partnerships and resources needed to scale what works.”

title: Space-Based Solar Power Could Reach the Grid by 2028 | OilPrice.com
description:
The artificial intelligence energy crisis is catalyzing the development pipeline for space-based solar energy.
The idea is this: by putting solar panels into orbit, the sun will never set on them, thereby solving the biggest problem associated with solar energy – its intermittency.
Space-based solar is not a new idea; scientists have been working on developing a logistically and commercially feasible model for decades now.
So why are we throwing so many resources into space-based solar power, especially when you consider that solar photovoltaics here on Earth is already the cheapest form of energy that there is?
Plus, solar panels in space would be dispatchable, as solar satellites can reach enormous portions of the planet.
text:
The artificial intelligence energy crisis is catalyzing the development pipeline for space-based solar energy. As the world rushes to build up more energy production capacity in a scramble to keep up with skyrocketing demand from data center hyperscalers, the public and private sectors alike are increasingly adopting an all-of-the-above approach to energy investing, including next-gen and emerging technologies like putting solar panels into space, where they can access sunlight 24 hours a day.

The idea is this: by putting solar panels into orbit, the sun will never set on them, thereby solving the biggest problem associated with solar energy – its intermittency. The energy captured by those solar satellites would then be beamed back down to Earth through the use of powerful lasers or through microwave beams, depending on the technology being applied.

Space-based solar is not a new idea; scientists have been working on developing a logistically and commercially feasible model for decades now. But with the new influx of interest and investing dollars coming from the tech sector, it might finally be time for that vision to become a reality. A small but growing group of startups think that they will be able to begin operations in just a handful of years.

One of those startups is Virginia’s Overview Energy. The company, which is setting up operations in one of the states struggling the most intensely with energy price hikes driven by sprawling data center campuses, thinks that it could beam solar power to the grid all the way from space as early as January 2028. “We really believe that we are able to provide utility-scale power with this technology,” co-CEO Darko Filipi recently told the Washington Post. And that’s not all. Filipi estimates that his company alone could supply one-fourth of the country’s energy demand growth over the next decade.

The four-year-old startup inked a deal with Meta earlier this year, agreeing to provide up to 1 gigawatt of space solar energy to the tech giant. That’s about as much as the output of a nuclear reactor. However, that agreement is based on a technology that still hasn’t been tested in a real-world setting. And even if the technology does get off the ground (so to speak) even the most optimistic of projections say that space-based solar won’t become cost competitive before the year 2040.

Other outlooks are far less rosy. “The technology may work,” Amory Lovins, a Stanford physicist and co-founder of the energy think tank RMI, told the Washington Post. “But I have serious doubts the economics do.” Lovins pointed to the many other forms of clean, abundant, proven, and even round-the-clock power options – such as nuclear and geothermal energies – that can produce electricity much more cheaply.

So why are we throwing so many resources into space-based solar power, especially when you consider that solar photovoltaics here on Earth is already the cheapest form of energy that there is? One of the most critical factors is competition over scarce land resources. Finding viable tracts of land for utility-scale solar developments has proven increasingly difficult, as pushback against massive renewable projects have gained traction in many rural areas.

“Utility-scale solar and wind farms require at least ten times as much space per unit of power as coal- or natural gas–fired power plants, including the land used to produce and transport the fossil fuels,” states a 2022 insight report from strategy & management consulting firm McKinsey & Company. “Wind turbines are often placed half a mile apart, while large solar farms span thousands of acres.”

Putting solar panels in space would therefore solve this issue of, well, space. This context makes the promise of companies like Overview Energy extremely attractive to developers. The company claims that it could meet a quarter of new energy demand in the United States without needing to do any new construction on land.

Plus, solar panels in space would be dispatchable, as solar satellites can reach enormous portions of the planet. A given satellite would be able to beam energy straight to the grids where it is needed most, when it is needed most. This ability to switch between grids and nations in real time would be a game-changer for energy security.
