Varanasi (Uttar Pradesh) [India], September 18 (ANI): The Indian Institute of Technology (Banaras Hindu University), Varanasi, has strengthened its international research collaboration in electric mobility with the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, with the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) for joint research and innovation in electric vehicles and sustainable mobility.

MoU was signed on September 8, 2026, at the Electric Vehicle Centre (EVC), University of Michigan, between Prof. Amit Patra, Director, IIT (BHU) Varanasi, and Prof. Todd Allen, Associate Dean for Research, University of Michigan.

A high-level delegation from IIT (BHU), led by Prof Amit Patra, visited the University of Michigan's Electric Vehicle Centre to formalise the collaboration and discuss opportunities for joint research, innovation and academic engagement in the rapidly evolving field of electric mobility.

Addressing the gathering, Prof Amit Patra highlighted IIT (BHU)'s contributions to e-mobility research and emphasised the complementary strengths of the two institutions. He said the collaboration would provide opportunities to combine IIT (BHU)'s expertise in e-mobility with the University of Michigan's capabilities in electric vehicle systems, thereby fostering joint innovation and creating a wider global impact.

Prof Rajeev Kumar Singh, Head of the Department of Electrical Engineering and Coordinator of the Centre for Transportational E-Mobility (CTEM), presented two sanctioned ongoing projects under the IIT (BHU)-University of Michigan collaboration. He also discussed possibilities for further engagement in other ongoing and proposed initiatives at IIT (BHU). Faculty members Debdip Bhandary, Abir Ghosh, Udita Ghosh and Prodyut Dhar participated in the discussions online.

IIT (BHU) delegation comprised Prof Amit Patra, Director; Prof Rajeev Kumar Singh, Head, Department of Electrical Engineering; Prof. Hiralal Pramanik, Dean (Resource & Alumni); Vish Narayanan, Distinguished Alumnus; and Sri Mirle, Senior Alumnus.

The University of Michigan delegation included Prof Alan Taub, Director, Electric Vehicle Centre; Christophe Mangin, Managing Director, EVC; Prof Todd Allen, Associate Dean for Research, College of Engineering; Prof. Jason Siegel; Prof Heath Hofmann; and Prof Amit Misra.

During the visit, the two institutions held detailed discussions on the two sanctioned projects and other projects under consideration.

Discussions on advanced materials also led to an agreement to constitute a Materials Research Team, which will work towards collaborative research and the development of a long-term white paper outlining potential research directions.

The visit also provided an opportunity to explore further avenues of collaboration with the University of Michigan and strengthen alumni and institutional engagement between the two institutions.

The MoU marks a significant step in IIT (BHU)'s efforts to expand its international research partnerships and advance cutting-edge work in electric vehicles and sustainable mobility. The collaboration is expected to create new opportunities for joint research, faculty and student engagement, and innovation in the global electric mobility ecosystem.

IIT (BHU) Varanasi expressed its gratitude to the University of Michigan and the Electric Vehicle Centre for their warm hospitality and support during the visit. (ANI)

text:
A fire that sparked Friday at the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County ignited in batteries that had not yet been removed after a larger fire at the same facility in January 2025.

The county issued shelter-in-place orders within a third of a mile of the Vistra battery energy storage facility at the power plant at 7301 state Highway 1 after the fire was first reported around 6:15 a.m. Friday. Those orders were lifted at around 4 p.m.

Authorities held a midday briefing to provide an update on the fire, which was expected to burn itself out by Saturday, but was brought under control Friday afternoon. The fire involved batteries that had not yet been removed from the site after the larger fire on Jan. 16, 2025.

Assemblymember Dawn Addis says about 1,500 hard-to-access batteries remain on the property.

Jess Cortez, fire chief with the North County Fire Protection District said the batteries were inaccessible after the 2025 fire because they were along a wall at risk of collapse. After they caught fire Friday, Cortez said the "best tactic is to let these batteries burn themselves out."

The batteries were still energized but were idle and that unit had been disconnected from the electric grid after the 2025 fire, according to Ron George, manager of the Vistra plant in Moss Landing. George acknowledged that until all batteries are removed from the site, there is a possibility of future flareups like the one that occurred Friday.

The shelter-in-place orders in the immediate vicinity of the facility remained in place until Friday afternoon. Authorities had also initially instructed students and staff at some schools in the area to stay inside Friday morning, but eventually allowed students to go outside. No injuries have been reported in connection with the fire.

Monterey County Supervisor Glenn Church, who represents the Moss Landing area, has led multiple community meetings about the 2025 fire and resulting investigation and said he is "deeply disappointed and frustrated" at having to deal with another fire at the same site.

Church said the fire underscores how volatile the battery storage systems can be and said it is "troublesome for the community when this continues to come up."

Officials with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Monterey Bay Air Resources District have been monitoring sensors around the facility and said they did not show readings out of the ordinary Friday. A meteorologist with the National Weather Service said light winds and a marine layer kept smoke from the fire from spreading very far.

The cause of the 2025 fire has not been released and authorities did not say what might have sparked Friday's new blaze. The EPA earlier in September said it was starting the final phase of battery cleanup and demolition of the battery storage building and was going to "take every precaution to mitigate the risk of a fire incident on-site."

Prior to Friday's fire, the EPA had estimated that the battery removal and building demolition process would be complete by mid-2027.

Monterey County sheriff's spokesperson Cmdr. Andres Rosas said there was no estimate yet for when the shelter-in-place orders will be lifted.

"We will update the community as soon as we make a decision," Rosas said.

Speaker of the Assembly Robert Rivas issued the following statement on the fire:

“The safety of our Central Coast community is always a top priority, and my team is closely monitoring the battery storage facility fire at Moss Landing. We are grateful to the firefighters and first responders on the scene, and our office is receiving regular updates. If you live in the area, please follow all emergency guidance and warnings, and heed the directions of local officials. Thanks again to the brave first responders and emergency personnel always working to protect our community.”

text:
New Mexico’s effort to require manufacturers to label consumer products that contain so-called ‘forever chemicals’ infringes on commercially protected speech, according to a preliminary injunction issued Wednesday by U.S. District Judge Margaret Strickland.

The disputed rule stems from the PFAS Protection Act, which the New Mexico Legislature passed and Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham enacted last year. It would require manufacturers to label consumer products containing PFAS — aka per and polyfluoroalkyl substances. The New Mexico Environmental Improvement Board sanctioned the rule in March.

Studies show PFAS is linked to kidney and reproductive cancers, decreased fertility, fetal developmental delays, disruption of immune responses and liver function in humans.

The American Chemistry Council, which advocates for chemical manufacturers, and several national manufacturer organizations, sued the New Mexico Environment Department on July 1. The organizations argued that the state requirement violates the First Amendment by enforcing manufacturers to communicate a government-mandated message and asked for the court to stop implementation of the rule set for next year.

In her order, Strickland wrote that New Mexico failed to demonstrate how the label “is a rational vehicle to achieve the goals of protecting consumer and environmental health,” and added that “the state proclaims the regulation exists to raise consumer awareness, but underneath intends the label to operate as a warning in disguise.”

The label itself does not comment on whether PFAS poses a risk to consumer or environmental health and safety, a requirement needed to supersede the plaintiff’s right to commercially protected speech, Strickland wrote.

“I’d be lying if I didn’t say I was disappointed,” New Mexico Environment Department Secretary James Kenney told Source NM.

Kenney said that New Mexico “absolutely” plans to move forward in challenging the injunction, adding that NMED won many of its arguments and that Strickland “made a solid roadmap” for the department to consider.

For example, the plaintiffs argued the PFAS label does not convey factual information due to the broad nature of what constitutes a PFAS chemical and that the label is controversial.

Strickland disagreed with both arguments, saying New Mexico’s labelling rule has the same definition of PFAS as other states that have passed similar regulations — Colorado, California and Connecticut. She added that the plaintiffs provided no evidence that consumers find the image inflammatory or controversial.

New Mexico’s labelling rule has faced backlash from the national manufacturing community since its inception. In addition to the American Chemistry Association, the National Association of Manufacturers and six other manufacturing organizations were parties to the lawsuit, with NAM issuing a statement welcoming the judge’s ruling.

“The NAM is committed to securing permanent relief to ensure manufacturers aren’t forced to redesign products, packaging and manufacturing lines to accommodate an unconstitutional labeling requirement that imposes tremendous costs on both businesses and consumers,” Linda Kelly, NAM chief legal officer, said in a statement.

But for NMED, the issue is about transparency.

“This preliminary injunction shows that the intent of industry is to keep New Mexicans in the dark and not educate them on what types of PFAS might be coming in from their grocery stores or big box retailers,” Kenney told Source NM. “Education shouldn’t scare the American Chemistry Council, but here in New Mexico — apparently it does.”

text:
This month, U.S. EPA has proposed approval of both the Indiana Department of Environmental Management and Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources coal combustion residuals (CCR) permit program applications. If finalized, the actions would shift authority from the federal government to the states. Indiana – home to the most CCR units in the nation – would issue permits for CCR disposal in landfills and surface impoundments. In Wisconsin, EPA would continue to regulate surface impoundments, as the state only sought approval for permitting CCR disposal in landfills.

EPA anticipates proposing CCR permit program decisions for at least two additional states soon.

The proposed approvals follow proposed or final EPA approvals for Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Texas, Virginia, and Wyoming. EPA has committed to take swift action on CCR, including state permit program reviews and updates to CCR regulations. Approved states cannot have CCR regulations and policies that are less protective of human health and the environment than the federal regulations.

text:
Mission Solar Energy’s solar panel manufacturing site in San Antonio, Texas, considered one of the longest-running panel assembly operations in the United States, may soon receive a boost from a global manufacturer.

Mission Solar has been making solar panels in the United States since 2014 and is owned by OCI Company, a South Korean chemical conglomerate that is involved with solar project development and polysilicon production. OCI started the assembler to supply panels to its own utility-scale projects in Texas. Mission Solar has since worked through solar panel distribution channels and mostly supplied the U.S. residential sector but was attempting plays into larger markets. The company is currently listed as having a 500-MW annual module assembly capacity in San Antonio.

Sam Martens, president of Mission Solar, submitted testimony in the ongoing antidumping/countervailing duty (AD/CVD) investigation into solar cell imports from India, Indonesia and Laos. In addition to reiterating to the U.S. International Trade Commission the challenges the U.S. solar industry faces from unfairly priced imports, Martens commented on Mission Solar’s Texas factory.

“Despite trying our best to be cost-competitive, our customers repeatedly told us that our prices are too high. Subject producers have even offered prices well below our cost of production. We simply cannot cut prices that far, and we often ended up losing the sale instead,” he said. “The continual loss of sales and revenue forced us to curtail our production, leaving us with significant excess capacity.

“Lower utilization has naturally resulted in reduced shifts and reduced employees,” Martens continued. “For example, we previously employed more than 200 workers. But, due to the market conditions caused by subject imports, we only had 70 employees by 2025, and have now temporarily ceased all manufacturing operations and related employment.

“If injurious subject imports remain unrestrained in the face of potentially shrinking demand, I am afraid that the domestic industry will once again face rising closures and mass layoffs,” he concluded.

There have been no layoff announcements by Mission Solar in Texas worker adjustment and retraining notification notices, so if employment has been temporarily ceased, it’s likely to have resulted in furloughs. When asked, Mission Solar representatives were unable to comment on the matter to Solar Power World.

It’s an unfortunate trend for long-established U.S. solar panel manufacturers. Silfab Solar furloughed workers in August at its South Carolina manufacturing site due to “temporary constraints affecting the availability of certain materials required for production.” Heliene laid off nearly 100 workers in August at its Minnesota solar panel assembly facility due to “unforeseen business circumstances.” Qcells furloughed 1,000 employees at its Georgia operations last year, but was able resume production four months later.

Mission Solar, which has long operated a small-output solar panel factory at a mixed-use community located on the former Brooks Air Force Base, announced in 2022 it would expand operations to reach 1 GW of annual module manufacturing capacity. The company built a 200,000-sq-ft addition on its property, but it was instead later described as a warehouse.

The warehouse was then assumed to become the starting point of Mission and OCI’s solar cell manufacturing operations, which the two companies announced in 2025. They would invest $265 million into the site to eventually reach 2 GW of annual cell manufacturing capacity. Martens confirmed in his ITC testimony that actual construction plans never progressed further.

That warehouse is back in play after a filing with the Texas Dept. of Licensing and Regulation in August. The filing says that $15 million will be spent to renovate the existing warehouse into the “Elite Solar factory [f]or manufacturing.” Construction is expected to begin in October and be completed in June 2027.

Elite Solar, a Singapore-headquartered panel brand (previously known as ET Solar), has affiliated panel manufacturing operations across the globe. The company’s flagship sites are now based in Egypt and Indonesia, but it has a longstanding relationship with OCI and is jointly developing a solar wafer production facility in Vietnam. This partnership could be extending to panel manufacturing in Texas.

Elite Solar provided no comment when asked by Solar Power World about the San Antonio factory plans.

title: THIS WEEK IN CLIMATE ACTION - SEPTEMBER 18, 2026 - League of Conservation Voters
description:
Data Centers have been reshaping communities.
Until today, that has been our path with data centers.
Across the country Republicans are attempting to kill clean energy and hand out massive giveaways to their Big Polluter billionaire donors.
The ads focused on how the Republican incumbent voted to cut clean energy driving up utility bills so the wealthy could get another cut.
Lawmakers must also address the significant concerns communities have about data centers’ impact on water, air, climate, and noise pollution.
text:
Your weekly resource to learn what the environmental movement is saying about the news of the day and the political fight of our generation. This week, we’re covering who’s responsibly (and irresponsibly) offering solutions to data center development, energy affordability, and air and water pollution.

Be sure to follow LCV on Facebook, Instagram, BlueSky, and TikTok.

QUOTES OF THE WEEK:

“In the past two years, I’ve watched and fought back with an angry fire in my heart as Trump’s reckless EPA leaders have advanced costly and harmful rollbacks to protections for our communities, our air, water, and land, all for the primary benefit of oil, gas, and coal CEOs.”

— Matthew Davis, LCV vice president of federal policy and former EPA scientist, during a press event where congressional Democrats introduced a bill to restore EPA’s mission of protecting the environment and public health.

“We need real solutions to rising costs of energy, like the Energy Bills Relief Act, rather than backroom deals that help to shield big polluters and data centers while doing very little to address the affordability crisis that people are facing.”

— Rep. Pramila Jayapal (WA-07) on the Ratepayer Protection Act, a bill that falls short of protecting ratepayers from skyrocketing energy costs and will have little practical impact on lowering bills.

“The Trump administration is spending nearly $4 billion in taxpayer funds to cancel 12 offshore wind leases at the same time when Americans’ utility bills are rising. Their priorities are completely out of whack.”

— Rep. Chellie Pingree (ME-01) at a press conference calling out Trump’s corrupt offshore wind buyouts.

TOP NEWS IN ENERGY AFFORDABILITY

STATE NEWS

SPANBERGER DATA CENTER PLAN: Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger announced her plan to enact new datacenter guardrails for the Commonwealth. Her data center accountability framework bans non-disclosure agreements for data centers, accelerates clean energy deployment and makes it easier for data centers to bring their own clean power, sets water usage and noise regulations, helps ensure data centers pay for their fair share of electric transmission and generation costs, and limits new gas energy generation.

VALCV TAKE: Virginia League of Conservation Voters Executive Director Michael Town spoke at the governor’s press conference today, saying, “You can’t go too many places in America today where people are not raising concerns about data centers. For us in Virginia, this is old news. Data Centers have been reshaping communities. Our electric bills keep going up. Neighborhoods have black clouds over them coming from diesel generators on the hottest days of the year. Local officials are cutting deals with companies and keeping the details secret from their voters. People are angry.”

“Virginians have been clamoring for action, and for the most part, their concerns have been falling on deaf ears. Virginia LCV represents voters from across the Commonwealth. We fight for a cleaner environment and for a healthier democracy. When the people are crying for help because their community is being polluted and no one is listening, both our environment and our democracy suffer. Until today, that has been our path with data centers. Today, that changes.“

“We and many of our partners are ready to work with Governor Spanberger as she leads Virginia into a new era of data center accountability. Together, we’ll cut pollution and we’ll protect communities. The path ahead will not be easy, and we will not always agree. Tomorrow the work begins. Today, we say thank you, Governor Spanberger, thank you for your commitment to tackle this issue and we stand ready to join you as we build a stronger, healthier and cleaner Virginia together.”

LCV TAKE: LCV President Pete Maysmith said, “People are fed up paying massive utility bills, watching Big Tech companies raise their rates to build new data centers that threaten more gas pollution in local communities’ clean air and water. This is why leadership matters. Governor Spanberger ran to address rising costs and today’s executive order and sweeping framework will help bring relief to Virginians and hold Big Tech accountable. We look forward to Gov. Spanberger working with Virginia LCV, other state partners, and the legislature to enact strong guardrails in the General Assembly. Across the country Republicans are attempting to kill clean energy and hand out massive giveaways to their Big Polluter billionaire donors. But the public is fighting back. We need more leaders like Abigail Spanberger who are ready to take on Big Tech and fight the source of rising energy costs.”

HAALAND DATA CENTER PLAN: Democratic candidate for New Mexico governor, Deb Haaland, announced her plan to establish a temporary moratorium on data centers on day one if elected. The pause would remain in effect until the state legislature enacts protections Haaland has called for, including clear standards for water use, clean energy, transparency and jobs associated with data centers.

CVNM ACTION FUND TAKE: On social media, Conservation Voters New Mexico Action Fund said, “Deb Haaland announced she will take executive action on day 1 as governor to put a moratorium on data centers until the state passes strong environmental and community guardrails and protections. She has made it clear that NM is ready to lead.”

NATIONAL NEWS

LCVVF RELEASES NEW POLLING ON CLEAN ENERGY AFFORDABILITY: New testing conducted by Tavern Research from June to August of 2026 determined that LCV Victory Fund’s early house program ads that ran in VA-01, MI-04 and AZ-02 improved results for Democrats by leveraging clean energy affordability. The ads focused on how the Republican incumbent voted to cut clean energy driving up utility bills so the wealthy could get another cut. After the ads aired, the named ballot moved a net 4 points toward the Democrat in all three districts. Read more here.

MEMBERS OF CONGRESS AND ADVOCATES CALL OUT TRUMP’S OFFSHORE WIND BUYOUTS: LCV joined labor, environmental advocates, and members of Congress to denounce the Trump administration’s attacks on offshore wind. As energy bills continue to skyrocket, the administration has used nearly $4 billion taxpayer dollars to buy out leases for offshore wind and force companies to invest that money into methane gas export projects, further increasing household costs and air and climate pollution.

OUR TAKE: LCV Legislative Director David Shadburn said, “As if energy costs were not high enough, the Trump administration has spent almost four billion taxpayer dollars to keep our energy costs high by blocking affordable clean offshore wind energy. Trump is instead directing our tax dollars to new LNG export projects, shipping gas overseas and actually driving prices back home even higher, all while enriching Trump’s fossil fuel donors. We stand with clean energy leaders in Congress who are fighting to hold this administration to account and lower costs for working families.”

HOUSE PASSES WINDOW DRESSING ON DATA CENTERS: The House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act, a bill that, on its own, falls short of addressing concerns about data centers and skyrocketing energy costs. The bill encourages states to consider protecting ratepayers from data centers, but fails to establish or require states to establish meaningful standards to address high consumer costs and the environmental impacts of data center development.

OUR TAKE: Last week, ahead of the vote, LCV Senior Vice President of Government Affairs Sara Chieffo said, “No Representative should feel like a vote for this bill solves the concerns people back home have with data centers. The public is looking for their elected officials to take on utility corruption and guarantee that Big Tech will pay the full costs of infrastructure for their data centers and build the clean, reliable grid we all need. Lawmakers must also address the significant concerns communities have about data centers’ impact on water, air, climate, and noise pollution. They are fed up with corrupt backroom deals that cut out communities and don’t want data centers powered by dirtier and more expensive gas, diesel, or coal.

“The job won’t be done until there are real, enforceable guardrails to ensure environmental and public health protections, meaningful community input and benefits for communities hosting these facilities, and until Big Tech — not the public – pays the full cost of electricity and water and broader infrastructure upgrades.”

CLIMATE ATTACKS FROM THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AND CONGRESS

TRUMP’S EPA REPEALS POLLUTION STANDARDS FOR POWER PLANTS: Trump’s EPA issued a final rule repealing climate pollution limits for coal- and gas-fired power plants. Rolling back these emissions standards will increase climate and other pollution, drive up our energy bills, and have disastrous consequences on public health… all to benefit Trump’s Big Polluter allies. In addition, EPA launched a proposal that would abdicate the agency’s responsibility to regulate greenhouse gas emissions altogether, which will be open for public comment through November 2nd.

OUR TAKE: Ahead of the final rule, LCV Vice President of Federal Policy and former EPA scientist Matthew Davis said, “Instead of holding polluters accountable, Trump and EPA administrator Lee Zeldin are determined to give free passes to Big Polluters at the expense of the health, safety, and budgets of our communities. By erasing limits on climate pollution for coal and methane gas plants while Trump is continuing to rush through data centers powered by coal and gas, the EPA is putting all of us, our health and our economy at tremendous risk. In order to benefit their Big Oil and Coal CEO donors, our families will get sicker, our utility costs will continue to skyrocket, our air will be dirtier, and we will face more extreme weather. Instead of repealing standards that are designed to protect us and provide billions of dollars in benefits, Lee Zeldin and the EPA should be protecting our communities by strengthening standards to reduce climate pollution and drive down energy, health, and disaster costs.”

CONGRESS’ BIG OIL HANDOUT WEEK: This week, congressional Republicans pushed for even more handouts to fossil fuel companies, including the House narrowly passing two Congressional Review Act (CRA) resolutions, H.J. Res. 210 and H.J. Res. 213, both of which seek to remove maritime ship air pollution limits that lower fuel oil use and ensure Big Oil profits remain sky-high. Before skipping town, Senate Republican leadership may bring up S.J. Res 208 and S.J. Res 207, both of which would drive up families’ costs at the pump by blocking longstanding air pollution and efficiency standards for cars.

OUR TAKE: LCV Vice President of Federal Policy and former EPA scientist Matthew Davis said, “In the last week before they head out for an extended recess, House Republican leadership decided to use their limited time to push for more handouts to Big Polluters, instead of passing legislation that will make life better and less expensive for everyday people. Across the country, people on both sides of the aisle are fed up with high prices fueled by Trump’s war in Iran, and they understand that the corrupt oil and gas industry is taking advantage of this crisis to drive prices to record levels, at all of our expense. Over 70% of respondents in recent polling support a windfall profits tax to return money to families and crack down on Big Oil’s war profiteering.

“This week, congressional Republicans proved that, even with midterms on the line, they are willing to sacrifice the health and financial well-being of their constituents to benefit Big Polluters. Sadly, it appears the public has come to expect this: by a 30 point margin they think the Republican party cares more about oil and gas CEOs than working families, and separate polling showed Americans view Oil and Gas as the ‘most corrupt’ industry in the country. Instead of padding oil and gas CEOs’ pockets, Congress should focus on deploying immediate relief, clean energy, and grid improvements to make electricity more affordable for families, and hold billionaire utility, oil and gas, and tech companies accountable.”

ICYMI: STATE NEWS

ARIZONA YOUTH ARE TURNING CLIMATE EDUCATION INTO ACTION: Through Chispa Arizona’s Plantando Semillas program, young people are building their knowledge of climate and environmental justice while developing the skills to advocate for their communities. Their work toward the Seal of Climate Literacy offers a look at how the next generation of Arizona climate leaders is learning, organizing, and making their voices heard. See youth in action here.

ICYMI: NATIONAL NEWS

LCVVF AND CFFE PAC LAUNCH $3.7 MILLION PAID FIELD PROGRAM: The Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy PAC (CFFE PAC) and LCV Victory Fund, along with state affiliates and partners, announced a combined $3.7 million investment in field organizing programs encompassing Senate, House, and gubernatorial races to knock over 300,000 doors in Michigan and Ohio. Read more about the program here.

LCVVF TAKE: LCV Victory Fund Senior Vice President of Campaigns Sara Schreiber said, “We need leaders who will prioritize people over polluters. We are thrilled to be partnering with the Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy to go door to door to meet voters where they are. Across the country we are facing an affordability crisis and voters need to know that there are candidates who have platforms and plans to actually lower costs, especially utility costs. Voters deserve better. They deserve leaders who will stand up to Big Polluters, advocate for their communities, and look for our health and safety.”

LCVVF LAUNCHES $2.6 MILLION AD BLITZ: LCV Victory Fund announced a $1.6 million ad campaign calling out Iowa Senate candidate Ashley Hinson’s record of voting against clean water protections, and a $1 million campaign targeting Mike Lawler (NY-17) and Scott Perry (PA-10).

LCVVF TAKE: LCV Victory Fund Senior Vice President of Campaigns Sara Schreiber said, “The folks back home are fed up with what these Republican Representatives have been doing in Washington to raise costs and roll back basic environmental protections. They’re helping us tell these stories because voters deserve to know why their utility costs have risen over the past year and corporate interests are put ahead of keeping families healthy and safe.”

LCVVF WEEKLY ROUNDUP: We are so back! With just 46 days until Election Day, LCV Victory Fund’s weekly report is back. Each week we will be sharing exclusives, new ads and organizing programing, paid media trackers, and the latest happenings on energy affordability this election season. Check out this week’s roundup here.

LCV, NRDC ACTION FUND LAUNCH PAID FIELD PROGRAM: LCV and NRDC Action Fund each launched a paid field canvassing program to work alongside campaigns in battleground states across the country. The LCV program, called the Clean Energy Corps, will run in three high-priority Congressional Districts and knock over 150,000 doors to mobilize voters in support of pro-environment, pro-democracy candidates, including Representative Kathy Castor (FL-14) and candidates Rebecca Bennett (NJ-07), and Paige Cognetti (PA-08).

OUR TAKE: LCV Vice President of Field Jennessa Agnew said, “Trump and his MAGA allies are doing all they can to take away voters’ right to free and fair elections while rolling back protections for our health and safety and making our lives more expensive. We’re utilizing every tool in our toolbox to mobilize voters, including those who have been historically excluded, by working alongside campaigns to reach more communities and talking about getting out the message that these candidates will fight for them, stand up to Big Polluters, and address the kitchen table issues impacting them every day.”

LCV, NRDC ACTION FUND LAUNCH AD URGING MEMBERS TO PROTECT THE CLEAN WATER ACT: LCV and NRDC Action Fund announced a six-figure ad buy to urge lawmakers to protect the Clean Water Act from further action by the Trump administration and Congress. This six-figure digital ad buy will run through October 2nd.

OUR TAKE: LCV Senior Vice President of Government Affairs Sara Chieffo said, “Trump and his allies have done everything in their power to gut critical protections for the water our communities rely on so that the fossil fuel industry, data centers, and corporate interests profit at our expense. We know the devastating costs to our health and safety when these protections fail and Big Polluters go unchecked. Families deserve clean water, no matter their income or zip code, and we’re urging members of Congress to reject polluters’ efforts to gut the Clean Water Act.”

CONGRESSIONAL DEMS INTRODUCE ENVIRONMENTAL HEALTH RESTORATION ACT: Senators Sheldon Whitehouse (RI) and Jeff Merkley (OR) and Representative Sean Casten (IL-06) introduced the Environmental Health Restoration Act at a press event with Protect our Winters on Wednesday. The bill aims to restore EPA’s mission and reinstate protections for public health and the environment.

OUR TAKE: LCV Vice President of Federal Policy and former EPA scientist Matthew Davis said, “We appreciate Senator Whitehouse and Representative Casten for fighting to restore the EPA’s mission and safeguards to protect public health, the environment and our climate in the face of the Trump administration’s reckless and dangerous rollbacks. People want more protections for their families and our air, water, and land, not less. They want officials who will hold accountable those corrupt utilities, data center developers, and fossil fuel companies that are driving up costs and making us sicker. EPA’s leaders must fulfill the agency’s mission of protecting human health and the environment and reject President Trump’s corrupt giveaways to his tech, coal, oil, and gas cronies. LCV is proud to support the Environmental Health Restoration Act to right the ship and deliver for American families.”

SENATE AGRICULTURE COMMITTEE REPUBLICANS PASS HARMFUL FARM BILL: Republicans on the Senate Agriculture Committee advanced a partisan Farm Bill that would slash investments in critical programs that help farmers engage in more sustainable and regenerative farming practices while doing nothing to address the upcoming Republican-caused food security crisis.

OUR TAKE: LCV Senior Vice President of Government Affairs Sara Chieffo said, “Farmers nationwide are struggling with extreme weather and rapidly rising costs under the Trump administration. To ensure our farmers can continue putting food on tables across the country, Congress should be investing more in the programs and agencies that help farmers thrive while fighting and adapting to the climate crisis. Instead, Republicans on the Senate Agriculture Committee advanced a bill that slashes investments in critical, already-oversubscribed conservation programs that help farmers engage in more sustainable and regenerative farming practices and fails to address the upcoming SNAP crisis that congressional Republicans created with the Republican Tax Law. We call on the Senate to reject this harmful proposal and pass a truly bipartisan Farm Bill that supports farmers, families, and our environment.”

LCVAF ENDORSED CANDIDATES WIN DELAWARE PRIMARIES: LCV Action Fund endorsed candidates Chris Coons (Senate) and Sarah McBride (DE-AL) won their respective primary elections in Delaware. All LCV Action Fund endorsed candidates for this cycle can be found here.

LCVAF TAKE: LCV Action Fund Senior Vice President of Government Affairs Sara Chieffo said, “Chris Coons and Sarah McBride are fighting to protect free and fair elections, the health of our communities, and a cleaner, more affordable energy future. While people are paying higher costs for gas and their energy bills due to Trump and his Republican allies’ actions, Big Polluters rake in massive profits. Voters have made it clear — they want clean air and water and affordable energy solutions. We’re all in to support candidates who will protect people and our planet.”

NEW ON THE POWER SOURCE BLOG AND SOCIALS:

ON THE BLOG: This week on the blog, we published our top five stories for fall 2026, including primary election victories, wins in the fight to rein in data centers, progress in the fight for clean energy, new laws to hold polluters accountable, and LCV Action Fund endorsements in the upcoming elections.

text:
Environmental and public health groups are suing the Trump administration over its most recent move to eliminate protections against climate-warming pollution.

The Environmental Protection Agency announced a plan on Monday, finalized in the Federal Register on Thursday, to revoke most of a Biden-era rule to limit greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuel power plants. The agency also proposed getting rid of all remaining greenhouse gas emission requirements for the plants, doubling down on climate denial.

Opposing the final rule, the American Lung Association, Natural Resources Defense Council, Environmental Defense Fund and others submitted a petition Thursday asking the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit to review the changes. Leaders from the groups called the EPA plan unlawful and said it would endanger human health and the environment by worsening climate change, while triggering billions of dollars of healthcare costs.

“By rolling back these critical protections, millions of Americans will get sicker, face more extreme weather, and pay more for energy and electricity, with vulnerable communities suffering the most,” said Lawrence Hafetz, legal director of the Pennsylvania-based Clean Air Council, one of the groups involved, in a statement. “EPA is supposed to protect people and the environment, not rewrite the rules to benefit polluters.”

The EPA’s announcement came on the heels of a summer of deadly and record-breaking heat, massive wildfires and, last month in Nepal, devastating floods from glacial collapse that killed at least 1,300 people—and which scientists confirmed this week were precipitated by human-caused climate change. Meanwhile, a new United Nations report said current emissions are rapidly pushing the world into even more intensifying dangers.

Globally, the U.S. is the largest historic emitter of greenhouse gases, which are primarily produced by burning fossil fuels.

The EPA said it does not comment on pending litigation. The agency did not respond to questions about critiques of its rule.

The second Trump administration’s efforts to claw back climate protections have been met with a wave of lawsuits, most of which still await a ruling. Among them are challenges to the repeal of the 2009 endangerment finding, which found that climate pollution threatens public health. Last week, federal judges ruled in favor of environmental groups who argued the administration’s use of emergency orders to keep old coal plants running was illegal.

“The courts are our last line of defense,” said Pat Parenteau, a climate law expert at Vermont Law & Graduate School. “I’m reasonably optimistic that the lawsuits are going to prevail against the Trump administration because [the administration’s] legal positions are frivolous, frankly.”

But Parenteau said the newest case will focus on whether it’s been “adequately demonstrated” that meeting the 2024 power plant rule’s requirements, including for carbon capture and sequestration, is feasible. That enters “new territory” for judicial review, he said.

“The courts are going to have to look very carefully at all of the evidence that’s being brought before them for how much has this technology matured, at what scales, for what purposes,” he said. “This will be a very technical review.”

Frank Sturges, a senior staff attorney at the Clean Air Task Force who represents some of the groups in the latest lawsuit, said the 2024 rule for coal and gas-fired power plants was based on scientifically, technically and legally sound evidence that the repeal failed to engage with. Scrapping the rule was unlawful, Sturges said, and fits into a broader pattern from the administration.

“What we see here is a rush to try to eliminate standards that are well-founded … and the arguments that have been put forward to repeal them really lack a lawful basis,” Sturges said. “This is not the only place we’re seeing that happening right now.”

The EPA’s choice to eliminate the Biden-era standards instead of attempting to replace them with weaker standards undermines the notion that the case is about a technical debate, added Sean H. Donahue, an attorney representing the Environmental Defense Fund in the lawsuit.

“They’re trying to make climate change disappear from federal policy across the board, and this is part of that,” Donahue said.

In 2024, during the Biden administration, the EPA estimated that its strengthened standards for coal and gas-fired power plants would avoid up to 1,200 premature deaths and 360,000 asthma symptom cases in 2035 alone, among many other health benefits. The agency projected a reduction of 1.38 billion metric tons of carbon pollution through 2047, the equivalent of taking 328 million gas cars off the roads.

A new analysis this week from the Environmental Defense Fund estimates the repeal of those standards will add 7.5 billion metric tons of climate pollution, equivalent to the annual pollution of 1.6 billion cars, and cause up to 84,000 premature deaths by 2047.

Donate Now

The lawsuit was “inevitable,” said Michael Gerrard, founder and faculty director of the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia University. He added that the groups have a strong case that the EPA’s actions violate the Clean Air Act.

“The claims by EPA that greenhouse gas emissions do not cause endangerment fly in the face of mountains of contrary scientific evidence,” Gerrard said. “So I think that’s very vulnerable.”

He added that nearly all of the Trump administration’s actions on the environment are being challenged in court.

A judicial review of regulatory policy during the first Trump administration from New York University School of Law’s Institute for Policy Integrity found that the Trump administration only won 23 percent of legal challenges to agency actions, compared with a rate of about 70 percent in previous administrations.

Gerrard said many of those defeats were based on procedural failures.

“They’re not being any more careful this time,” he said, “so I wouldn’t be surprised to see a comparable success rate at the end of the second Trump administration.”

description:

It will support this growing demand while expanding domestic production of critical conductive additives in the United States.
The grant reflects a collaborative effort between Cabot and DOE to redirect funding from the company’s originally announced Michigan project to a two-site brownfield expansion program.

text:
Cabot Corporation announced a modified $50 million grant from the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation (CMEI) that will support the company’s recently announced plans to expand its North American battery materials platform.

Supported by this DOE grant and approximately $75 million of Cabot investment, the company plans to expand domestic production of advanced conductive additives at its facilities in Franklin, Louisiana, and Pampa, Texas.

The planned investments are designed to address rising demand for advanced battery materials driven by the expansion of energy storage systems, increasing power requirements from artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure and data centers, ongoing grid modernization efforts, and broader electrification trends. It will support this growing demand while expanding domestic production of critical conductive additives in the United States.

The grant reflects a collaborative effort between Cabot and DOE to redirect funding from the company’s originally announced Michigan project to a two-site brownfield expansion program. By leveraging existing manufacturing assets, Cabot expects to accelerate the development of a local and secure supply of critical conductive additives for the growing domestic battery supply chain while strengthening its ability to serve customers globally. The planned investments are also expected to support high-quality manufacturing and construction jobs and contribute to U.S. leadership in advanced battery materials technologies.

Cabot is well-positioned to capitalize on growing demand for advanced battery materials through its decades of materials expertise, longstanding relationships with many of the world’s leading battery manufacturers, global manufacturing footprint, and broad portfolio of conductive carbons, carbon nanotubes, and carbon nanostructures. Together, these capabilities enable the company to scale production efficiently, support customers with localized supply, and compete across the major battery markets of North America, Europe and Asia.

“This investment represents an important step in our strategy to build a differentiated battery materials business that supports some of the most significant growth trends shaping the global economy,” said Sean Keohane, president and chief executive officer of Cabot Corporation. “Demand for advanced batteries continues to expand across energy storage, electrification, and emerging AI-related infrastructure. By leveraging our existing manufacturing assets, we can efficiently expand our battery materials platform, strengthen our position in the North American battery ecosystem, and support our customers’ growth with localized supply.”

Investment outlook for Cabot

Cabot’s planned investments will support production of LITX® advanced battery-grade conductive carbons at its Franklin, Louisiana, 100 miles west of New Orleans, facility and establish the first commercial-scale production of carbon nanostructures (CNS), Cabot’s most advanced conductive additive technology and part of the ENERMAX® product family, at its Pampa, Texas, 55 miles northwest of Amarillo, facility. These conductive additives are designed to help improve battery performance and support the evolving needs of next-generation energy storage and electrification applications. Both projects are expected to be operational by the end of 2028.

“Cabot is a trusted partner and technology leader in conductive additives for the battery industry, delivering innovative solutions backed by a global manufacturing footprint and technical expertise,” said Keohane. “These investments reinforce our commitment to the North American battery market and position us to be a reliable, long-term supplier as our customers scale production. Together with our technology leadership, broad portfolio, and established customer relationships, we believe these investments will strengthen our competitive position globally and advance battery materials as an increasingly important growth platform for Cabot.”

title: NC denies Duke Energy request to expand gas turbine for future data centers
description:
In a rare move, North Carolina regulators will not allow Duke Energy to expand an existing natural gas power plant in Richmond County.
Duke Energy had requested a permit last year from the Utilities Commission to add a sixth natural gas turbine to the complex, which would’ve added about 255 additional megawatts of generation capacity.

text:
In a rare move, North Carolina regulators will not allow Duke Energy to expand an existing natural gas power plant in Richmond County.

Although Duke Energy said the project is necessary to provide power for expected data centers, members of the state Utilities Commission said they’re concerned that Duke is overestimating how much power these data centers will need, and that everyday customers could end up paying for the project.

Greenlighting the project at this point, commissioners wrote in a Friday decision, “will increase substantially the costs that ratepayers will need to bear and will impose a significant risk that new generation is approved before the need for that generation is determined.”

The Utilities Commission, a five-member group that oversees North Carolina’s utilities, rarely denies permits for major projects like this one.

The Sherwood H. Smith Energy Complex currently has five natural gas turbines and two other combined-cycle turbines, which generate over 2,200 megawatts in total — enough to power between 1.5 million and 2 million households. Duke Energy had requested a permit last year from the Utilities Commission to add a sixth natural gas turbine to the complex, which would’ve added about 255 additional megawatts of generation capacity.

Duke spokesperson Craig Wilson said in a statement that the company is “disappointed” in the decision and is “assessing potential next steps.”

“We believe we have demonstrated that the Smith [turbine] is part of a least-cost path to maintain reliable and affordable service for customers as energy demand continues to grow across North Carolina,” the statement reads. “We remain committed to working constructively with regulators and stakeholders to identify the best path forward to meet our customers’ future energy needs while maintaining reliability and keeping costs as low as possible.”

To justify why it needs to expand the plant, Duke modeled how much power demand it expects to be added to the Eastern North Carolina grid, and estimated that it will need more than 25,000 new megawatts of power generation by 2035 to keep up with demand. Much of that demand will come from more data centers, which often require massive amounts of energy for their day-to-day operations.

However, state authorities haven’t finished independently reviewing and vetting Duke’s analysis to make sure it’s accurate. They’re set to complete that review in late 2026, but Duke told the Utilities Commission that they need a decision on this turbine before that review was over.

Waiting, a Duke Energy representative told the commission, “would inherently delay initiation of construction, and in turn, materially delay the in-service date” for this project of January 2030; it also “could increase construction costs.”

Building the expansion to the natural gas turbine would cost $584 million, a price tag that the Utilities Commission’s Public Staff called “staggering.” Yet Public Staff ultimately decided to recommend supporting Duke’s project.

“Duke has continued to [add customers] at a rate that exceeds their ability to build generation, and so we’re in this position where we feel compelled to recommend approval of this facility simply because there’s no other options, even though this is a facility that costs half a billion dollars and you’re not getting a lot of value out of it for that amount of money,” an expert witness from Public Staff previously told the Utilities Commission.

Commission members, though, decided that they can’t yet confirm if the huge surge in electric demand that Duke projects is accurate.

Under a new state law that allows Duke Energy to charge customers for construction projects before they are completed, Duke’s existing customers would still pay for the expansion even if more data centers do not end up on the grid. The utility also profits from building new infrastructure — it currently has a state-set return on equity of 9.48%, meaning it will earn about that much back from any new capital investments it makes.

The Smith Energy Complex sits right next to the site of an Amazon data center in Richmond County. The data center has faced pushback from local residents over its plan to use diesel generators for its first several months of operation, and as backup power once it’s connected to the energy grid.

“The Commission held today that Duke’s rush to gas to support speculative data center build-out in North Carolina is too rapid and too expensive,” said Will Scott, policy director of the Environmental Defense Fund, in a statement. “Clearly, Duke’s desire to satisfy short-term demand should not saddle customers with what are, over the long-term, likely to be inefficient, stranded assets.“

Duke could still re-file its permit application for the turbine expansion, but would need to respond to several specific concerns from the Utilities Commission if it did re-file.

Through a portfolio of wind energy resources serving the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) market, ENGIE will help supply up to 568 MW of renewable electricity for Oracle’s Texas operations. These agreements reflect the strength of our portfolio and our ability to deliver customized energy solutions that help customers meet their business objectives.”

ENGIE's capabilities to deliver

“Oracle is taking a responsible approach to meeting the energy needs of our growing AI and cloud operations in Texas — investing in carbon-free electricity without shifting costs to consumers,” said Julia Robin, Head of Infrastructure Planning and Sourcing for Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. “Our agreements with ENGIE advance Oracle’s goal to match 100 percent of our AI data center electricity use with carbon-free electricity by 2035, while supporting long-term economic growth with no cost impact to the state of Texas .”

Key points in the Hitachi Energy announcement: Mississippi facility investment: Hitachi Energy announced plans to build a $528 million transformer manufacturing factory in Gallman, Mississippi, creating over 700 jobs.

text:
Hitachi Energy announced plans for a new $528 million transformer manufacturing facility in Gallman, Mississippi, 35 miles southwest of Jackson, creating over 700 jobs.

The Mississippi facility will be the cornerstone of Hitachi Energy’s around $1.5 billion U.S. manufacturing expansion program, the largest in the industry, increasing domestic production of transformers and other critical grid infrastructure to meet rapidly growing energy demand across the country.

Key points in the Hitachi Energy announcement:

Mississippi facility investment: Hitachi Energy announced plans to build a $528 million transformer manufacturing factory in Gallman, Mississippi, creating over 700 jobs.

Capacity expansion: Construction begins late this year with production starting in 2029, doubling current output and serving as the flagship project of Hitachi's $1.5 billion U.S. manufacturing expansion strategy.

Broader U.S. footprint: The move addresses surging U.S. electricity demand from data centers and advanced manufacturing, adding to other recent expansions in South Boston, Virginia ($457M), Alamo, Tennessee ($106M), and Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania ($70M).

The new facility in Mississippi, Hitachi Energy’s largest single investment in the United States to date, deepens a long-term commitment to American manufacturing rooted in more than a century of building and strengthening the U.S. power grid, a heritage spanning Westinghouse Electric, ABB Power Grids, and Hitachi. The investments will help meet growing American energy needs through the expansion of U.S. manufacturing, contributing to the advancement of Hitachi's efforts in support of the strategic investment initiatives promoted by the governments of Japan and the United States. It also aligns with the Trump administration's and Governor Reeves' goals to promote domestic access to these critical grid technologies.

New factory specs

The new factory in Gallman will be approximately 6.5 miles (ten kilometers) from Hitachi Energy’s existing Crystal Springs facility. At over twice the size of the current plant, it will more than double capacity. Construction is expected to begin late this year, with transformer production at the facility scheduled to start in 2029. Once the new factory is completed, transformer production will transition from Hitachi Energy’s existing Crystal Springs facility to Gallman.

The project will significantly increase output of power transformers manufactured in Mississippi. The additional capacity will help address rapidly growing demand for electricity across the U.S., driven by the expansion of advanced manufacturing, industrial electrification, data centers, and other energy-intensive industries, as well as the continued modernization and expansion of the nation’s power grid.

The investment reflects Hitachi Energy’s collaboration with federal, state, and local leaders to strengthen domestic manufacturing, grow the skilled workforce, and expand the critical infrastructure needed to meet rising electricity demand. The partnership will also help ensure continued economic development and long-term investment in Mississippi and the U.S.

Recent Hitachi projects

The project follows several major Hitachi Energy manufacturing investments across the country. In June, the company broke ground on a $457 million expansion of its large power transformer factory in South Boston, Virginia, which will be the nation’s largest of its kind and create 825 new jobs. Last August, Hitachi Energy announced a $106 million expansion in Alamo, Tennessee, that will increase production of critical transformer components and create more than 100 jobs, and last year, the company announced a $70 million expansion of its facilities in Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania, which focuses on the production of high-voltage equipment for the grid.

Together, these projects represent a historic investment in U.S. transformer manufacturing, creating over 1,600 jobs. This broader footprint will support the modernization of the nation’s power infrastructure, enhancing grid resilience, reliability, and security.

Production will continue at Hitachi Energy’s existing Crystal Springs facility until the new Gallman factory is complete. Once transformer production transitions to Gallman, the Crystal Springs building will continue to be used for warehousing, training, or other operational needs, reinforcing Hitachi Energy’s long-term and sustained commitment to the region and its local workforce.

text:
The Electric Reliability Council of Texas, or ERCOT, has made public the data center community impact survey that more than 400 projects must complete as part of an audit ordered by Gov. Greg Abbott last month.

The governor has ordered a pause on approvals for new, large data center projects that want to connect to the ERCOT grid until the state's utility and power grid regulators complete an audit of the projects.

The survey, which includes more than 250 questions, is divided into nine sections: facility information, reasons for development, financial assistance, power self-sufficiency, water sources and consumption, cooling technologies, community impact, ownership and controlling interests, and an attestation confirming that the survey responses are accurate.

Sign up for the Hello, Houston! daily newsletter to get local reports like this delivered directly to your inbox.

Skip to PDF content

University of Houston Energy Fellow Ed Hirs said the survey goes beyond what ERCOT needs to determine what projects to connect to the grid. While questions about data centers' energy and water usage are relevant to state regulators, Hirs said developers may chafe at questions that ask about their projects' finances and ownership.

"This is going to be considered to be very, very intrusive in a state that usually has a good reputation for free market principles," he said.

Hirs said the survey may deter some data center developers from building in Texas.

"What this survey kind of communicates with everybody is that the state is looking to regulate all of these different aspects, and that will change the economics for the developers," he said.

ERCOT did not immediately respond to a request for comment Friday about criticisms of its community impact survey.

The community impact survey includes 247 large data centers, classified as projects that are requesting at least 75 megawatts of power from the Texas grid. It also includes 214 “medium” data centers, which are requesting between 25 and 75 megawatts of power from the grid. One megawatt can power about 250 Texas homes during a hot summer day or cold winter night, according to ERCOT.

Data centers will have until Oct. 12 to complete the survey. ERCOT said it may publicize responses in the aggregate, but individual survey answers will remain confidential.

Projects that do not complete the survey will be reported to the Public Utility Commission of Texas and the governor’s office. Sarah Fischer, a spokesperson for the commission, said in an email that projects that do not comply "will be evaluated on a case-by-case basis.”

Texas has the fastest-growing data center market in the country. As of late July, large energy consumers had requested 474 gigawatts of electricity from the Texas power grid, more than five times the amount of energy needed to power the state during record-breaking demand. Roughly 90% of the requests came from data centers.

But even as Texas has seen an influx of proposed data projects, it's struggled to assess how much water these facilities will use. Data center developers have failed to respond to water usage surveys from the state, according to the Texas Tribune. Gov. Greg Abbott has ordered the Texas Water Development Board to penalize developers who did not respond to its past survey and help ERCOT develop its data center audit.

The audit survey released Friday includes questions about how much water these projects are using, the source of the water used, wastewater produced, and other cooling methods used by these projects.

In addition to the survey published Friday, ERCOT and the Public Utility Commission of Texas are conducting a "verification" process for data centers included in "Batch Zero" — a group of large data centers that the agencies are evaluating so they can connect to the state's power grid.

The verification process will confirm that these projects are actually ready to be built — for example, by providing a lease or property deed and permits. This “verification” process does not involve evaluating data centers’ water usage, noise or other community impacts.

Once ERCOT completes the "verification" process and the community impact survey, it will complete a report about the findings of its audit in December. The agency has said it will share its findings with the state’s utility regulators, the governor and state lawmakers.

Maria Faconti is a partner with the law firm K&L Gates, which specializes in Texas' energy regulations. She said some of her clients have already begun to anticipate that the governor may require data centers to bring their own power generation, rather than connecting to the state's power grid, and are beginning to plan accordingly.

As the legislative session begins early next year, Faconti said, developers will be watching to see what new regulations become law.

"I think there are a lot of people who think that the legislature will make changes, but no one knows really what those changes will be," she said. "So it's hard to plan for something that's currently not predictable."

title: Plasma Technology Could Help Plant-Based Packaging Replace Plastic
description:

CNF films are derived from renewable biomass such as wood pulp.
Widespread industrial adoption of more sustainable alternatives like CNF films remains limited in part because of their poor moisture barrier performance.
In fact, the technology is already used in the packaging industry, meaning the DBD plasma treatment process can be seamlessly integrated into existing manufacturing lines.
The paper “Surface modification of cellulose nanofibril films via organosilicon deposition using dielectric barrier discharge plasma (DBD) plasma for packaging applications,” is published in the journal Applied Surface Science.
text:
A new study has found a sustainable and scalable way to improve the durability of plant-based packaging; it’s a discovery that researchers say could help curb the environmental footprint of plastic.

In the study, researchers used advanced plasma technology to apply layered, protective coatings to the surface of cellulosic nanofibril (CNF) films, with the goal of reducing water absorption and improving moisture resistance.

They found that one of the plasma-treated coatings reduced liquid water absorption in CNF films to less than 1%, while another weakened the film’s moisture barrier and allowed more water vapor to pass through.

According to the researchers, the results show that the plasma technology — dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) plasma — can be used to precisely control how CNF films interact with moisture, opening new possibilities for plant-based packaging.

“This research provides a practical strategy for turning natural plant and tree fibers into functional, water-resistant packaging. It moves society one step closer to replacing everyday plastic wraps with truly renewable, biodegradable materials,” said one of the study’s lead authors Nathalie Lavoine, an associate professor in the Department of Forest Biomaterials at North Carolina State University.

CNF films are derived from renewable biomass such as wood pulp. They are completely biodegradable and provide strong barriers against oxygen and grease, offering a more sustainable alternative for additives, coatings and films in packaging products.

Many conventional packaging products such as potato chip bags, candy wrappers and squeeze pouches are made by fusing multiple layers of petroleum-based plastics with materials like aluminum foil or paper.

Because the layers are difficult to separate, standard recycling facilities often cannot process this type of packaging. As a result, it may end up in landfills, where it can eventually break down into microplastics that can contaminate soil and water.

Widespread industrial adoption of more sustainable alternatives like CNF films remains limited in part because of their poor moisture barrier performance. Because cellulose naturally attracts water, the films rapidly absorb moisture from the environment.

Moisture absorption can compromise the structural integrity of CNF films, causing them to lose strength and experience a significant reduction in gas barrier performance. In packaging, this can compromise product protection and shorten shelf life.

If CNF films were used in a potato chip bag and that bag were exposed to high humidity, for example, moisture could permeate the film and reach the chips. This could cause the chips to lose their crispness and become stale. For some foods, moisture can promote the development of bacteria, resulting in foodborne illness.

Plasma treatment helps address these problems by modifying the surface of CNF films to block water, while preserving the original mechanical performance and structural integrity of the cellulose.

Lavoine said one of the primary advantages of plasma treatment is that the technology itself is more sustainable than traditional chemical coating processes that use large amounts of water, generate high heat and produce toxic waste.

The technology is also scalable, according to Lavoine. In fact, the technology is already used in the packaging industry, meaning the DBD plasma treatment process can be seamlessly integrated into existing manufacturing lines.

Still, Lavoine said that she and her collaborators must address several key challenges before DBD plasma treatment can reach real-world production. That includes refining the process so that it doesn’t allow water vapor to leak through.

While that permeability can be useful for tailoring CNF films for medical products such as breathable wound dressings, it would need to be minimized for packaging applications where moisture resistance is essential.

Lavoine said additional testing and optimization are also needed to assess coating speeds, energy use and physical durability, ensuring the material can withstand real-world handling while remaining economically viable and environmentally and socially safe.

The paper “Surface modification of cellulose nanofibril films via organosilicon deposition using dielectric barrier discharge plasma (DBD) plasma for packaging applications,” is published in the journal Applied Surface Science. Co-authors include Mirela A. Artner of NC State University, Lucia Švandová of Masaryk University, and Jacopo Profili of the University of Quebec in Rimouski.

This research was supported in part by the College of Natural Resources at NC State University, the 2022-23 NC State Internationalization Seed Grant, the Mitacs Globalink Research Award (#IT35099) and the intramural research program of the U.S. Department of Agriculture, National Institute of Food and Agriculture, McIntire-Stennis, grant number NI22MSCFRXXXG054.

title: Why is South Korea alone so lenient on Chinese EVs? 8% in South Korea vs. 128% in the ...
description:

The United States applies tariffs of up to 127.5% on Chinese EVs, while the European Union imposes tariffs of up to 45.3%.
Japan operates an economic security fund that directly subsidizes one-third of facility investment costs, as well as production-volume-linked tax credits, alongside consumer subsidies.
Despite these defensive measures, Chinese EVs are spreading rapidly.
The rise in sales of Chinese EVs in the South Korean auto market is far outpacing growth in the overall EV market.
text:
As Chinese EVs rapidly penetrate the South Korean market on the strength of their price competitiveness, voices are growing within the auto industry calling for the swift introduction of EV production tax credits. Unlike the United States and the European Union, which are simultaneously strengthening tariffs and support for domestic production, South Korea lacks policy tools to directly support local manufacturing.

The Korea Automobile & Mobility Association (KAMA) and The Korean Association of Mobility Studies emphasized the need for support schemes linked to domestic production to counter the advance of Chinese EVs at a seminar titled "Measures to Strengthen the Competitiveness of the Domestic EV Industry," which they jointly hosted at the National Assembly on the 18th.

Major auto-producing nations are raising tariff barriers while expanding support for domestic production. The United States applies tariffs of up to 127.5% on Chinese EVs, while the European Union imposes tariffs of up to 45.3%. Japan operates an economic security fund that directly subsidizes one-third of facility investment costs, as well as production-volume-linked tax credits, alongside consumer subsidies. As of March this year, the support allocated to the finished-vehicle and materials and equipment sectors totaled as much as ¥671.1 billion, or approximately ₩6.3 trillion.

Despite these defensive measures, Chinese EVs are spreading rapidly. Chinese brands' share of new-vehicle registrations in Europe rose from 4.5% in the first half of 2025 to 11.2% in July this year. Their share more than doubled in just over a year despite tariff barriers of up to 45.3%.

Warnings that market protection measures are needed are also emerging from the global auto industry. José Muñoz, president and CEO of Hyundai Motor, said at Hyundai Motor Group's "Tech Talent Forum" in San Jose, California, on the 17th local time, "In the United Kingdom, where there are no trade barriers, all of the top-selling vehicles are Chinese brands. A similar thing could happen in the United States if certain conditions are not in place. To minimize the shock, the United States must impose conditions on Chinese companies."

By contrast, South Korea's tariff on Chinese passenger cars is 8%, lower than China's 15% tariff on South Korean-made automobiles. There is also no separate production tax credit for EVs made domestically. Park Jeong-gyu, a visiting professor at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) Graduate School of Management of Technology, warned at the seminar, "A market without defensive measures can be overtaken within one or two years."

The rise in sales of Chinese EVs in the South Korean auto market is far outpacing growth in the overall EV market. According to KAMA, 235,000 EVs were sold domestically from January through July this year, up 99.3% from the same period a year earlier. Of these, 83,000 were made in China, a surge of 148.9%. The share of China-made vehicles, including Teslas made in Shanghai, rose from 12.6% in 2023 to 35.3% this year, while BYD ranked fourth in domestic EV sales.

The auto industry has long called for the introduction of production tax credits that provide tax benefits to EVs made domestically in proportion to production volume. Unlike purchase-stage subsidies, such credits directly increase domestic production and demand for parts, helping sustain automakers' facility investments, employment at partner companies, and local economies.

Yoon Kyung-sun, an executive director at KAMA, said, "We need to establish production-linked support schemes, including domestic production tax credits, to help offset the production-cost gap with Chinese EVs. While maintaining purchase subsidies over the medium to long term, we also need to strengthen differentiated support for vehicles made domestically."

Chinese EVs' price competitiveness is the result of long-standing government support, the internalization of battery and rare-earth supply chains, low production costs, and economies of scale built on the world's largest domestic market. As domestic competition and overproduction intensified, vehicle exports by Chinese automakers increased 12.1-fold in Russia, 8.1-fold in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), sixfold in Latin America, and 5.3-fold in the Middle East between 2020 and 2025.
